title: Mission Accomplished? Rehab in Scotland, Five Years On
content:
When I started working in addiction treatment to reliably access residential rehab in Scotland you had to live in the right area, be wealthy or just plain lucky. I heard it too often from patients and families who could see what was needed and, despite their best efforts, couldn’t get near it. When we argued for change, we’d hear the same weary rebuttal from the doubters: ‘there’s no evidence that rehab works’. (Ten years earlier, they were saying precisely the same thing about mutual aid.)
So, it was with some excitement that I read the final report of Public Health Scotland’s evaluation of the Scottish Government’s Residential Rehabilitation programme, published in September. Official evaluations are always careful things. They are cautious, and caveated, though if you look underneath the hedged language, the story this one tells is remarkable.
Headline: the target was passed.
Back in 2021, the Scottish Government committed £100M (about $135M) over five years to residential rehab and set two targets: 650 beds, and 1,000 people a year publicly funded to go through rehab. In 2025/26, 1,125 Scottish residents started a publicly funded placement – a comfortable overshoot. This is likely an underestimate, since not every provider was submitting data. Overall access for Scottish residents is up by around 60% since 2019/20, and publicly funded placements have more than doubled.
Capacity
Bed capacity grew by 35%, from 425 to 574. More to the point, the growth was aimed at the gaps so that capacity was directed to where it was most needed. Mums can now be treated alongside their children. Aberlour’s Discovery Grove in Dundee and the Burrow in Falkirk were simply not there when this journey started. Rae House brought new provision to the North East. Nevis House extends reach across the Highlands and Islands. These were aimed precisely at the unmet need we mapped in the Working Group’s earlier days.
Referrers have changed their minds.
Three-quarters of staff surveyed say they now discuss rehab more often with the people they support. Two-thirds report making more referrals. Referrers are now far more willing to consider a placement for someone who has been through rehab before – up from 45% to 66%. That’s a positive because of the cumulative effect. Anyone who works in this field knows recovery is rarely linear. To be offered a second or third chance should be routine, and now it increasingly is. Meanwhile, the proportion worried that rehab increases overdose risk has fallen sharply. As referrers get more experience, they get more confident.
For the first time, we know what happens to people.
When the Residential Rehabilitation Working Group reported in December 2020, one of our nine recommendations was straightforward: outcomes should be measured, published and monitored. At the time, nobody in Scotland (or to be honest, anywhere in the UK) could tell you who was going to rehab and what happened to them. Now we have a national individual-level dataset, built from scratch, with almost all providers across the private, third and NHS sectors signed up.
The first full year of data shows that 55% of people starting publicly funded rehab finish it with a positive status – substance free, or stabilised – rising to 70% for alcohol placements. This compares very favourably with international completion rates. Nine out of ten of those assessed on the validated Outcomes Star improved in at least one area of their life, and most in several. Deaths following rehab were rare: one drug-related death in the six months after placement among the subset of 146 individuals who were followed up. Given our grim record on drug deaths and the potential risks, that really matters.
What still needs fixing.
None of this means the job is done. The report has a shopping list of problems waiting to be addressed. Waiting times for detox remain a serious bottleneck. Bed capacity still falls short of the 650-bed target, and funding still trails demand. The post-rehab pathway: housing, mental health support and aftercare needs to be the next focus. People going from structured, supportive rehabilitation back into the same challenges that contributed to their problems is not recovery. The good news is that the new Alcohol and Drugs Strategic Plan 2026–2035 contains commitments addressing these gaps. The evaluation gives all of us fresh ammunition to hold everyone (myself included) to them.
So what?
Over five years a postcode lottery became much more of a national pathway. A treatment that was for the rich, the insured or the lucky became a right for anyone for whom it is deemed clinically appropriate. A sector that operated largely in the dark now has a dataset that, to my knowledge, is unique in Europe. Huge thanks are due to all of those who have contributed to the Working Group over the years and to Ministers for accepting and enacting our recommendations.
A personal note, and a full circle.
Twenty years ago, frustrated at watching patients and families bounce off the same walls I’ve described here, I helped set up a rehab service rooted in the NHS, along with council and third sector partners, based on the therapeutic community model. Plenty of people told us the NHS couldn’t run an effective rehab programme. The premise was simple: services to aid recovery from addiction should be available on the same basis as services for cancer, diabetes or broken bones – comprehensive and free at the point of delivery.
We learned early that if you build it, they will come. Demand was never the problem. Because we wanted to know whether it worked rather than just believe it might, we commissioned rigorous evaluation from the outset: one-year outcomes, four-year outcomes, independently followed up and then published in peer-reviewed journals. Almost half of our patients were abstinent at four years; among those who completed, more than 60%. Remarkable.
Those lessons – make it easy to access and free at the delivery end, evaluate honestly, expect demand, and treat addiction like any other condition – are precisely the ones now scaled up across Scotland. The principle behind the now-established national dataset came from the same frustration we felt in 2005 when I couldn’t find rehab outcome data anywhere in Scotland, so we had to create the means to collect our own. The Mother and Child Units, the prison-to-rehab pathway, the commissioning framework – all of it started life as a recommendation from people who had run out of patience with the lottery.
When I see the PHS data now, I see the lessons of one small NHS-based therapeutic community in Edinburgh, learned slowly and at a cost, becoming ordinary practice across a whole country. Of course we had learned from others and ‘stood on the shoulders of giants’ (thank you Providence Projects and others) to some extent, but there was much new learning from our unique service too.
There are good reasons to be positive, and plenty of evidence with which to challenge the naysayers. The future looks brighter, not just for rehab, but for recovery from substance use disorders generally. And if we keep our nerve, our data and our funding commitments, the next five years can build on the last because the lesson of LEAP, and of the national programme, is the same: set the bar high.
Now, let’s get on with the rest of the work.

title: Documenta historiadora la esencia del son huasteco, forjador de gran cohesión social
content:
Brenda Lira Montero realizó una investigación de dos años en Pahuatlán, Puebla, para comprender cómo se mantiene vivo este arte y cuál es su aportación a la comunidad
Jueves 17 de septiembre de 2026, p. 2
Pahuatlán, enclavado entre las barrancas y los cafetales de la Sierra Norte de Puebla, es un baluarte del son huasteco. Ahí, cada Jueves Santo, tríos de huapangueros se reúnen para lanzar versos hasta el amanecer entre el sonido de violines y el repiqueteo del zapateado.
La esencia de esta tradición ha quedado documentada en el libro El eslabón constante de la música: Son huasteco en Pahuatlán, de Brenda Lira Montero, maestra en historia por la Benemérita Universidad Autónoma de Puebla. El título es producto de un trabajo de investigación realizado entre 2019 y 2020.
“Puebla está ceñida a su identidad barroca colonial y ése es su elemento más visible, promocionado y lo que le da identidad. Pero también tenemos otras expresiones, como el son huasteco de Pahua-tlán, y es importante visibilizarlas”, afirmó.
En entrevista con La Jornada, la autora explicó que esta obra surgió a partir de su gusto por la música –estudió flauta transversal en alguna etapa de mi vida–, así como por una visita al pueblo mágico que la cautivó.
“Me encantó el sonido del violín, la participación de las bailarinas en la tarima y la alegría que ahí se produce. Fue a partir de esa visita que me decidí a estudiar ese vínculo entre música, alegría y comunidad”, agregó.
Durante el trabajo de campo, que incluyó una inmersión en la comunidad, sus fiestas y largas entrevistas con sus pobladores, fueron varios los hallazgos que le permitieron comprender cómo esta expresión se mantiene viva y cuál es su aportación a la comunidad.
Uno de sus descubrimientos fue la cohesión social que se produce a partir de los sones, incluso entre personas que ya no residen en Pahuatlán. Explicó que durante la festividad familiares de los lugareños, quienes por motivos de trabajo o estudio ahora viven en Tamaulipas, Veracruz, San Luis Potosí o Querétaro, regresan al pueblo.
“Pude observar los vínculos sociales tan fuertes que se forjan a partir de la música”, apuntó.
Otro elemento que surgió es cómo la música puede ser una manera de romper las barreras y vencer la desconfianza. “Yo preguntaba: ‘¿me puede contar más sobre cómo bailaba su abuela?’ Y ahí las personas sacaban las fotos del cajón y me compartían de una manera muy sensible y emocional las experiencias de sus antepasados”.
Para Lira Montero uno de los aspectos más relevantes durante la investigación fue el papel protagónico de las mujeres en la organización de los bailes, los versos y el zapateado. “En la ciudad de Puebla las mujeres tenían una participación muy distinta, más limitada, pero en relación con el son huasteco su presencia era más destacada”.
Fusión con sonidos nuevos
En El eslabón constante de la música: Son huasteco en Pahuatlán, organizado en una introducción, seis capítulos y las conclusiones de la autora, se reconstruye la historia del son huasteco de la primera mitad del siglo XX, periodo en el que el nacionalismo musical coincide con el auge de sonidos nuevos.
En medio de los sones tradicionales (por ejemplo, El caimán, La petenera y El gusto), se registra el auge de compositores nuevos, entre otros, Nicandro Castillo, Elpidio Ramírez y Valeriano Trejo, quienes crearon sones como El andariego, Rogaciano el huapanguero y El hidalguense.
El volumen también registra que si bien los versos o los temas de los sonetos se han mantenido a lo largo del tiempo, hay algunas variaciones en el humor o la picardía que se les imprime según la región. Otro aspecto interesante son los cambios que se han hecho en la ejecución de los instrumentos.
Las nuevas generaciones, advirtió Lira Montero, en lugar de la quinta huapanguera usan un bajo eléctrico. “He llegado a escuchar algunas fusiones, e incluso algo de jazz, pero siempre tratan de mantener la estructura base, lo que los une a sus raíces”.
Instrucción musical
Para que esta tradición se mantenga viva por más tiempo, los habitantes han señalado la importancia de contar con programas musicales. Hasta ahora los niños aprenden de forma empírica de sus familiares, pero para los pahuatecos una escuela de música sería ideal.
“Más que talleres esporádicos, ellos quieren una escuela de música que les permita una verdadera instrucción musical: de canto, de ejecución de instrumentos, pero también que se les permita ser incluidos en festivales y en eventos culturales”.
A Lira Montero le gustaría que cualquier persona que lea su libro se quede con la inquietud de conocer más sobre esta expresión de son huasteco que se ejecuta en la Sierra Norte de Puebla. “Ojalá pudieran sentir curiosidad por los violines, por la quinta huapanguera, la jarana y por la gente que está detrás de estos instrumentos”.

title: The mystery of drums with 'ears' in Vietnam’s Central Highlands
content:
Unique drums belonging to ethnic communities in the Central Highlands, from the collection of Dang Minh Tam, a resident of Da Lat, are being showcased to visitors at the Temple of Literature in Hanoi.
The collection includes drums with 'ears' as well as drums whose buffalo-hide surfaces still retain a thick layer of hair.
Tam’s drum collection is displayed alongside drums from Doi Tam Village in Ninh Binh Province and Binh An Village in Tay Ninh Province as part of the 'Nhat Trong: One Drumbeat - A Thousand Years of Civilization' exhibition at the Temple of Literature.
The exhibition is being held as part of the second Thang Long - Hanoi Festival in 2026.
Mystery of drums once owned only by the wealthy
While the Doi Tam and Binh An drums stand out for their eye-catching colors and fashionable designs, the Central Highlands drums have attracted even more visitors, not only because of their distinctive, rustic appearance but also because of the fascinating stories behind each drum that Tam is always willing to share with anyone interested.
Speaking to Tuoi Tre (Youth) online newspaper, Tam said each Central Highlands drum tells an interesting story, and all of them carry a special sacred meaning.
People in the Central Highlands treat drums as sacred objects. As a result, the drums must be made according to strict rules, and only wealthy people could afford to own them.
There are no drum-making villages or drum shops in the Central Highlands.
When wealthy families in a village wanted to make a drum, they would first slaughter a large male buffalo and make offerings to the tree spirit, drum spirit, sky spirit, and forest spirit for permission to make the drum.
Only then would they begin selecting a tree for the drum. Unlike drums made by other ethnic groups, which are assembled from pieces of wood, Central Highlands drums are carved from a single solid tree trunk.
The tree therefore had to be a high-quality, perfectly straight trunk with a diameter of about one meter.
The tree also had to meet a number of other conditions: it could not have vines wrapped around it, a beehive on it, a broken top, or any blemishes on its trunk.
In the past, people in the Central Highlands had to venture deep into the forest to find such a tree. Today, this is no longer permitted in order to protect the forests.
Once a suitable tree had been selected, a group of seven strong young men would carry shields and spears, and bring along a 6-7kg pig and alcohol into the forest to make offerings to the tree spirit.
There were also strict taboos along the way to cut down the tree. The group was not allowed to hear a cuckoo's call, see a black snake crossing the path or encounter a dead fish.
When they reached the tree, they would dance around its trunk, slaughter the pig they had brought as an offering to thank the tree spirit, and apologize to the spirit before asking permission to cut down the tree.
To determine whether the tree spirit agreed to offer itself for the making of a drum, the strongest man in the group would stand at a distance and throw an ax into the tree trunk before everyone returned home.
The next day, when they came back, if the ax was still firmly embedded in the tree, it meant the tree spirit had agreed to let the tree be cut down. If the ax had fallen, they had to continue searching for another tree.
After the tree was felled, a section of the trunk about one meter long was cut off, shaped and hollowed out into the drum body in the forest before being taken home.
The drum with 'ears'
Once the drum body was brought home, the owner would slaughter a female buffalo to hold a feast for the entire village and use its hide to cover the head of the main drum.
Among some Central Highlands ethnic groups, the main drum is made only from female buffalo hide, while others make drums with both male and female heads.
The Central Highlands follow a matrilineal system, so things associated with femininity are highly respected.
The main drumhead is about 2-3cm larger than the male drumhead and is stretched very tightly.
The main drumhead is struck only during major village ceremonies, such as those to celebrate a new communal house or offerings to the water source.
By contrast, the male drumhead, made from male buffalo hide, is used only within the immediate family.
Another distinctive feature is that the main drumhead has its 'ears' pierced so the drum can hear the spirits’ voices from the left and right.
The hide used to cover Central Highlands drums can be as thick as a finger joint because local people do not thin the hide as is done elsewhere.
As a result, many Central Highlands drums still retain a thick layer of hair on the buffalo hide.
Drums in the Central Highlands are not placed on the ground but kept on chairs or in sacred positions.
In communal houses, drums are respectfully hung in the center, while in longhouses, they are placed on the sacred Kpan bench.
No one would dare turn their back to a drum or touch its drumhead. Visitors to a home are also not allowed to play the drum without permission.
For people in the Central Highlands, all of these acts would be considered disrespectful to the spirits, known as Yang.
To play the drum, the owner must perform a ritual offering a chicken, a jar of rice wine and some porridge to ask permission from the spirits.
Only the drum’s owner or the village elder or chief is allowed to sound the sacred drumbeats.
Tam said that today, making a solid, one-piece drum like those made in the past is almost impossible.
As a result, Central Highlands drums are becoming increasingly rare.

title: Indigenous ‘turtle women’ help vulnerable reptiles recover in Ecuadorian Amazon
content:
On the banks of the Aguarico River in the Ecuadorian Amazon, a group of Indigenous Siekopai women are combining traditional knowledge and modern technology to help a threatened native turtle recover.
Their efforts center around charapa turtles (Podocnemis unifilis), also known as the yellow-spotted Amazon River turtle, Mongabay Latam’s Astrid Arellano reported. The animal’s populations have declined due to hunting adult turtles, harvesting eggs from nests and pollution from garbage, oil and gasoline.
“Sometimes we see plastic, garbage bags,” Janeth Piaguaje, a Siekopai community leader of the project, told Mongabay Latam. “We also see dead animals floating down the river. We can’t control all of that, but we do make a significant effort to clean the beaches where we work.”
Boat traffic is also eroding riverbanks, and climate change has caused water levels to rise, flooding the flats where turtles make their nests. Charapa turtles are listed as vulnerable by the IUCN, the global conservation authority.
To help the turtles recover, a group of seven Siekopai women, who call themselves Tari Nomiowa’i, or “turtle women,” patrol the riverbanks looking for turtle tracks and nests. When they find nests, the women carefully collect the eggs, a skill Piaguaje said she learned from her father.
“He taught me how to handle the eggs, how to see on what dates and in what months the turtles lay their nests,” she said.
The women document the date, time, location and number of eggs in each nest using the Epicollect5 app, a field data collection tool.
Then they take the eggs to an incubation facility where they are protected from predators, flooding and pollution. Once the eggs hatch, the women continue to care for the baby turtles for another month, feeding them cassava, sweet potato and taro leaves.
Their painstaking work has paid off. Over the 2025-26 nesting season, the women collected 235 eggs and successfully hatched and released 208 hatchlings into the Aguarico River over March and April this year. The group invited the local community, including schoolchildren, to participate in the turtle release and attend workshops.
“A little girl said, ‘I’m going to take care of them, I’m going to tell them not to touch the eggs,’” Piaguaje recalled.
A driving force behind the work of the Tari Nomiowa’i is their culture and the ancestral belief that the turtles are a link between the visible and spiritual worlds, each swimming with protection from Koouwajëo, the spiritual chief, mother and ancestral guardian of the turtles.
“I want Koouwajëo to be proud,” said Piaguaje. “When we protect turtles, we don’t just care for a species; we honor the spirits of the river, strengthen our culture and maintain the sacred pact between our community and nature.”
Read the full story by Astrid Arellano in Spanish here.

title: Proyecto educativo "La página oculta" visibiliza líderes afrodecescendientes
content:
Lundu Centro de Estudios y Promoción Afroperuanos y la agencia Cheil Perú se unieron para desarrollar el proyecto educativo y de memoria histórica "La Página Oculta", mediante el cual vienen distribuyendo 50 mil ejemplares impresos en instituciones educativas de Lima, Callao, Ica, Lambayeque y Piura. La iniciativa busca integrar en las aulas los aportes de líderes afrodescendientes del siglo XIX .


A partir de una investigación liderada por la historiadora Maribel Arrelucea y el uso de referencias históricas y familiares, el equipo creativo logró recrear los rostros y trayectorias de cuatro figuras clave: Alberto "Grumete" Medina, héroe de la Guerra del Pacífico; Catalina Buendía de Pecho, lideresa de la resistencia en Ica; Francisco Congo, fundador del Palenque Huachipa; e Ildefonso, combatiente de la causa independentista. Los materiales impresos han sido diseñados e insertados estratégicamente para complementar los textos escolares existentes.
"Con esta iniciativa queremos contribuir a visibilizar en la escuela a personajes referentes de los procesos de libertad y emancipación de las comunidades afrodescendientes. Al compartir estos ejemplares, vemos que se despierta la curiosidad del alumnado por conocer otros aspectos de la historia, transformando la percepción hacia los aportes afroperuanos más allá del ámbito musical, gastronómico o deportivo", destacó Brenda Garay, directora de proyectos de LUNDU.
El desarrollo de la iniciativa cuenta además con un video documental producido por Cheil Studio, el cual registra el proceso de investigación, diseño e impacto del proyecto en las escuelas.
El audiovisual, disponible en las plataformas digitales de Lundu, está musicalizado por los percusionistas Carlos Yamasaki y Gustavo Silva, e incluye análisis sobre ciudadanía e interculturalidad a cargo de la actual senadora Susana Matute, así como valiosos testimonios de exintegrantes de la organización, entre ellas su fundadora Mónica Carrillo y la comunicadora Ysabel Omega.
Lee también:
["La púrpura de la rosa, primer ópera prima de América, regresa a Lima 325 años después"]Con la distribución de estas 50 mil publicaciones en cinco regiones del país, "La Página Oculta" se consolida como una herramienta pedagógica que promueve una revisión crítica y representativa de la historia nacional en las nuevas generaciones.
Más en Andina

title: The ‘National Park’ That Stretches From Coast to Coast
content:
On Doug Tallamy’s 10-acre property in rural Pennsylvania, the evidence arrives on wings. Wood thrushes now nest in shrubs that were once cut for hay. Luna moths — emerald-green giants that had become increasingly rare — have reached record numbers. Tallamy recounts enthusiastically that he has documented more than 1,380 species of moths on the land, along with 62 breeding bird species. “We hear the birds in the morning. I see the gray tree frog sitting on my window sill,” he raves. “That is a real reward for me.”
When he and his wife Cindy bought the 300-year-old farm in 2000, its surroundings looked green. But when Tallamy walked the property he noticed it was overrun by invasive plants — like the Japanese stiltgrass and the aptly named mile-a-minute-weed, a smothering vine — that supported few pollinators. “There were no caterpillars!” he recalls. That recognition turned him from a researcher with a passion for insects into a passionate advocate for native plants. The transformation of his land didn’t require expensive engineering or high-tech equipment. Tallamy simply weeded out invasives and put native plants back. “I think in the last 26 years we spent about $100,” he says. “Because I simply go get seeds and put them in the ground.”
For more than two decades, the bestselling author and entomologist at the University of Delaware has argued that the biodiversity crisis won’t be solved only in national parks or on other protected lands. It will be solved — or lost — in millions of ordinary backyards and schoolyards, on corporate campuses and apartment balconies. “Nearly 80 percent of land east of the Mississippi is privately owned, and 135 million acres are now in residential landscapes,” he says. “That puts the private property owner in charge of conservation. If 10 to 20 percent of landowners planted native plants, this would add up to a habitat larger than 10 Yellowstones.”
National parks are much needed and beloved, but Tallamy points out that many species migrate beyond their borders and won’t survive if they don’t find sustenance and habitat along the way. “In between protected areas is no man’s land for most creatures and plants,” he says. “All of the parks and preserves, including Yellowstone, are too small and too isolated.” Connecting those islands with habitat on private land, he argues, “is going to be the solution.”
This premise led to his creation of Homegrown National Park, a nonprofit that encourages people to replace conventional lawns with native habitat and register their efforts on a nationwide biodiversity map. The initiative has now grown to over 52,000 registered participants who tend to more than 187,000 acres, figures Tallamy says are rapidly rising. “The real argument is that natural systems are generating your life support,” he urges. “They make your oxygen, they manage your watershed, they minimize extreme weather conditions, sequester carbon to help [mitigate] climate change. They’re doing all kinds of things to keep you alive on this planet.”
While the current administration guts the Endangered Species Act, reduces national monuments, defunds national parks and opens millions of acres of public lands to drilling and grazing, Tallamy is urging every American to give nature a boost where they can. “Everything we plant, don’t plant, or apply to our yard impacts the greater ecosystem in which our yard exists, and thus everything that depends on that ecosystem,” he writes in his most recent book, How Can I Help? Saving Nature with Your Yard. He argues that we don’t have the luxury to ignore that simple truth. “Everybody requires healthy ecosystems whether they know it or not,” he says. “That means it’s everybody’s responsibility to contribute to taking care of these systems.”
Tallamy emphasizes the urgency: “When you read that we’ve lost three billion breeding birds and have 22 percent fewer butterflies just since the year 2000, global insect decline, two-thirds of wildlife gone — that’s upsetting to a lot of people,” he says. “Even if they don’t know anything about biology, they don’t want to hear that everything on the planet is dying.”

Rather than stopping there, Tallamy pivots toward agency. “Our simple message is: There are things you can do. You can see the results. It empowers you to be part of the solution instead of part of the problem.” He argues that the reward of taking action is immediate: “If you plant an oak tree in your yard, you can see the difference tomorrow.”
Homegrown National Park’s website and Tallamy’s books give detailed practical advice on what anybody can do, from planting keystone species to shrinking one’s lawn and leaving the leaves as shelter for pollinators. But even people without a yard can find plenty of useful information. “If everybody did container gardening on their balcony, it [would become] a resource for native bee species in cities,” he says. “Migrating monarchs will use these plants.” And if someone really does not want to handle plants, Tallamy has hands-on advice for them, too: “Then change the light bulb outside from a white bulb to an amber bulb to stop killing moths all night long. You don’t need a PhD to do that, but it would make a huge difference.”
Whether this grassroots movement can scale fast enough to make a measurable ecological difference remains an open question. But as governments struggle to halt biodiversity loss, Tallamy is betting on changing culture.
Referring to the U.N.’s initiative of conserving 30 percent of land and water by 2030, commonly referred to as 30 x 30, he says, “You’ve got to count what’s happening on private property. And nobody’s doing that. Nobody’s recording it. That’s what that biodiversity map is all about.”
In his books, which have sold over half a million copies, Tallamy propagates a stubbornly upbeat view. “The cultural change from an adversarial relationship with nature to a collaborative one is starting to happen,” he writes in his latest book, “and it gives me hope about the future of biodiversity and thus our own future.”
Tallamy’s initiative is especially trying to reach people not usually interested in ecosystem health. “That is of course most people,” he acknowledges. “We try to create a social network to motivate people who don’t have a clue, who don’t know they are responsible for good earth stewardship right where they live.” He tours the country relentlessly giving speeches “and there is usually someone who has been dragged in by their neighbor.”
In parts of the Deep South, Tallamy says, traditional landscaping culture remains resistant to rewilding. Many homeowners associate tidy lawns with safety and social acceptance.
Tallamy is refreshingly candid about the limitations of his approach. Even converting every targeted lawn would represent less than one percent of U.S. land, he acknowledges. Critics argue that such a change cannot solve biodiversity loss on its own. “I never said Homegrown National Park is going to solve the biodiversity crisis,” he says. “Getting everybody involved and changing the culture is going to help. It’s going to help a lot.”
A recent feature in the New York Times questioned whether his insistence on native plants is out of date because some species adapt to a changing habitat. But Tallamy has shown in dozens of studies that native plants are crucial for many species’ survival.
The real metric, he argues, isn’t simply acreage restored but whether ecological thinking becomes mainstream. Evidence of that cultural shift, he believes, is already emerging. Demand for native plants now exceeds supply in many regions. Conservation landscaping is beginning to increase property values rather than diminish them. Native plant professionals are increasingly booked months in advance.
Still, Tallamy admits the movement remains tiny relative to the challenge. Even counting the two million people who visit Homegrown National Park’s website annually, “That’s nothing compared to 340 million people in the U.S. we need to reach.”
Mostly, he wants people to stop thinking of conservation as something professionals do somewhere else. “The object is to get people to realize that they have agency over what happens on their little piece of the Earth,” he emphasizes. “And that it matters.”

title: Barcelona, una ciudad que educa más allá del aula
content:
CIUDAD EDUCADORA
Barcelona, una ciudad que
educa más allá del aula
La capital catalana consolida un modelo de Ciudad Educadora que extiende el aprendizaje a los barrios e implica equipamientos, entidades y ciudadanía en la construcción de una Barcelona más equitativa, sostenible y cohesionada
Un sábado por la mañana, un patio escolar abierto se transforma en un espacio de juego y encuentro. Familias que no se conocían comparten espacio, criaturas que no van a la misma escuela juegan juntas y el barrio gana un punto de convivencia. En otro rincón de la ciudad, niños, niñas y adolescentes participan en actividades culturales, artísticas o deportivas fuera del horario lectivo. Son escenas que responden a una misma idea: en Barcelona, educar va mucho más allá de la escuela.
La ciudad trabaja con esta mirada desde 1990, cuando firmó la Carta de Ciudades Educadoras. Más de tres décadas después, el modelo afronta una etapa de consolidación y actualización. "La educación es una tarea compartida por toda la ciudad", explica Pilar Lleonart, responsable de Ciudad Educadora. Calles, plazas, equipamientos culturales y deportivos, entidades y vecindario tienen, desde esta perspectiva, una función educativa.
De la idea al barrio
El reto es convertir estos principios en actuaciones tangibles. Una de las más visibles es Transformem els Patis, que convierte los espacios escolares en entornos más verdes, inclusivos, coeducativos y abiertos al barrio. Actualmente se han realizado 79 transformaciones, 48 de las cuales cumplen los requisitos de refugio climático.
La transformación no es solo física. Infancia, profesorado, familias, entidades y vecindario participan en el proceso de definición de los espacios. La misma concepción hay detrás del programa Patis Oberts, que pone los espacios escolares a disposición de la ciudadanía los fines de semana y durante periodos de vacaciones. La ciudad dispone actualmente de 66 patios abiertos distribuidos por los diez distritos. La escuela deja así de ser un recinto que cierra cuando acaba el horario lectivo y se convierte en un equipamiento del barrio.
Los programas, en cifras
Que el código postal no marque
La equidad es otro gran eje del modelo. El programa Tardes Educatives nació después de detectar que las oportunidades fuera del horario escolar variaban mucho según el territorio. En algunos barrios predominaban actividades como el refuerzo escolar o el fútbol, mientras que el acceso a propuestas artísticas, culturales o científicas era menor. El programa busca ampliar esta oferta y eliminar barreras económicas. Los últimos datos sitúan la actividad en 2.035 propuestas con 222 entidades participantes, acompañadas de ayudas y becas. "Lo que queremos es que el código postal no implique que puedas hacer unas determinadas actividades y dejes de hacer otras", explica Lleonart.
La Xarxa Educació i Ciutat, que articula la colaboración entre administración, centros educativos y entidades, amplía todavía más este ecosistema: el curso pasado ofreció 2.260 propuestas educativas y 42.970 plazas de equidad (gratuitas), con la participación de 146 entidades. Las actividades pasan, además, por una evaluación de calidad pedagógica. "La ciudad educa si todo el mundo facilita recursos que lleguen a todos", remarca.
La mirada abarca todas las edades. Por ejemplo, el Espai de Joc 0-99, que ofrece propuestas lúdicas y educativas para todas las edades, ha recibido durante el curso 2025-2026 más de 35.000 usuarios y promueve el juego intergeneracional, mientras que la Escola Municipal de Segones Oportunitats acompaña a jóvenes que han quedado fuera de los itinerarios formativos ordinarios para que puedan retomar su recorrido educativo y laboral.
Una estrategia de ciudad
Barcelona Ciudad Educadora no es una política exclusiva de la Direcció d'Educació ni de una única institución. Es una estrategia de ciudad compartida que implica al conjunto de las administraciones y agentes educativos, con un papel destacado del Consorci d'Educació de Barcelona, y también de los ámbitos de urbanismo, cultura, deportes, salud, derechos sociales y movilidad.
Esta mirada se hace especialmente visible ante la emergencia climática con programas como el Pla Clima Escola Barcelona, que en 2029 habrá climatizado con energía renovable 170 escuelas, o Transformem els Patis, con más árboles, sombra, agua o biodiversidad para mejorar el confort, pero también para educar en sostenibilidad.
Los programas, en cifras
"El gran reto hoy es pasar de una idea inspiradora a una estrategia operativa, capaz de traducir sus principios en acciones concretas y visibles en los barrios. En definitiva, se trata de hacer de la educación un proyecto colectivo de ciudad que la ciudadanía pueda reconocer, vivir y sentir como propio", resume Pilar Lleonart.
"La 'escola bressol' no es solo cuidar: es educación desde el primer día"
Barcelona consolida un modelo de Ciudad Educadora que extiende el aprendizaje a los barrios e implica equipamientos, entidades y ciudadanía en la construcción de una Barcelona más equitativa, sostenible y cohesionada
La capital catalana continúa ampliando la red de escoles bressol municipales. Este curso, la ciudad cuenta con 106 centros y unas 9.000 plazas de 0 a 3 años, después de la apertura de la EBM Tramuntana, en Sant Andreu de Palomar, y de la ampliación de la EBM La Mar, en la Barceloneta, con dos nuevos grupos. Además, hay diversos proyectos que se encuentran en diferentes fases de desarrollo.
Crear más plazas es solo una parte del reto. La otra es decidir dónde hacen más falta. Para planificar la ampliación de la red, el Ayuntamiento, a través del Instituto Municipal de Educación (IMEB), analiza la situación de los 73 barrios de la ciudad a partir de indicadores como: número de niños empadronados, demanda no atendida, nuevas promociones de vivienda, oferta privada, niveles de renta o vulnerabilidad de las familias. "Esto nos permite ordenar los 73 barrios y definir cuál es la prioridad de necesidad de escuela infantil", explica Alícia Aguilera, gerente del Instituto Municipal de Educación de Barcelona (IMEB).
