El modelo conecta directamente con la idea de Barcelona Ciudad Educadora. La escuela infantil no funciona de manera aislada, sino en relación con los servicios sociales, culturales y de salud y con el conjunto del barrio. Las familias también tienen un papel central. Participan en las asociaciones de familias o el consejo educativo de la escuela, y se pueden organizar también para hacer uso del patio una vez acabada la jornada (Pati en família); lo hacen un 75% de las escuelas. "Se promueve que las familias formen parte de los espacios participativos donde se toman decisiones en el ámbito comunitario y también se organicen para hacer actividades con sus hijos e hijas después del horario escolar", indica Aguilera.
Igualdad de oportunidades
Dos aspectos muy presentes en la red son la inclusión y la igualdad de oportunidades. En este sentido, las escuelas infantiles disponen de plazas reservadas para niños con necesidades educativas específicas y también para los que se encuentran en situación de vulnerabilidad y/o exclusión social. La red dispone de un equipo de educación inclusiva y trabaja con servicios sociales y servicios especializados.
La red de escoles bressol municipales de Barcelona afronta los próximos años con tres prioridades alineadas con la Garantía Infantil Europea: garantizar la equidad, reforzar la calidad educativa y ampliar la accesibilidad. También es prioritario avanzar en la ampliación de plazas públicas para que todas las familias que las necesiten puedan acceder a ellas. Para el IMEB, el papel de las escoles bressol y de los espacios familiares es clave para el bienestar de la infancia y la igualdad de oportunidades.

title: Más de cinco años para llevar su cultura a las aulas: “Me decían: no hables en tu idioma”
content:
Más de cinco años para llevar su cultura a las aulas: “Me decían: no hables en tu idioma”
Las nacionalidades amazónicas Siekopaai y A’i Cofán y Waorani lograron que el Ministerio de Educación de Ecuador reconozca sus tejidos curriculares e incorpore sus propios modelos de enseñanza, saberes ancestrales y lenguas en la educación pública
EL PAÍS ofrece en abierto la sección América Futura por su aporte informativo diario y global sobre desarrollo sostenible. Si quieres apoyar nuestro periodismo, suscríbete aquí.
Gaba Guiquita tuvo que aprender a hablar español a la fuerza. Sus primeras clases no fueron en su lengua materna: el wao terero. “Siempre hablaba en wao, pero algunos profesores me daban con la regla por hacerlo”, cuenta este waorani de 38 años. “Me decían: ‘No hables en wao’. Era un trauma para aprender español”, recuerda. Como Guiquita, generaciones de indígenas de las nacionalidades Siekopai y A’i Cofán y Waorani han crecido con una educación que no recogía su cultura. Ahora, después de una lucha de cinco años de trabajo, los niños y niñas de estas nacionalidades comenzaron este nuevo año escolar con clases en su idioma, materias que les cuentan sobre sus tradiciones, cosmovisión y el conocimiento de sus abuelos.
Más de un centenar de indígenas llegaron hace varios días a Quito desde la Amazonía y marcharon por una de las vías más transitadas de la ciudad. “¡Qué viva la educación propia!”, gritaban. Era un día de celebración. Bajo la consigna: ¡Sembramos saberes, cosechamos futuro! niños, niñas, maestros y padres, con sus vestimentas tradicionales, caminaron hasta el Ministerio de Educación de Ecuador, en un acto histórico. Ahora, por primera vez, cuentan con currículos educativos elaborados de forma autónoma desde las propias nacionalidades y reconocidos por el Estado. Una pancarta con el lema: “Educación propia para un futuro con identidad” encabezaba la marcha. En el Ministerio los esperaba el Secretario de Educación Intercultural Bilingüe para registrar oficialmente sus Proyectos Educativos Comunitarios (PEC) y permitir su implementación en las escuelas de estas nacionalidades.
En Ecuador, la Educación Intercultural Bilingüe se institucionalizó hace 38 años, cuando en 1988 se creó la Dirección Nacional de Educación Indígena Intercultural Bilingüe (DINEIB). Se logró desarrollar un currículum de acuerdo con las necesidades de los pueblos y nacionalidades indígenas. Aunque para ese momento fue un logro, gran parte de la estructura tenía un modelo que no respondía a las diferentes realidades lingüísticas y culturales de las 14 nacionalidades. “Era un documento traducido. Ahí hablaban del Inti Raymi [una ceremonia ancestral andina], que no tiene nada que ver con nuestra cosmogonía. Y los profesores no podían enseñar eso a cabalidad”, dice Wilmer Piaguage, dirigente de educación de los Siekopai. Muchos acababan la escuela sin conocer sobre su cultura ni su idioma. Ahora, los nuevos textos incluyen conocimientos que durante años quedaron relegados de las aulas.
Mireya Nenquimo, una de las profesoras de la nacionalidad waorani, viajó hasta Quito para la marcha. Llevaba una corona de plumas amarilla y pintura roja alrededor de sus ojos, tradicional de las mujeres de su nacionalidad. La maestra resalta que este es un gran paso y que las clases, que iniciaron este lunes, partirán de lo cotidiano. Los niños aprenderán a trabajar la chambira—una fibra tradicional extraída de hojas de palma—para hilar pulseras, hacer canastos y, para terminar el año, elaborar una hamaca. También aprenderán a identificar la madera para fabricar una lanza. El objetivo es que la educación salga del aula y aprendan en el territorio. Nenquimo cuenta que los miércoles, por ejemplo, la clase será de recorridos por la comunidad. Los niños tendrán que observar lo que encuentran en el camino, registrar las plantas medicinales y animales que reconocieron.
Pero el conocimiento ancestral va de la mano de un elemento clave: el idioma. Todos reconocen que jóvenes y niños han dejado de hablar su lengua materna. Ahora el reto de los maestros, como Nenquimo, será recuperar y fortalecer su idioma. “Ha sido necesario rescatar nuestra cultura e idioma. Hemos visto que la mayoría habla español y queremos que se rescate nuestro idioma y se sientan orgullosos”, dice Nenquimo. En su comunidad, las clases serán dictadas en wao terero los lunes, miércoles y viernes; mientras que los martes y jueves las impartirán en español.
Pero no serán las únicas habilidades que aprenderán y tampoco se busca que se aíslen del resto del mundo. Wilson Criollo, líder de la nacionalidad A’i Cofán, cuenta que la nueva malla también incorpora el conocimiento del “mundo occidental”. “Un niño tiene que tener su conocimiento ancestral, pero también conocer estas tecnologías del siglo XXI”, reflexiona. “Si no, ¿cómo podemos defender el territorio de las amenazas?”, se pregunta.
En el caso de los Siekopai, el nuevo currículum de estudios introduce los conocimientos que debe tener un siekopai. “Los estudiantes deben aprender los nueve mundos. Uno de ellos, el mundo del agua, donde hay seres espirituales”, explica. “Era algo que no nos enseñaban. Solo aprendíamos desde la visión de la iglesia y lo evolutivo”, agrega Piaguaje, quien ha trabajado durante tres años en la construcción del tejido curricular, sin contar los dos años que dedicó al diagnóstico de la educación en su nacionalidad.
Cinco años para aprender en su idioma
El proceso comenzó en 2019, cuando los waorani se preguntaron cómo continuar con la defensa de su territorio cuando los pikenani (abuelos y sabios de la comunidad) ya no estén. Las respuestas apuntaban al futuro de las nuevas generaciones y la educación que estaban recibiendo. En 2021 se sumaron los Sikopai y A’i Cofán, que comenzaron sus propios procesos de diagnóstico en sus territorios. Todos encontraron una preocupación común con la extinción de su cultura: la pérdida del idioma. “Los más pequeños conocían lo más mínimo. Incluso muchos jóvenes y niños no querían ni hablar el paikoka [el idioma de los siekopai], solo hablaban el castellano porque pensaban que se iban a burlar de ellos”, dice Wilmer Piaguaje.
Ese año se aprobó la primera propuesta para construir un modelo de educación propia. Para Gladys Vargas, lideresa A’i Cofán, crear el currículum desde cero significó preguntarse qué conocimiento debía llegar a las aulas. “Pensamos en qué temas poner, dónde están y cuáles son los nombres de los ríos, cómo es la cultura. Si se enseña eso, van a ir valorando el territorio”, cuenta.
La construcción del currículum educativo no quedó en manos de técnicos. Fue más allá: participaron abuelos, padres de familia, jóvenes y dirigentes que se reunieron para recordar sus conocimientos: desde las historias hasta sus técnicas de construcción de casas, cestos y comidas tradicionales. Pero, en 2024, las nacionalidades se encontraron con otro desafío: para que estos saberes pudieran impartirse en las escuelas públicas, necesitaban el reconocimiento del Estado.
Fue entonces cuando en 2025, las tres nacionalidades amazónicas terminaron sus Proyectos Educativos Comunitarios y las mallas curriculares. Y, este año, los entregaron al Ministerio de Educación para exigir su registro. Pasaron ocho meses de reuniones, viajes a Quito y cambios hasta conseguir que fueran aprobados e ingresados a las plataformas nacionales de evaluación. Ahora comienza un nuevo camino, el reto es poner en práctica todo el conocimiento dentro y fuera de sus comunidades.
Este logro tiene un significado especial para las nacionalidades indígenas del Ecuador. Cada una tiene sus propios saberes y formas de entender el mundo. Y, aunque todavía quedan otras nacionalidades por recorrer el proceso, este es un paso más para asegurar su existencia en el tiempo. Para Gaba Guiquita y una generación de indígenas, este cambio tiene un significado personal. Él, como otros indígenas de su generación, aprendió español a la fuerza, después de que le prohibieran hablar su idioma en la escuela. Ahora, los niños Siekopaai y A’i Cofán y Waorani podrán aprender en su lengua apenas entren al aula.

title: Culture That Made Me: Clonakilty guitarist Bill Shanley picks his touchstones
content:
Culture That Made Me: Clonakilty guitarist Bill Shanley picks his touchstones
Bill Shanley, 54, grew up in Clonakilty, Co Cork. In 1992, he was a guitarist on the iconic album, an early collaboration from many with international artists, as he has toured and contributed to albums with Ray Davies, Gilbert O’Sullivan, Sinéad O’Connor, amongst others.
Memorable gigs include playing with Davies at the closing ceremony of the London Olympics in 2012. He will perform at the Clonakilty International Guitar Festival, September 16-20. See: clonguitarfest.com
I grew up in the school of music in Shanley's Bar in Clonakilty. I started playing there as a nine-year-old in the early ’80s. My father was a great musician. He was a piano player, a great session man. The beauty of that was that I was amongst musicians. There was young Noel Redding. There were always visiting musicians that became lifelong friends like Paul Brady or Eric Bell. I came of age there. I was set up to move on in a life of music.
Noel Redding and his partner, Carol, started finding their feet again in Clonakilty in terms of going out and doing gigs around the same time that I started playing. Noel took me on as a student for about a year. He had never taught music. In his own way, he gave me great lessons. It would be – learn a song, learn a rock'n'roll [riff]. He'd draw pictures, beautiful artwork. He was an art student. I still have his notebook.
What Noel brought to Clonakilty was an eccentricity, a colour. Locals recount the day he arrived in the early ’70s. He came in his big yellow 3-litre Ford Capri. He was probably dressed in tie-dye colours. He came as he was and he shook it up. Bands used to follow over, be it Manfred Mann or his old buddies from Status Quo. He had a big house; he had “the rockstar mansion”, so people came and hung out and played.
Shanley’s was his regular haunt in the early ’80s up to maybe ’87. He had this reputation. People knew him because of his association with Jimi Hendrix, the power trio, but he didn't hold back from getting stuck into the local town. He was a great community man and a brilliant musician.
I went to see and meet Eric Bell recently. He played in Dublin. It was Philip Lynott’s anniversary. He did a gig in Whelan’s. I went down. I said hello. It was an amazing gig. You’d forget how good he is. Eric comes from that era where his contemporaries were people like Jimi Hendrix and Eric Clapton. He still brings that high level of playing. He played , the big Thin Lizzy song. As a kid, I remember him teaching me that note for note in the kitchen of our house. Amazing.
is the coming together of a great story, great casting. It's so beautifully shot. Every scene is a classic, every nuance is just perfect. As Al Pacino’s character is getting more involved in taking over the family mafia business, you can see him getting more distant, colder, less affectionate as a character. He dismisses his family. Kay, his wife, wants to leave him because she can't handle it. She doesn't come from that background. The development of that one character in the movie is so good. It's a masterpiece.
Eric Bell sent me an album in the mid ’80s. He was living in London. I still have it here in my studio. He posted over a cassette of Django Reinhardt and Stephane Grappelli, who was his sparring partner, the great fiddle player. This was an album from way back, from 1935. I've listened to it a thousand times. I listen to it for the beauty and how pleasant it is. Django Reinhardt was a gypsy. His caravan as a kid went on fire. He spent a year in hospital. He came out with two fingers that he could play guitar with, so he created this left-hand technique. He made great music.
Paul Brady's is a great Irish rock album. It came out in 1981. I came to it late. It was Paul's first time delving into his own songs. When I listen to the album, it conjures up those pictures of the early 1980s, which were tougher times. There's emigration. He talks about less savoury characters in Dublin, robbing cars, this or that. , , great songs. It’s a classic album – the musicianship on it, Paul's production, his guitar playing, his delivery. It’s a thing of beauty.
I was a real fan of ’60s music. People said, “Are you a Beatles or Stones fan?” I would say, “I'm a Kinks fan.” Ray Davies is incredibly prolific. I've seen his process up close. I was in a dressing room with him once. We were in Canada doing a festival. We were going on stage in about an hour. He was over at a desk writing a lyric. He was putting together a show that involved a choir. He was shooting off the cuff, putting down lyric ideas. He's so good at his craft that he instinctively gets it right firsthand. There isn’t much editing. He’s totally on it as a lyricist, and as a music producer. The thing about Ray is that as well as writing all the Kinks music, he also produced it. He didn't bring in some big time American producer. He didn't make it easy on himself. Amazing.
The Olympics was all kept under wraps, as to who would be performing. I was with my family down in West Cork, on holidays. We [Ray Davies + Friends] had come back from an American and an Asian tour. I got to Clonakilty. Then I headed over for a day to Dagenham, London to rehearse. All under wraps. The show was on a Sunday, the closing ceremony. We put on a gig in Shanley's Bar on the Saturday night because there was no point in sitting around thinking about what was happening too much. Next morning, I flew to London. The show was spectacular – the magnitude of it.
Being involved in the Olympics, what I noticed was on the day – every band was there, from Pink Floyd and The Who to Ed Sheeran – everyone was humble because no one band was bigger than the Olympics. Everyone was just glad to be there. From Ray's point of view, we sang , the quintessential London song. So here we were in Ray's lifetime doing his song at London 2012. These things won't come around again. It came off well. I was delighted to be part of it. The next day, I flew back in the morning. I was down in Inchydoney with my family enjoying the beach, thinking, did I just do that?
John Steinbeck’s is a brilliant story. It’s fabulously written. When I first read it, it seemed a very modern, hip book even though it was written in an era going back over a century ago in California. It's a great story about intertwining families and hardships, and how their lives overlap. The imagery is very vivid. It’s a classic.
I loved the recent Dónal Lunny documentary, , on RTÉ. It was written and directed by Nuala O'Connor. It’s a very enjoyable watch, a great portrayal of Dónal Lunny. It puts across his immense contribution to the music world.

title: A Homeland Remembered: Crimean Tatars and the Question of Indigenous Identity in Europe
content: A Homeland Remembered: Crimean Tatars and the Question of Indigenous Identity in Europe Country Russia Ukraine agnes Wed, 09/09/2026 - 10:12 Issues Human Rights Program 5 Main Image By Mara Moldavan (CS Intern) For centuries, the Crimean Tatars have lived on the Black Sea peninsula of Crimea, where their language, traditions, and history are closely tied to the land. But since Russia’s annexation of Crimea in 2014, many Crimean Tatars have been forced into exile or now live under occupation. Their situation raises a question that Europe still struggles to answer: what does it mean for an Indigenous People to defend identity, continuity, and political belonging when access to their homeland is disrupted by occupation and war? “Our homeland is Crimea—and no one else's,” says Liudmyla Korotkykh (Crimean Tatar), a lawyer and manager at the Crimean Tatar Resource Center, an organization that documents human rights violations in Crimea. Speaking from Kyiv, where she has lived since leaving Crimea in 2015, Korotkykh describes a Peoples whose identity is inseparable from the land itself.​ ​Who are the Crimean Tatars? The Crimean Tatars are recognized in Ukraine as one of the Indigenous Peoples of Crimea, alongside the Karaims and the Krymchaks. Outside of Eastern Europe, many people are unfamiliar with the idea that Indigenous Peoples live within Europe at all. Korotkykh believes this misunderstanding stems partly from the way Indigenous identity is often depicted. “People often think Indigenous Peoples are those who were colonized,” she explains. “And historically, Europeans were the colonizers. Because of this, many people don’t imagine Indigenous Peoples existing in Europe.” Tatar Youth. Photo by Crimean Tatar Resource Center. A Relationship Rooted in Land Crimea is located on the northern coast of the Black Sea and consists of mountains and prairie lands. Over generations, communities developed ways of living with these environments. “It’s more than territory,” Korotkykh says. “It’s a special way of life.” One example lies in the mountains, where traditional orchards known as chayır rely on natural water flows shaped by the terrain. These mountain gardens allow communities to grow fruit and crops in places where irrigation would otherwise be difficult. According to Korotkykh, the unique conditions of these landscapes produce fruit that is known for its distinct flavor. Even among those who grew up far from Crimea, that connection remains. Korotkykh’s mother was born in Uzbekistan after the deportation. “We grew up hearing stories about Crimea,” she says. “People would say that the fruit there tastes better, that even the sun shines more brightly.” Displacement and Survival In 1944, Joseph Stalin, then leading the Soviet Union, ordered the mass deportation of Crimean Tatars to Central Asia, accusing the entire population of collaborating with Nazi Germany. Families were forced onto trains and deported thousands of kilometers away; many did not survive. For decades afterward, Crimean Tatars weren’t allowed to return. Their culture was suppressed, yet families continued to maintain traditions and language in private, passing them from one generation to the next. Over time, small acts of cultural preservation became forms of resistance. Weddings, for example, took on a significance beyond celebration. In Crimean Tatar communities, large gatherings allowed people to share music, language, and news while raising funds to support cultural activities and the growing movement. During the late Soviet era, Crimean Tatars began returning to their homeland after generations of exile. Many found their homes gone and land ownership uncertain, but through persistence and collective effort, they slowly rebuilt community life. By the early 21st century, Crimean Tatar culture was beginning to reemerge across the peninsula. A Homeland Under Occupation That recovery was interrupted in 2014, when Russia annexed Crimea. In February 2014, thousands gathered outside the Crimean parliament building in Simferopol to support Ukraine’s territorial integrity and protest Russia’s actions. “Crimean Tatars were in the center of opposition to the occupation,” Korotkykh says. In the years that followed, many Crimean Tatar activists and journalists faced arrests and criminal charges widely criticized by human rights organizations. “Russia uses these accusations to create the image that Crimean Tatars are extremists,” Korotkykh says. “But in many cases, people are targeted simply for their activism or for their beliefs.” Despite pressures, Crimean Tatars continue to safeguard their identity. As Korotkykh explains, language remains a powerful marker of belonging: “When you hear Crimean Tatar language or see traditional clothing, you understand you are among your people.” For younger generations, cultural expression has become a form of resistance. “In conditions where political activity is dangerous, culture becomes a way to show who you are. Young people are increasingly interested in traditions because they want to keep that identity alive,” Korotkykh says. What Is at Stake The broader war between Russia and Ukraine has added new pressures to Crimean Tatar communities. After Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, reports of arrests and political prosecutions in Crimea intensified. The stakes, Korotkykh argues, extend beyond one community. Crimea’s location on the Black Sea makes it strategically important for the region, and it has become a central element of the conflict between Russia and Ukraine. For Korotkykh, the international response to Crimea since 2014 shows just how easily the concerns of Indigenous Peoples can be overlooked in geopolitical debates. “When the occupation began, many people said a full-scale war in Europe was impossible,” she recalls. “But we warned that Russia would not stop in Crimea.” Eight years later, those warnings proved prescient. Only a few hundred thousand Crimean Tatars now live worldwide. Korotkykh worries that continued displacement could slowly fade the identity of Crimean Tatars. “If the world closes its eyes to Crimea,” she says, “our People could disappear.”​ ​ Liudmyla Korotkykh A Future Tied to Home Today, Korotkykh documents human rights violations in Crimea while also advocating internationally for the rights of Crimean Tatars and the other Indigenous Peoples of Crimea. Her work extends to engagement with United Nations mechanisms and international forums, where she brings attention to the situation on the peninsula. Like many Crimean Tatars living outside Crimea, she still has family there. “I’m Crimean Tatar. I’m from Crimea,” she says. “And of course, I want to go home.” Despite the ongoing war and uncertainty about the future of Crimea, Korotkykh remains hopeful that the rights of Indigenous Peoples will play a greater role in shaping Ukraine’s future. In 2021, Ukraine adopted a law recognizing Indigenous Peoples, including the Crimean Tatars, Karaims, and Krymchaks, marking an important step toward acknowledging Indigenous identity within Europe. “Each person can make the world more just,” she says. For the Crimean Tatars, the memory of Crimea continues to shape daily life—whether on the peninsula itself or across the diaspora. Even after decades of deportation, exile, and conflict, that connection endures. Crimea remains not only the land remembered, but the homeland many still hope to return to.

title: Wonder Rooster, historic Mango tree put Lundo Island’s cultural heritage under tourism spotlight again
content:
Wonder Rooster, historic Mango tree put Lundo Island’s cultural heritage under tourism spotlight again
AT the shores of Lake Nyasa, beneath an old mango tree closely associated with the history of Lundo Island, domestic tourists recently encountered something more enduring than scenery: a living account of culture, tradition and memory. Gathered around the tree, they listened to island elder Vincent Tadei, popularly known as Mzee Magogo, as he recounted stories and beliefs that have helped shape Lundo’s cultural identity across generations.
The encounter offered visitors an opportunity to understand Lundo beyond its waters and natural beauty. It presented the island as a place where history survives through people, places and oral traditions. At the centre of the experience was the old mango tree, whose history, according to accounts shared with visitors, is linked to lepers who lived on or visited the island in earlier times. It was beneath and around this historic tree, close to the lakeshore, that the visitors participated in a traditional moment of prayer.
Mzee Magogo explained that, according to local tradition and belief, visitors to Lundo may make prayers through traditional practices by directing their requests towards the island’s famous “Wonder Rooster.” The rooster is among the most intriguing stories associated with Lundo. For years, local people have regarded it as a distinctive part of the island’s traditional heritage. Its exact age is unknown and even those responsible for managing the island do not know precisely how long it has lived there.
According to Mzee Magogo, the rooster remains within the island’s reserve and appears to visitors according to patterns that are not readily understood. Some people arrive hoping to see it and leave without doing so, while others encounter it during their visit. That uncertainty has become part of the story surrounding the bird and contributes to the curiosity it generates among visitors.
For the domestic tourists who travelled from Mbamba Bay to Lundo Island through an initiative organised by Jogoo FM Radio, the encounter was particularly memorable. They became the second known group of tourists in 2026 to see the Wonder Rooster, according to information shared by people familiar with visits to the island.
A group of Namtumbo District Council employees who recently visited Lundo was also reported to have seen the bird, while many other visitors during 2026 had not. Across Tanzania, generations have passed knowledge through elders, stories, sacred places, songs, dances, ceremonies and traditional practices. Lundo is one of the places where elements of that inheritance remain part of community identity.
Mzee Magogo therefore serves a role extending beyond that of a guide. As an elder familiar with local traditions, he provides a link between the island’s past and present. Lundo’s history cannot be understood only through its lake, mountains, birds or wildlife. It is also contained in memories associated with people and places. The old mango tree illustrates this point. For those familiar with its history, it is more than vegetation; it is a physical reference to an earlier period in the island’s life and to experiences that shaped how the place is remembered.
This form of heritage gives cultural tourism a deeper purpose. A visitor who comes only to admire the lake may leave with photographs, while one who listens to local stories may leave with a stronger understanding of the community’s identity and relationship with its surroundings. Domestic tourism can therefore create opportunities for Tanzanians to discover histories and traditions within their own country that might otherwise remain unfamiliar.
The experience also raises questions about preservation. What happens when elders who carry such knowledge are no longer available to tell it? Cultural heritage can disappear gradually when stories stop being transmitted, historic places lose their meaning or younger generations grow up without understanding why certain traditions matter.
Preserving heritage does not mean accepting every traditional belief without question. It means documenting, understanding and respecting cultural knowledge while ensuring that traditions are presented responsibly and that practices remain consistent with safety, human dignity and conservation.
This approach allows communities to retain their heritage while engaging with changing social realities. People such as Mzee Magogo are important to that process because their knowledge may contain histories unavailable elsewhere.
Local authorities, tourism institutions, researchers, schools and communities can collaborate to document oral histories, traditional stories, significant sites and cultural practices associated with Lundo Island. Young Tanzanians can also participate by interviewing elders, recording stories, studying local history and sharing cultural knowledge responsibly with visitors. Such efforts can turn heritage into a living inheritance rather than something remembered only after it has disappeared.
The visitors from Mbamba Bay did not merely reach an island; they encountered an elder, listened to traditions and experienced a cultural narrative rooted in the place. Such encounters can broaden the meaning of domestic tourism by encouraging curiosity, respect and learning. Lundo Island consequently offers more than scenery. The Wonder Rooster, the old mango tree and Mzee Magogo’s stories form different elements of a wider cultural narrative. For visitors, they can inspire curiosity; for the local community, they represent heritage; and for younger generations, they provide lessons about preserving history.
As domestic tourism expands, destinations such as Lundo have an opportunity to place culture alongside natural attractions. The lake may draw visitors and the island’s landscape may encourage exploration, but stories can give the destination a deeper identity. The gathering beneath the old mango tree was therefore more than a moment of prayer.
It was an encounter between the present and the past and an opportunity to hear a cultural history that cannot be measured only through visitor numbers or economic value. Lundo’s enduring lesson is that heritage exists not only in monuments and historical objects, but also in stories, memories, elders and places. Preserving those elements requires documentation, responsible tourism and intergenerational learning.
For the island, preserving these accounts can strengthen cultural pride while helping visitors appreciate heritage beyond the landscape itself. For the visitors beside Lake Nyasa, the journey became an encounter with memory and tradition. In that sense, one of Lundo’s greatest treasures is a story still being told.

title: Regina Askia-Williams: My 10 Defining Moments from Nigeria to America
content:
Latest Headlines
Regina Askia-Williams: My 10 Defining Moments from Nigeria to America
From the village streams that shaped her childhood and identity to the stages of Nigeria and the clinics of America, the life of Regina Askia-Williams has been a remarkable journey of culture, courage, transformation and resilience, spanning what feels like several lifetimes. In this interview, she recounts the experiences that shaped her, from her university days and pageantry to modelling, memorable acting roles and her iconic years in Nollywood. Ferdinand Ekechukwu brings the excerpts:
1
. MY CHILDHOOD — AT MY GRANDPARENTS’ KNEES
My first ten years were among the most beautiful and foundational years of my life. During the summer, we left the city to stay in my maternal grandmother’s village and my paternal grandparents’ village. We picked fruit, swam in streams, made earthenware pots, attended church, watched Christmas masquerades and listened to folklore and tales by moonlight. We were not silver-spoon children, but we had every comfort. Extended family surrounded us, aunties helped raise us, a driver took us to school, and we even had an Italian cook. From my parents and grandparents, I learnt culture, community and survival. I can sew, sculpt, make earthenware, keep a home and live from the land. Those early experiences gave me identity, values and personhood. Today, I thank God that my mother is still with us at 94.
2. MISS UNIVERSITY OF LAGOS, 1988
Being crowned Miss University of Lagos in 1988 changed the direction of my life. I was studying Biology, but the crown introduced me to a larger public. It opened doors and taught me that visibility comes with responsibility. I began to understand that whatever platform I received should ultimately serve something greater than myself.
3. REPRESENTING NIGERIA INTERNATIONALLY
In 1990, I represented Nigeria at Miss Charm International in Leningrad, Russia, and emerged first runner-up. I also became the first Nigerian to compete at Miss International in Japan, where our traditional costume received outstanding recognition. I was not standing there only as Regina Askia; I was carrying Nigeria—our beauty, culture and dignity—with me.
4. MODELLING AND BECOMING A FAMILIAR FACE
Pageantry opened the way for a successful modelling career. I appeared in print and television campaigns for brands including Visine by Pfizer, Kessingsheen Hair Care and Collectibles. Modelling taught me discipline, confidence and how to communicate without words. Every image had to tell a story.
5. TOKUNBO JOHNSON IN FORTUNES
My acting breakthrough came in 1993 when I played Tokunbo Johnson in the NTA television series ‘Fortunes,’ later known as ‘Mega Fortunes.’ Tokunbo was bold, complicated and unforgettable. The role connected me with audiences across Nigeria and transformed me from a beauty queen and model into a nationally recognized actress.
6. MY NOLLYWOOD YEARS
The 1990s and early 2000s were defining years. I appeared in films including – Most Wanted, Full Moon, Suicide Mission, Vuga, The President’s Daughter and Festival of Fire. We created powerful stories with limited resources but enormous passion. I am proud to have contributed during the formative years of the industry now celebrated worldwide as Nollywood.
7. BEST ACTRESS — AFRO HOLLYWOOD, LONDON
Receiving the Best Actress in Nigeria award from Afro Hollywood London in 2000 was a memorable affirmation of my work. It reminded me that the long hours, demanding roles and personal sacrifices had been seen. It also confirmed that African stories and the artists who told them had value beyond our shores.
8. BEGINNING AGAIN IN AMERICA
This was the most daunting phase of my life. Relocating to the United States required me to begin again. Fame did not exempt me from struggle, hard work or responsibility. I returned to school and embraced nursing from the ground up. It was humbling and demanding, but it taught me that reinvention does not erase who you were—it reveals who you are still capable of becoming. Funny how my first experience of “hard life” was in America…
9. BECOMING A FAMILY NURSE PRACTITIONER
Graduating from Wagner College and becoming a Family Nurse Practitioner was one of my proudest achievements. Success now had a face. It was tangible. In acting, I helped tell people’s stories; in healthcare, I became part of their most vulnerable moments. My advocacy grew through the Campaign for Nursing Excellence in Nigeria, African Health Dialogues, Saturday Online Clinic and the Regina Askia-Williams Foundation.
10. FOUNDING REGINA MEDICAL SERVICES
Founding Regina Medical Services brought the different chapters of my life together—science, service, communication, beauty, wellness and advocacy. Opening our doors in 2023 fulfilled a dream of making quality healthcare more accessible, particularly to underserved communities in New Jersey. My journey has taught me that a woman does not have to be confined to one identity. She can wear the crown, face the camera, raise a family, return to school, care for the sick, build an institution and continue dreaming.

title: Holy Trinity Oak Tree Chapel in Čibukovac, Serbia
content: The Holy Trinity oak chapel in Čibukovac, a small village near Kraljevo, is built inside a pedunculate oak believed to be over 500 years old. It is thought to be the oldest oak in Serbia. The tree stands more than 30 metres tall, with a trunk circumference of about 8 metres and a diameter of roughly two and a half metres, wide enough that villager Mihailo Erotijević, with the help of Father Radojko and others, was able to hollow out its trunk and turn it into a small working chapel. Since the feast of the Holy Trinity is the village's main Slava (a custom in the Serbian Orthodox tradition), the chapel took that dedication naturally. The interior was coated with wax to help preserve it, and small niches hold icons of the Holy Trinity, the Theotokos (Mother of God), the Great Martyr George the Victorious, St. Basil of Ostrog, the Crucifixion, and St. Paraskeva (Petka), a saint especially beloved across the Balkans. Villagers still gather there for major feast days in the Serbian Orthodox Calendar, and some visit alone simply to pray. There is also a local detail that adds to its mystery and why it is special. Before the tree became a chapel, it was frequently struck by lightning, something residents see as part of its passage from an ordinary ancient oak into a site of devotion. The Holy Trinity Oak Tree Chapel a striking, living echo of zapis meaning "inscription", an old Slavic traditions of venerating sacred trees across Serbian villages.

title: Ganjasar Monastery reflects legacy of Albanian Church — chairman
content:
AGHDARA, Azerbaijan, September 21. The Ganjasar Monastery is part of the heritage of the Albanian Church, Robert Mobili, chairman of the Albanian-Udi religious community, told reporters during a visit to the Ganjasar monastery complex, Trend's Karabakh bureau reports.
He noted that members of the community recited prayers in Ganjasar and honored the memory of the martyrs.
“Today is the Nativity of the Most Holy Mother of God. Yesterday was State Sovereignty Day, and today is World Peace Day. It is especially important for us to visit the Ganjasar monastery complex on such significant days,” said R. Mobili.
According to him, the Ganjasar monastery complex is one of the most important examples of the Christian heritage of Caucasian Albania.
“This is our first visit to Ganjasar. We have visited many churches in the liberated territories, prayed, and lit candles. The Ganjasar Monastery is an important example of the surviving Albanian ecclesiastical heritage of Caucasian Albania,” noted the community chairman.
Mobili said that the ancient Christian churches in Azerbaijan are part of the heritage of the Albanian Church.
“The legacy of the ancient Albanian churches that exist today in Azerbaijan is the legacy of the independent Apostolic Albanian Autocephalous Church. It is a very rich legacy. These churches have no connection whatsoever to the Armenian Church,” he emphasized.
The community chairman said that after Christianity was adopted as the state religion in Caucasian Albania, many churches were built in the region.
According to him, the cessation of the Albanian Church’s activities in 1836 and its subordination to the Armenian Church had a serious impact on the Albanian Christian heritage.
“The decree-statute of March 11, 1836, put an end to the activities of the Albanian Church. The center of the Albanian Church was located in Ganja. After that, the heritage of the Albanian Church was Armenianized. Part of the Albanian community left for Georgia, including the Udis. Some converted to Islam. “We, the Udis living in Gabala, have preserved our native heritage,” Mobili said.
He noted that the opportunity to visit Christian churches in the region following the liberation of Karabakh from occupation is a significant event for the Alban-Udi community.
“Today, the doors of the churches are open, and services are being held there. We can pray in our native churches. This is a great blessing bestowed upon us by God,” the community chairman said.
Mobili also emphasized that the sphere of influence of the Albanian Church is not limited to the current territory of Azerbaijan. He cited the ancient churches in Eastern and Western Zangazur, including the Tatev Monastery, as well as those in the Derbent region, as part of the historical heritage of the Albanian Church.
The community chairman also drew attention to the existence of the Albanian alphabet and religious texts in the Albanian language.
“Caucasian Albania had its own centers of scholarship. Religious books were translated into Albanian. In this regard, ancient sources have also been preserved at the Monastery of St. Catherine on Mount Sinai,” R. Mobili said.
He noted that the ancient church located in the village of Sheki Kish is also an example of Albanian Christian heritage.
R. Mobili also noted that depictions of crosses and other religious symbols in Azerbaijan are part of the heritage of the Albanian Church.
“At a UNESCO event held in Geneva in 2010, we expressed our position regarding the affiliation of cross-shaped elements and symbols found in Azerbaijan to the Albanian Church,” he added.
The community leader emphasized that the atmosphere of tolerance prevailing in Azerbaijan allows the Alban-Udi community to preserve its religious heritage.
“One of the most heartwarming moments for us is the tremendous support we receive in Azerbaijan, where the overwhelming majority of the population is Muslim. The tolerance of the Azerbaijani people and the atmosphere in the country allow us to attend our own churches. This is our heritage,” Mobili said.

title: Yosemite National Park highlights Indigenous arrowhead crafting
content:
There is a simple reason why Indigenous arrowhead crafting has remained largely the same for thousands of years—if something works, it works. The earliest examples of these lethal tools date back around 74,000 years ago to Stone Age Ethiopia, but the skill is still practiced today by trained artisans around the world. Yet, the process isn’t only a matter of breaking rocks into sharp-edged projectiles.. As Yosemite National Park officials recently highlighted, there is more to this very specific technique called knapping.
Proper knapping largely hinges on choosing the correct stones. These usually include chert, flint, and most notably obsidian due to their surgically sharp fracture lines. Artisans then slowly and purposely break off flakes of rocks to shape them into not only aerodynamic arrowheads, but knives, scrapers, and spear points.
Interestingly, obsidian isn’t native to the Yosemite, yet the region’s Indigenous communities have prized the material for generations. The volcanic glass was introduced into the area via ancient trade routes that crossed over the Eastern Sierra’s Mono Lake in present-day eastern California near the Nevada border. Tribes separated by hundreds of miles relied on these and similar exchange networks to swap tool materials for animal skins, medicinal plants, as well as nutritious pine nuts and acorns.
Yosemite’s earliest Indigenous communities initially knapped obsidian into larger points for spears and spear throwers known as atlatls. As hunting technology evolved over hundreds of years towards a reliance on bows and arrows, the obsidian points shrank in size to make them more aerodynamic.
The national park celebrates the ancient tradition of knapping at its annual Knap-In event, which includes demonstrations, workshops, and other hands-on opportunities. While this year’s Yosemite Knap-In took place in August, numerous others are held across the United States throughout the year.

title: HYPREP: Ogoni Cleanup Enters New Phase as Women’s Participation Rises to 45%
content:
Latest Headlines
HYPREP: Ogoni Cleanup Enters New Phase as Women’s Participation Rises to 45%
• Mangrove restoration, health projects advance
Blessing Ibunge in Port Harcourt
The Hydrocarbon Pollution Rehabilitation Project (HYPREP) has said women’s participation in the Ogoni cleanup programme has risen from five per cent in 2023 to 45 per cent, as the federal government intensifies efforts to make the project more inclusive and sustainable.
HYPREP Project Coordinator, Prof. Nenibarini Zabbey, disclosed this on Wednesday in Port Harcourt, Rivers State, during the 2026 third quarterly meeting of key regulators and asset owners involved in the Ogoni cleanup.
Zabbey said the project was being implemented through a human-centred and multi-stakeholder approach designed to ensure that the environmental restoration programme delivers lasting benefits to the people and ecosystem of Ogoniland.
“We are implementing the recommendations of the UNEP report on the environmental assessment of Ogoniland and, in doing that, we have decided to adopt a multi-stakeholder and human-centric approach,” he said.
According to him, regular meetings with asset owners, regulators, civil society organisations and other stakeholders were critical to sustaining collaboration, reviewing progress and addressing challenges affecting the cleanup.
He said the quarterly meeting was particularly significant as it coincided with activities marking the 10th anniversary of the Ogoni cleanup.
Zabbey said HYPREP had recorded significant progress in mangrove restoration, urging stakeholders to support the protection of the Ogoni mangrove wetland, which has been designated a Ramsar site of international importance.
He also called for greater investment in ecotourism, saying it would help conserve Ogoni’s biodiversity while creating economic opportunities for residents.
On healthcare, the project coordinator said HYPREP had gone beyond the recommendations of the United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP) by implementing a series of health interventions across Ogoni.
He said four health facilities had been strengthened with modern medical equipment and solar power systems, while five fully equipped ambulances had been provided to health facilities to improve emergency and referral services.
“Those that have visited the Onne Health Centre recently will attest to the fact that since we installed our solar system in February this year, light has not blinked in that facility,” Zabbey said.
He added that HYPREP had completed construction of the 43-bed cottage hospital at Buwa and was awaiting the posting of personnel by the Rivers State Government to commence operations.
Zabbey further disclosed that the Ogoni Specialist Hospital was about 80 per cent complete, with an oncology unit expected to provide cancer screening and treatment.
He said the hospital would be equipped with a state-of-the-art MRI machine, adding that HYPREP had inspected the equipment in Germany.
“We are bringing the latest MRI, and what that means is that it will be the second latest MRI in this country,” he said.
The coordinator also disclosed that HYPREP had commissioned the World Health Organisation’s International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC) to conduct a three-year comprehensive health study of the Ogoni people.
He said the study had entered its second year, with blood sample collection already underway.
“This is not just for Ogoni. HYPREP is doing the cleanup in Ogoni to develop a sustainable template that will be applicable to other impacted communities in Nigeria,” he said.
On challenges, Zabbey identified flooding and communal land disputes as major obstacles to the remediation programme.
He explained that heavy rainfall had flooded some remediation sites, particularly those located around floodplains, forcing work to stop temporarily.
“When they are flooded, remediation activities will have to stop. You cannot, under that condition, excavate the soil and treat it. You cannot, under that condition, install your bioburging devices,” he said.
He, however, assured that HYPREP would fast-track remediation activities after the rainy season to recover lost time.
On communal disputes, Zabbey said the agency had adopted mediation and alternative dispute resolution rather than force, while training community leaders and members of its conflict-resolution structures in dispute management.
He said the agency had also made progress in preventing repollution linked to illegal artisanal refining and oil theft by engaging former artisanal refiners in its programmes.
According to him, hundreds of former artisanal refiners are currently being trained in commercial diving and underwater welding to equip them with skills for employment in the oil and gas and maritime sectors.
Zabbey said HYPREP was also training 300 persons living with special needs in five skill areas selected by them.
He stressed that the project was determined not to leave vulnerable groups behind.
The HYPREP coordinator also urged asset owners, regulators and other stakeholders to remain committed to collaboration, saying the success of the Ogoni cleanup was ultimately in the public interest.
Coordinator of the Centre for Environment, Human Rights and Development (CEHRD), Dr Nabie Nubari commended HYPREP for adopting a community-centred approach.
Nubari said civil society organisations were motivated to support the cleanup because of HYPREP’s engagement with communities.
“If HYPREP is doing this massive cleanup, and there is an act of sabotage and there is repollution while cleanup is ongoing, we find it like mopping the floor while the tap is on,” he said.
He commended HYPREP for the reported reduction in repollution and pledged CEHRD’s continued support for the project.
“We will continue to support HYPREP in any way possible, and we encourage that HYPREP, please keep it up with a community-centred approach,” Nubari said.

title: Martha's Rule rolled out at every A&E department in England
content:
Martha's Rule rolled out at every A&E department in England
- Published
The NHS is expanding Martha's Rule to all hospital emergency departments in England to help patients and families challenge staff and seek a rapid review about their care if they want.
It is named after Martha Mills, who died aged 13 in 2021 after developing blood poisoning, or sepsis. Her family's concerns were not listened to, which later prompted her parents, Merope and Paul, to change that culture by creating the rule.
Patients, loved ones and staff in A&E units will be able to call a dedicated phone number to trigger an urgent review if a patient's condition is deteriorating and they are concerned this is not being listened to.
The nationwide expansion should be complete by March 2028, after a trial at seven trusts. It is already being rolled out in all inpatient wards.
Scotland is beginning to use Martha's Rule and Northern Ireland is considering using it, while Wales has a similar scheme called Call4Concern.
Martha's story
In 2022 a coroner ruled, external Martha would probably have survived if she had been transferred earlier to intensive care and given appropriate treatment.
She was in King's College Hospital in London after a cycling accident on a family holiday where she fell heavily onto the handlebars after skidding on some sand.
It left her with serious injuries to her pancreas.
After a few weeks, she developed an infection and then signs of sepsis - when the body's response to an infection is overwhelming and ends up injuring its own tissues and organs - but this was not managed properly.
Prof Aidan Fowler, national director of patient safety at NHS England, said the expansion of Martha's Rule would give families and NHS staff "a critical new lifeline" to help improve care and save more lives.
Prof Fowler told the BBC that a Martha's Rule call would mean a patient receives an "appropriate response", for example, a senior nurse or member of the critical care outreach team could conduct a review of the case.
Staff can themselves also ask for a review from a different team if they are concerned the appropriate action is not being taken.
During an eight-month pilot of the scheme at seven emergency departments, 69 calls were made to dedicated Martha's Rule phone numbers, including some calls relating to acute deterioration following an urgent clinical review. In some cases, it led to a patient having immediate surgery or being transferred to intensive care.
Prof Fowler told the BBC's Today programme that, while these numbers might seem relatively small, the decision to roll out Martha's Rule further "is on a background of very, very extensive experience in other settings".
This included in-patient wards, where Prof Fowler said his teams had received "nearly 20,000 calls"; three quarters of which came from families.
Prof Fowler said: "Early testing has shown that Martha's Rule can work well in busy A&Es and builds on the evidence from our adult and children's wards, where thousands of calls have been made by patients, families and staff to date, with many leading to changes in treatment and potentially life-saving interventions."
Questioned whether busy A&E staff might struggle with a sudden influx of calls, Prof Fowler told the BBC this had not played out in the recent tests.
"There was a concern we would receive an overwhelming number of calls, and that would be a distraction and actually divert staff from the important work they're doing," he said.
"But that hasn't been the case, actually people have used it very sensibly," he added. "We've tested it through winter and across this busy summer and therefore I am not concerned that when we roll this out we are going to be overwhelmed with calls."
Health minister Baroness Merron said the initiative was part of "wider efforts to put patient safety at the heart of the NHS."
Actor Jason Watkins, whose two-and-a-half-year-old daughter Maude died from sepsis in 2011, praised the rollout, saying Martha's rule "is making a difference on the wards".
"It enables a parent to have a voice and if there is an issue, that is addressed," he told BBC Breakfast, and urged parents: "if you're at all worried when you go into A&E, ask for a second opinion."
Watkins said the rollout of Martha's law could benefit medical professionals too, explaining: "Those extremely dedicated medical practitioners, nurses, doctors and consultants, it gives them a pause and a thought 'am I doing everything I can to assess this child accurately?'".
The phased rollout in England will be completed by March 2028.
Patients and their families can check with their local hospital or NHS trust where Martha's Rule is available by visiting the trust's website or asking hospital staff.
