title: Jonah: An uncomplicated man surrounded by highly complicated situations
content:
Vea Mafile’o isn’t particularly interested in rugby and jokes that before the advent of AI it would take her a whole afternoon to write an email.
Yet the 44-year-old film director has just completed the most arduous and lucrative assignment of her career – enapsulating the complex life story of the rugby star and Tongan legend, Jonah Lomu.
On Thursday, Lomu, a new documentary about the All Blacks winger, is being released nationwide. UK production company Sylver Entertainment made Lomu, having previously produced documentaries about US tennis legend John McEnroe and British racing driver Damon Hill.
Mafile’o laughs: “I’m not a great talker and a worse writer, one of those people who has to Google-check spelling and even then Google doesn’t recognise the words. I even did that once trying to spell ‘because’.
“I’m artistic and dyslexic. I love drawing, creating, filming, letting things speak for themselves. If I want to tell you something, I’m not going to talk it or write it. I’m going to talk in pictures and say, ‘Look, here it is’.”
For co-director and lifelong rugby fan Irishman Gavin Fitzgerald the project was an obvious fit. Mafile’o arrived later, with trepidation.
“When I say I’m not a rugby fan, I wouldn’t say in my spare time, ‘hey let’s go to a rugby game’, but I do feel some loyalty to it,” she explained.
”My father, Saia Mafile’o, was a First XV coach. He went to school with Amanaki Palavi, who coached Jonah at Wesley College. Later Tonga College played Wesley. I have a little brother who just scored a contract in France, so it has always been in my environment.
“If you’re making stories about people, you need the right people in place. Gavin was encyclopaedic on rugby detail; however, Sylver probably realised that culturally and around Jonah’s family, it would be easier if someone knew all the nuances.
“There have been all kinds of different films made about Jonah that mostly focused on just his rugby and a sanitised narrative of that. I feel like this was the opportunity to share something different about the man.”
Lomu differs from other films about Jonah because his Tongan family is much more present than in previous efforts. Jonah’s brother John Lomu supplied 160 VHS tapes of privately captured family footage, much of it never seen before.
“It was really fascinating because at the time, late 80s, early 90s, it was very rare for there to be a camera around,” Mafile’o said.
“The footage covers a wide scope of people and places, a snapshot of Tongan migration life growing up in South Auckland. We’re very lucky to have the opening of Lotofale’ia, the church he went to. The big Wesleyan church, Tuingapapai, is also there, with a whole lot of rugby games and private, intimate moments. I would love to transcode all the tapes and return them to the family in a more compact form, but that’s another time and budget process.”
More crucially, his mother, Hepi, is interviewed in Tongan. This has never happened before.
In 2019, Mafile’o made a critically acclaimed film, For My Father’s Kingdom, that debuted at the Berlin Film Festival. The film about her father Saia raises thorny questions about the relationship between money and the church in Tongan culture and addresses tensions within Mafile’o’s family, including Saia’s marriage. They attend a Misinale, an annual church festival and fundraising event in Tonga, an experience that almost resembles an open catharsis.
Mafile’o believes Lomu was a similar experience for members of Lomu’s family.
“Everything that I went through with putting my own family on the line, maybe that’s something that they see and understand: I’m not about to throw people under the bus,” Mafile’o said.
“From the first day that I met Hepi to more recent trips to their house, there has been this energy shift; the confidence has grown, she smiles because at first she was weary and pretty dam scary,” she quipped.
The movie does not feature Jonah’s wife Nadine or his two sons; an offer was made for them to be involved, but declined.
On July 29, a historic, free public premiere of the film was held at the Teufaiva Rugby Stadium in Tonga, which Hepi attended. A massive crowd of over 8,000 attended, the first time a major production company has allowed such an event in the Pacific Islands.
Mafile’o believes the event has been “magic” for the Lomu family, “unlocking doors,” reopening old connections and developing new ones. She hopes the story will inspire a new generation. Lomu was a trailblazer for superstar Tongan athletes like Jason Taumalolo and Daniel Tupou.
And though reluctant to admit it, Mafile’o is a trailblazer herself. She was raised on a dairy farm in Hamilton before moving to Auckland. Her first serious job was as a scuba diver before she undertook a Bachelor of Visual Arts at the University of Auckland, graduating in 2006. Her paintings have explored natural and man-made environmental issues in Tonga. An early success was the Digital Kava Circles video installation series featuring interviews she conducted in Tonga in 2006 following the death of King Tāufaʻāhau Tupou IV.
Fast forward a decade and with her sister, Emily, she founded Taro Patch Creative, a Pacific-led creative agency, studio, and community trust in Papatoetoe, Auckland. According to its website, it “functions as a safe, culturally grounded space for Māori and Moana Pasifika artists, filmmakers, and storytellers to connect, run creative workshops, host events, and preserve cultural identity.”
For My Father’s Kingdom (co-directed by her husband Jeremiah Tauamiti) came from the studio, as did Lea Tupu’anga/Mother Tongue, which is about Katherine, a young speech therapist of Tongan and European heritage who lied about her Tongan language skills to work with Siaosi – an elderly Tongan patient with aphasia who lost his ability to speak English. It was chosen from 17,000 submissions to play at the 2024 Sundance Film Festival.
In 2021, Mafile’o etched her name in history as the first Pacific female director of a prime-time TV drama in New Zealand with The Panthers. Set in Auckland in 1974, The Panthers focuses on how a group of Polynesian students and young people of the street, led by Tongan student Will ‘Ilolahia, formed a revolutionary movement called the Polynesian Panthers, drawing inspiration from the American Black Panther Party. The mini-series is set against the backdrop of racial tensions between European and Pasifika New Zealanders during the dawn raids on overstayers under Prime Minister Sir Robert Muldoon.
For one deeply rooted in Tongan culture and storytelling, what was the most interesting thing Mafile’o learned about Jonah Lomu?
“Jonah was a very uncomplicated person, but almost everyone and every environment around him was highly complicated,” Mafile’o responded.
“He always had a drive and a bigger purpose, and I think that’s something people just don’t really understand: that he did the mahi, he did the work, he’s just not naturally talented, he actually was so dedicated, so young.
“When the All Blacks lost the Rugby World Cup semi-final to France in 1999, Jonah stayed out on the field an hour after every player had left, signing autographs. There’s a great humility in that. Or in Tonga we would call that living by one of the four main pillars of Fā Kavei Koula.”

title: Sale of 100-year-old Vancouver church reflects hard choice facing many congregations
content:
Sale of 100-year-old Vancouver church reflects hard choice facing many congregations
Many are facing a difficult decision: Continue despite waning attendance or close and sell their place of worship to a more prosperous congregation or to a property developer?
On a warm July day outside a church at 12th Avenue and Trimble in Vancouver, a small crowd gathered for a brief ceremony that was bittersweet for some but exciting and promising for others.
In the early afternoon, Rev. Richard Watson, representing West Point Grey Presbyterian Church, handed a symbolic cardboard cutout key to Pastor Joseph Concepcion of the Pentecostal Missionary Church of Christ (4th Watch) and, with it, ownership of the 100-year-old landmark.
It was a day of celebration as children paraded with red-and-yellow balloons while parishioners crowded around, and photographers and videographers captured the moment.
Now a minister at Kerrisdale Presbyterian Church, Watson prayed the new parishioners would continue ministry there for another 100 years.
The three-lot prime location in affluent Point Grey had just sold for $6.4 million, even though a year earlier a developer offered $7.5 million and, two years ago, it was listed at $10 million.
Ian Rokeby, chair of the committee overseeing Presbyterian real estate in the Lower Mainland, said after initial expectations that the church would be demolished and redeveloped, he is glad it is being passed to another congregation — one that is growing.
“The number of worship spaces in the Lower Mainland is diminishing every year, so we were anxious,” Rokeby said. “One of our priorities is to preserve houses of worship.”
When it closed three years ago, West Point Grey Presbyterian had only 19 people attending. With dwindling attendance, the 200-seat church couldn’t afford a full-time minister or keep up maintenance of the aging building.
Many mainline congregations are facing the same difficult choice — continue despite waning attendance or close and sell to a more prosperous congregation or property developer.
“(There are) a handful of people who are doing way too much, and so they actually aren’t doing any outreach in the community, which is one of the primary objectives of the church,” said Rokeby.
It is dispiriting when all a congregation can manage to deal with is broken plumbing, he said.
Many congregations are relying more on rent revenue to cover the costs of building maintenance, pay the pastor, minister or priest, and finance community outreach.
When Jeff Rock, coordinating minister at Canadian Memorial United Church in Vancouver, was ordained 15 years ago it wasn’t unusual for 90 per cent of a congregation’s income to come from tithes or offerings.
Now, he said, that number has dropped to 50 per cent, with the other half coming from rent.
In Vancouver’s competitive land market, churches often rent space to daycares, community events, concerts and support groups.
“I get a request for space usage almost every day. People are just desperately looking,” he said. “A lot of spiritual communities have found themselves becoming, really, rental agencies.”
According to Statistics Canada, religious demographics in B.C. have changed over the decades. Between 2011 and 2021, the proportion of people identifying with mainline Christian denominations has decreased, with Anglicans down 42.9 per cent, United Church members down 49 per cent ands Presbyterians down 40 per cent, since 2011.
Anglicans in that decade dropped to 2.8 per cent of the B.C. population from 4.9 per cent, United members dropped to 2.6 per cent from 5.1 per cent, and Presbyterians dropped to 0.6 per cent from one per cent.
Over that period, the proportion of the B.C. population identifying as “non-religious” or secular grew from 44.1 per cent to 52.1 per cent.
Other denominations are offsetting the decline.
For example, the proportion of people identifying as Sikh increased 25.5 per cent, the number sayibg they were Muslim was up 44.4 per cent, and the number of Hindus was up 54.5 per cent respectively.
The Pentecostal Missionary Church of Christ (4th Watch) in Vancouver has grown, despite those identifying as Pentecostal or other charismatic denominations also dropping 42.9 per cent since 2011.
Rock said that over the past decade places of worship have felt the same financial squeeze as many households and residents.
Attendance levels drop and people who still attend church are not able to donate as much as before, he said.
“I’m lucky that I’m in a spiritual community that’s vibrant and is thriving. But I know many of my neighbours are feeling that attrition rate more and more.”
Ownership out of reach
When Watson handed over the key of the Presbyterian church, one door closed while another opened for another congregation. But the prospect of church ownership is out of reach for many religious groups.
Growing congregations look, often for years, to purchase places of worship. Many are priced out of the market entirely. With few churches available, their capacity to grow and practise their faith hinges on whether congregations selling their churches view the property as financial assets or as community institutions.
Growing congregations often don’t have the capital to buy, and they are purchasing from a limited supply of land that is also sought after by other congregations and property developers.
Rokeby said many religious communities have “dreams” of owning a place to worship, but “no cash.”
Devin Roberts, the church realtor representing the Pentecostal Missionary Church of Christ, compares those congregations that are growing to the average millennial unable to break into the housing market. If they can’t afford to buy, their only option is to rent. But renting comes with its own challenges.
Compared to Vancouver, Surrey and Maple Ridge, where zoning is more flexible, Roberts said Burnaby, the Tri-Cities, Pitt Meadows, Mission and White Rock have stricter regulations that limit where congregations can gather in commercial areas.
“A big fat ‘no’ to anything other than an actual church building,” Roberts said.
The Pentecostal Missionary Church of Christ had not had a permanent home since it was established in Vancouver nearly 26 years ago. Members gathered in hotels, industrial and commercial buildings, and even in family homes.
For eight years, Pastor Miziel Rivera searched for a permanent place for her congregation in New Westminster, Richmond and Surrey. When they did find a potential location in Surrey, another congregation outbid them by $1 million.
When they gathered Sundays at a hotel, a volunteer had to arrive at 6 a.m. to set up chairs, musical instruments and the pulpit. For weekday services, when the hotel wasn’t available, congregants would gather in restaurants or parishioners’ homes.
Founded in the Philippines in 1977, the Pentecostal Missionary Church of Christ has grown steadily in Vancouver since the 1990s. As more people joined and the congregation grew from 80 to 100, hotel space became inadequate.
At the first meeting after the Pentecostal Missionary Church of Christ purchased the church, everyone was in tears, Rivera said.
“We’ve been negotiating, and it was a back and forth. I’m just grateful to West Point Presbyterian Church. (They were) very patient with us,” Rivera said.
However, without the financial support of the global Pentecostal Missionary Church of Christ denomination they are a part of, Rivera said they wouldn’t have been able to purchase the church.
Of the more than 30 congregations that Philippines-based Pentecostal Missionary Church of Christ has across Canada and the Caribbean, only three own their places of worship, in Edmonton, Toronto and, now, Vancouver. It was hardest to find a church in Vancouver, said Concepcion, who serves as the church’s Canada district coordinator.
It’s difficult for congregations to host events, programs and fellowship without a space of their own, he said. “I believe that these programs in the church help believers to mature and grow and to be connected.”
Unlocking revenue to continue
While the Point Grey church sale represents a continuity of faith, other church sales represent a combination of faith and property development.
Acquiring and consolidating lots for a traditional land assembly is costly and difficult for developers. Collaborating with a church is relatively simple and a more attractive form of property development, according to Tim Law, a lawyer at Lawson Lundell in Vancouver.
Law, himself a regular churchgoer, said property development, whether for social or market housing, is a way for congregations to “unlock” revenue and continue.
Lawson Lundell posted in February 2026 about the opportunity congregations have to redevelop their property for major projects. They said congregations with old or aging churches can build new developments to help pay for new facilities and infrastructure.
Marcela Corzo, the founder of LinkQuest Development, said religious institutions in Vancouver are sitting on more than $3.4 billion in asset value, giving congregations a unique opportunity to continue their worship and mission.
The common denominator for congregations deciding to redevelop their land is the age of their churches, she said. “They have 100-plus years of lifespan, and they are coming to an era when they need to spend a lot of money in capital expenditures. More than 50 per cent (of places of worship) are facing very expensive capital expenditures.”
Tim Dickau, director of the non-profit Citygate Vancouver and former pastor of Grandview church, said congregations aren’t just developing property to keep their lights on.
Citygate works with a community network to support social programs, including by helping churches better utilize their properties to engage in neighbourhoods. For many congregations, Dickau said, it’s part of a larger mission to support community.
Rock said redevelopment projects represent a balancing act between competing interests. For example, in a space that might have housed an education wing or gym, a congregation might choose to partner with a developer to prioritize condos or commercial space instead.
For example, Oakridge United Church, which redeveloped in 2018 to include 49 residential units and a coffee shop, now has fewer rental spaces than before, said Rock.
“I think most churches that do some kind of a redevelopment are downsizing their space rather than creating more community spaces for rent,” he said.
One municipality encouraging property development at places of worship is Burnaby. It allows up to six storeys of housing if it’s for uses such as dormitories, supportive and transitional housing, and non-market housing. If congregations or property developers want to build higher than six storeys and include market-rate housing on the property, they need approval from council.
“They really see churches as a low-density use with kind of underused land,” said Roberts. “They really see housing as a big issue. They don’t see churches as a big issue.”
Carl Isaak, city liaison to the Burnaby Housing Authority, said the city is prepared to allow even more housing to be built on place-of-worship property if community amenities are built with it. Isaak said the density of the residential housing is “essentially unlimited” provided churches and developers include community benefits and amenities reflective of the development potential.
One door closed, another opened
In Point Grey, the Presbyterian church tried for more than two years to sell. When the property was listed at $10 million near the peak of the booming real estate market, there were discussions about developing housing while retaining a place of worship on the property.
As the property market cooled, they eventually received an offer for $7.5 million from a developer. Zoning allowed for up to six dwellings in a small apartment building, or eight rental homes. But if they agreed to the sale, the church would have to take on risk for rezoning of the property, Rokeby said.
Eager for a clean sale, the church approached Leonardo Di Francesco and Rav Rampuri, two church realtors with more than 30 years experience. The two helped find the Pentecostal Missionary Church of Christ. They say they have sold nearly 100 churches to Christians, Sikhs, Muslims and others, sales that reflect shifting religious demographics and immigrant trends of the past three decades.
But it’s difficult for local congregations to break into a market with such limited supply, they say. When a church does become available, many don’t have enough capital to purchase, or can’t get financing.
Francesco said banks are hesitant to give loans to religious institutions. “If they foreclose on a church, it will be all over the newspaper.”
It leaves congregations like Pentecostal Missionary Church of Christ, which exist within large international groups, and property developers as the only customer base for the region’s expensive places of worship.
For six months, the two groups negotiated before settling on $6.4 million, which was $3.6 million less than the original listing price.
Rokeby said they accepted the offer for several reasons: the cooling property market, fatigue from the length of the sale, and the opportunity to have their church pass to another congregation.
Buying a church was the conclusion of a long-held dream, says Wilma Calica, a member of the Pentecostal Missionary Church of Christ and one of those at July’s key-exchange ceremony.
There are “no words” to describe how she feels, she said, adding that congregants are “overwhelmed” with happiness.
After the key exchange, and before entering the church sanctuary, Concepcion prayed with the congregation.
He prayed for church communities to grow, for the few to become many: “This is not material treasure. This is not money. These are people … I pray that this place will be filled with rare, beautiful — not material things, not beautiful clothes — (but) beautiful people.”
On Sept. 27, The Pentecostal Missionary Church of Christ in Vancouver will celebrate 26 years.
It will also be the first time they celebrate an anniversary in their new church. The first time in a place of their own.
Marc Guido Bolen is a 2026 recipient of the Langara College Read-Mercer Journalism Fellowship. This feature was produced through the fellowship.

title: BROOKE ROLLINS, MONICA CROWLEY: America’s family farms have kept us strong for 250 years
content:
Half a century before America declared independence, John Lester broke soil on a 150-acre plot of land in East Hampton, New York. Little did he know, the next 300 years would see nine generations of his direct descendants cultivate that land. As our young nation took root and endured hardship, so did Round Swamp Farm. Today, Carolyn Lester Snyder carries on the family tradition by growing and selling produce on the property, with the help of her husband, children and grandchildren. They are a living, breathing, working testament to the American Dream and to America’s long legacy of family farming.
This summer, the Trump administration is honoring that glorious inheritance by launching the American Family Farm Legacy 250 Program. In partnership with the National Association of State Departments of Agriculture, the U.S. Department of Agriculture is building on proud traditions established during America’s bicentennial and elevating them into a unified national commitment.
A long chain of uninterrupted family ownership is no small feat. That’s why this program publicly recognizes the inspirational perseverance of multigenerational farm families, from 100-year legacies to the extraordinary handful of patriots who have stewarded their land for 250 years or more.
TRUMP ADMINISTRATION EXPANDS 'PRODUCT OF USA' LABEL AS PUSH FOR AMERICAN-RAISED BEEF GROWS
From the Eastern Shore of Maryland to the wooded hills of western Massachusetts, from the South Fork of Long Island to the country roads of rural North Carolina, these farms remind us just how much rural America matters to all of America. Critically, they have sustained us with the food we eat and the clothes on our backs. But even more importantly, they have been the wellspring of our most cherished values and time-honored traditions.
In times of tranquility and times of crisis, these men and women stand in the gap, reaffirming their commitment to the American way of life. To faith and family. To patriotism and civic responsibility. To standing where their mothers and fathers stood. And to remaining steadfast in hope for what’s on the horizon.
STEVE MOORE: POLITICIANS ARE BLAMING THE WRONG VILLAIN FOR AMERICA’S RISING FOOD PRICES
When the first generations of these family farmers planted the seeds of liberty, they laid the foundation for an unrivaled American agricultural might that has only grown stronger across each generation. During droughts and depression, through war and peace, their forebears kept the plows turning, the tractors running and our rich American soil fertile for freedom.
These powerful legacies remind each of us that we are part of a larger story — a story we did not originally author and the ending of which we will not see. Our duty is to honor the magnificent inheritance we’ve been gifted by fighting for the prosperity of American agriculture with every fiber of our being. This is at the heart of the Farmers First agenda we are carrying out across the Trump administration. Empowered by President Donald Trump’s leadership, we are putting our farmers, ranchers and rural communities back at the center of policymaking.
REP ROGER WILLIAMS: 250 YEARS OF HARD WORK PAYS OFF FOR MAIN STREET BUSINESSES
While the American Family Farm Legacy 250 Program is primarily meant to put a spotlight on farms with centuries of continuous operation, it also celebrates the future of American agriculture and the next generation of farmers who dare to take up the noble mantle of stewardship.
After all, America’s success is bound up in theirs. This is what Thomas Jefferson meant when he wrote in 1785, "Cultivators of the earth are the most valuable citizens. They are the most vigorous, the most independent, the most virtuous, and they are tied to their country and wedded to its liberty and interests by the most lasting bands."

The family farms honored by the American Family Farm Legacy 250 Program are bound more closely to our nation than any others. As we continue celebrating America’s 250th birthday, it is only fitting that we salute the families whose grit, sacrifice and stewardship have fed our nation, strengthened our communities and preserved our agricultural heritage across generations.

Five of those families joined us on the National Mall this summer, and we are eager to visit more in person in the coming months. President Trump has made restoring pride in America’s history a national priority, and together, we are ensuring our farmers receive the recognition and support that they deserve.

title: Sustainability, Vol. 18, Pages 9102: African American Family Fishing as Food Provision, Communal Learning, Wellness, and Social-Sustainability Exploration
content: This narrative literature review examines African American family fishing as a historically grounded practice of food provision, cultural continuity, place-based learning, and environmental stewardship, and considers its conceptual relationship to the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). The review synthesizes an analytical corpus of 41 works spanning history, fishing participation, food insecurity, food sovereignty, foodways, place attachment, environmental education, and social-ecological systems. The literature indicates that Black fishing cannot be understood as recreation alone; historically and contemporarily, it has connected food acquisition, family interaction, livelihood, cultural memory, and community identity. These functions are conceptually aligned with SDGs 2, 3, and 10 through plausible pathways involving culturally meaningful food access, family-centered outdoor activity, and attention to racial disparities in food security, environmental access, and institutional representation. Family fishing may also provide a place-based learning context relevant to SDG 4, while responsible harvesting, reduced waste, and ecological literacy may contribute to SDG 12. Repeated engagement with local waters may cultivate belonging and stewardship; freshwater relationships are most directly relevant to SDG 6, whereas coastal, estuarine, and marine contexts may contribute to SDG 14. These are interpretive alignments, not measured SDG outcomes. The review concludes that family-centered pilot initiatives may productively integrate cultural history, ecological education, food skills, mentorship, and community leadership, subject to feasibility testing and empirical evaluation. Contemporary family-level research is needed to examine harvest, food sharing, learning, health, access, and stewardship across generations.

title: Gov't prioritizes human-centered AI principle for inclusivity
content:
"AI is a tool. Who operates it? Humans do. So we need to look at it from the human-centered AI perspective, with humans serving as the operators who use it," Triyanto said during a discussion held by OpenAI here on Thursday.
To uphold this principle, the ministry pursues an approach of "AI for all, for many, and for few", especially in AI-specific digital talent literacy activities.
Through this approach, the ministry expressed hopes that every AI digital talent in Indonesia can produce innovations and solutions that remain human-centered.
According to him, the AI development principle is also reflected in every step taken by the ministry and other ministries responsible for AI development.
He cited the ministry's initiative in issuing a joint decree with seven ministries focused on ensuring young people can use AI responsibly without losing their critical thinking skills as the nation's future generation.
The joint decree refers to guidelines on the use of digital technology and AI in education.
Under the guidelines, students from primary to secondary school levels are not allowed to use instant AI services to directly answer school assignments.
However, AI use remains permitted if the technology is specifically designed for educational needs and guided learning purposes.
Another example is Government Regulation Number 17 of 2025 on Electronic System Governance for Child Protection in Digital Spaces (PP TUNAS).
The regulation prioritizes children's safety, including when accessing AI services provided by electronic system operators.
The government is also translating this principle into concrete programs so AI can be introduced even to regions with limited digital infrastructure access.
"Now there is integrated Sekolah Rakyat, as well as Sekolah Unggul Garuda, and others. At the education level, social facilities (for AI access) have been provided," Triyanto said.

title: Kaushik Kappagantulu’s Greenhouse in a Box Is Aiding India’s Farmers
content:
Kaushik Kappagantulu’s grandmother raised eight kids and 20 grandkids, including him, mostly by herself in the bustling Indian city of Hyderabad. An educated woman, she taught Kappagantulu that if you work hard, you will succeed. But after graduating from engineering college and doing a volunteer program teaching homeless kids, Kappagantulu realized this was not the case for everyone. “In rural India, most of the people work really hard, but because of a lack of access to different things, their hard work does not convert into success,” he tells TIME.
This revelation prompted Kappagantulu to dedicate himself to uplifting others. For six years he worked with school dropouts, helping them access jobs through vocational training. “Every single one of those kids was from a farming family and they were coming to us because farming was failing,” he says.
Sensing a systemic problem that needed addressing, Kappagantulu pivoted to agriculture. In 2015, he launched an agri-tech enterprise called Kheyti, which means farming in Hindi. The goal was to help the more than 100 million smallholder farmers who produce the bulk of India’s staple foods like rice, wheat, and pulses. And one of the biggest challenges facing farmers today is the changing climate.
In India, the combination of extreme heat, unseasonable rain, and depleting groundwater is making it difficult for farmers to grow during the summer season from March to June. During a heatwave this April, sensors installed by Kheyti recorded ground temperatures on multiple farms hitting 125 degrees Fahrenheit. “Climate change is wiping out their hard work,” says Kappagantulu, adding that the average Indian farmer earns about $1,000 a year. “It is not even enough for them to make ends meet,” he says.
Kheyti’s solution was a low-cost modular “greenhouse-in-a-box.” These net houses are designed to be smaller than conventional greenhouses, suitable for the one-acre farmer. They have shade cloth on top, which reduces internal temperatures by about 9 degrees Fahrenheit, and drip irrigation. Each greenhouse is also paired with an AI-powered tool that offers farmers advice on things like choosing the best crops and managing pests. This model works: Farmers reduce their crop losses by 58% while using 67% less water and 70% less fertilizer. Farmers using Kheyti’s structures also increased their net income, earning three times what non-Kheti farmers did on the same amount of land. And thanks to Kheyti’s partnerships with local governments, subsidies and low-cost loans mean the greenhouses are relatively affordable, each costing between $200 to $300. “We have to be the bridge that makes high tech agriculture accessible to the poorest farmer,” Kappagantulu says.
The greenhouse-in-a-box concept won the Earthshot Prize in 2022. It’s been growing ever since, with Kheyti now working with roughly 7,000 farmers across eight Indian states. Kappagantulu aims to double this over the next 12 months with the support of the Indian government, which has recommended states partner with the company.
Kappagantulu hopes to take the greenhouses global in the next three years and has a pipeline of other products, including flexible solar panels that can be installed on top of the greenhouses. His aim is to help one million farmers build secure, climate-smart livelihoods by 2033. But he knows he can’t do it alone. “Long-term change in the climate sector for agriculture doesn’t happen through one solution or one organization,” he says, “but through forming coalitions.”

title: Rarámuris de Norogachi piden respeto a su autodeterminación
content:
Funcionarios locales intentan imponerles proyectos
Domingo 13 de septiembre de 2026, p. 22
Integrantes de los gobiernos indígenas rarámuri de la región de Norogachi, de la sierra Tarahumara en Chihuahua, exigieron respeto a su derecho a la libre autodeterminación, pues señalaron que a través del Fondo Federal de Aportaciones para la Infraestructura Social para Pueblos y Comunidades Indígenas y Afromexicanas (Faispiam), funcionarios locales intentan imponerles los proyectos, proveedores y prestadores de servicios, cuando éstos necesitan ser decididos en asambleas comunitarias.
Ejemplificaron que en el presente año se les planteó invertir en letrinas, pero muchos pobladores prefieren que el recurso sea para otras obras, además han detectado que las personas quienes les recomiendan los servidores públicos para ejecutar los proyectos son familiares o gente cercana a ellos.
En un escrito dirigido a la presidenta Claudia Sheinbaum y al Instituto Nacional de Pueblos Indígenas (Inpi), rechazaron “cualquier forma de tutelaje sobre nuestros derechos comunitarios, los cuales se encuentran plenamente reconocidos tanto en instrumentos jurídicos internacionales como nacionales y locales”.
Isidro Gardea García, primer siríami de Norogachi; Jesús Raúl Naba Peña, primer siríami de Pawichíki, Juan Espino Hernández, comisario policial de Siquirichi, Guachochi, entre otros, resaltaron que actualmente el pueblo rarámuri está en proceso de adquisición y desarrollo de habilidades, las cuales “nos permiten organizar y administrar nuestro capital social, humano, económico y político”.
Frenan empoderamiento técnico y operativo
Por ello, afirmaron, “la imposición de una tutela gubernamental frena nuestro empoderamiento técnico y operativo, reduciendo con ello nuestra autonomía a una simulación burocrática”.
Así, rechazaron la imposición de proveedores, prestadores de servicios y logística externos para la ejecución de sus proyectos comunitarios. “Somos nosotros quienes poseemos la capacidad y el derecho legítimo de decidir con qué constructores trabajar, a qué fleteros locales contratar y dónde adquirir materiales a implementar para materializar infraestructura comunitaria, de modo que el beneficio económico se quede y circule dentro de nuestra propia región indígena”.
Defendieron que sus asambleas comunitarias, en las cuales se planea, proyecta y deciden las obras, cuentan con los mecanismos internos de control, consenso y transparencia para administrar los recursos entregados a través del Faispiam, a cargo de la Secretaría del Bienestar.
Asimismo, los integrantes de los gobiernos indígenas rarámuri señalaron que el hecho de limitar los rubros de inversión a obras preestablecidas “anula las prioridades reales de nuestras comunidades”.

title: No Doors, No Locks: How a Maharashtra Village Has Lived by a 300-YO Belief
content: In Shani Shingnapur, a house can stand empty for days without a locked front door. There are no padlocks on many entrances, no metal gates guarding homes, and often little more than a curtain separating a family from the street. The same belief extends to shops and public spaces. Even the local branch of a nationalised bank once opened with a glass entrance that had no lock. In a country where even rural homes increasingly rely on security grilles, CCTV cameras and heavy locks, this Maharashtra village has followed the opposite idea for generations: leave the doors open, and trust that no one will steal. Shani Shingnapur sits in Maharashtra's Ahilyanagar district, formerly Ahmednagar, about 240 km east of Mumbai. Home to around 15,000 people today, the village has become known across India for something remarkably simple — its houses do not traditionally have doors. For generations, residents have believed that theft invites punishment from Shani, the deity associated with the planet Saturn, who is said to protect the village. The belief is so deeply embedded that locking a home has traditionally been seen as unnecessary. But this isn't simply a story about a village without locks. It is about what happens when a religious belief becomes a community-wide social rule — and what happens when that rule encounters a changing world. A 300-year-old promise The custom traces its roots to a legend that villagers have passed down for nearly three centuries. Around 300 years ago, when a shepherd living near the Panasnala river reportedly prodded a strange black slab that had washed ashore after a flood, blood is said to have emerged from the stone. The village’s open-door tradition is rooted in a nearly 300-year-old belief that theft invites punishment from Shani, the deity worshipped here. That night, according to local belief, Shani appeared in a villager's dream and revealed that the stone was his own self-manifested form. He asked that it remain in the open, without a roof, and promised to protect the village. The story eventually became more than a legend about a mysterious stone. It shaped the way people lived. If Shani was protecting the settlement, residents believed there was little reason to protect their homes from one another. Over time, the absence of doors became part of everyday life. How an entire village adopted the custom For residents, the practice is less about deliberately rejecting modern security and more about growing up with the assumption that it simply isn't necessary. Homes traditionally have open entrances, sometimes softened with curtains for privacy. Shops follow similar practices. Families can leave their houses unattended without necessarily worrying about locking them first. Housewife Jayashree Gade, for instance, has spoken about keeping her family's savings in an unlocked tin barrel — a practice that would seem unthinkable in most homes. Even public institutions embraced the tradition: a bank in Shani Shingnapur once operated with an unlocked glass entrance, while its cash remained secured inside. The belief is also reinforced socially. Children grow up hearing that stealing from another person will invite Shani's punishment. The idea becomes part of the village's moral code: the consequence of theft isn't simply arrest or social shame, but divine retribution. That shared belief may be what makes the system work. A lock is a physical barrier. In Shani Shingnapur, faith has traditionally served as the barrier. Even the bank followed the rule Perhaps the clearest example of how deeply the custom has entered village life came when a state-owned bank branch opened here in January 2011. Its glass front door was deliberately fitted without a conventional lock, with the decision presented as an extension of the village's long-standing faith. But the arrangement also revealed an interesting compromise between tradition and modern life. While customers could walk through an unlocked entrance, the bank did not leave its money unprotected. Cash was kept inside a secured strongroom. The distinction was telling: the village could preserve its symbolic open-door tradition while still using conventional security where financial risk demanded it. As Shani Shingnapur changes, some families are adding doors and locks, raising questions about whether faith alone can continue to provide a sense of security. As the village grew and attracted increasing numbers of visitors, that balance became more important. When the belief met reality The tradition has not gone entirely untested. In October 2010, a visitor from northern India reported that cash and valuables worth Rs 35,000 had been stolen from a vehicle. A case involving stolen jewellery followed the next year. The incidents challenged the image of a settlement where theft simply did not happen. When the bank opened without a front lock in 2011, district police were also reported to have privately raised concerns about an unsecured cash counter in a village that could see tens of thousands of pilgrims on busy weekends. The outside world was changing too. For decades, the nearest police station had been several kilometres away, something locals had cited as further evidence that serious crime was virtually unheard of. But as the population and visitor numbers increased, the village eventually got its own police station. Even the local bank once had no lock on its front door, though its cash was kept secured inside a strongroom. Even that building reflected the unusual relationship between tradition and modern administration. Its door was installed without a lock, out of respect for local sentiment. When tradition comes at a personal cost Not everyone has found the open-door tradition easy to live with. For Sukhadev Bajira Shete, the belief became difficult to accept after his mother's wedding necklace was stolen from their home when he was a teenager. His father, a temple trustee, continued to oppose installing a door while he was alive. For Shete's wife, that meant living for years without the privacy most people take for granted. Only after his father's death did Shete install a sliding metal gate with a padlock, becoming one of the few residents to openly break with the village's traditional practice. His decision highlights a tension that is easy to miss when the custom is viewed only as an intriguing cultural curiosity. For generations, Shani Shingnapur’s open entrances have reflected a community-wide belief that faith can protect what locks cannot. For some residents, an open doorway represents faith and community trust. For others, a door can represent something equally fundamental: privacy, autonomy and the right to feel secure inside one's own home. Can a village really be crime-free? The reputation of Shani Shingnapur has also attracted scepticism. Critics argue that the village's image may partly survive because smaller incidents are not always reported. Documented cases of theft have also made the idea of a completely crime-free settlement difficult to defend. There are contradictions too. While homes traditionally go without locks, the temple's donation box has a lock — an irony that sceptics often point to when questioning how absolute the custom really is. Yet for many residents, these contradictions have not been enough to abandon the tradition. Trust here is not necessarily being presented as a replacement for every form of security. Instead, it has become a deeply rooted part of the community's identity. A village caught between faith and change The Shani Shingnapur of today is very different from the small settlement of three centuries ago. Its population has grown to around 15,000. Thousands of visitors arrive regularly, particularly on busy weekends. What was once a relatively isolated village is now connected to a much larger world. The Shani Shingnapur temple has become the centre of a village whose unusual open-door tradition has drawn visitors from across India. That brings new pressures. More people means more movement. More visitors mean more strangers. And modern life increasingly comes with expectations of privacy and security that did not exist when the open-door tradition began. Yet the custom continues. Residents still leave homes and shops without conventional locks. The police station has an unlocked door. The bank maintains modern security behind its open entrance. And families continue to make their own choices about where tradition ends and personal security begins. Will the doors eventually return? For nearly 300 years, the open doorway in Shani Shingnapur has represented more than the absence of a lock. It has represented a collective agreement — that neighbours can be trusted, that stealing is unthinkable, and that a divine presence is watching over the community. But change rarely arrives all at once. Families like the Shetes have begun quietly putting doors and locks back into their lives. Younger generations are growing up in a village that is increasingly exposed to the realities of the outside world. The question facing Shani Shingnapur may therefore no longer be whether its ancient belief can survive. It may be whether the next generation will still believe that being watched is enough. Sources: 'Theft in Maharashtra's crime free temple village': by IANS for Deccan Herald, Published on 26 October, 2010 'Temple town with doorless homes gets a bank with no lock': by IANS for Deccan Herald, Published on 10 January, 2011 'Maharashtra's Ahmednagar officially renamed to Ahilyanagar': by Mrityunjay Bose for Deccan Herald, Published on 5 October, 2024

title: Jóvenes indígenas k’iche’ interpretan el clima para salvar cultivos en Guatemala
content:
- Comunidades indígenas k’iche’ de Totonicapán, en Guatemala, combinan monitoreo climático y saberes ancestrales para adaptarse a heladas, sequías y cambios extremos de temperatura.
- La información climática compartida a través de audios, mensajes y redes sociales permite que las familias campesinas tomen decisiones que evitan pérdidas agrícolas.
- La iniciativa es parte de un proyecto mayor que incluye estaciones meteorológicas, viveros agroforestales y la conservación de los bosques y fuentes de agua en otros departamentos de Guatemala.
- En 2026, los indígenas k’iche’ de Totonicapán sembraron 500 árboles y planean plantar 2000 más en los bosques de siete comunidades.
Antonela Huinac recuerda las historias que su papá narraba sobre la vida en Tacajalve, una aldea de San Francisco El Alto, municipio del departamento de Totonicapán. “Él nos contaba que, entre 1985 y 1995, la comunidad no sufría mucho calor. No había plagas, todo era muy ‘natural’”, dice.
Pensar en calor parecía una utopía en Totonicapán pues se ubica en el altiplano, en el occidente de Guatemala, e históricamente los informes del Instituto Nacional de Sismología, Vulcanología, Meteorología e Hidrología (Insivumeh) lo identifican como la región con las temperaturas más bajas del país, donde su población, en su mayoría indígena k’iche’, vive de la agricultura, especialmente de granos como el maíz y el frijol.
Sus habitantes aseguran que cosechaban bastante durante el invierno, tanto que podían almacenar una porción para consumir en verano, cuando no había cosechas porque éstas dependían del ciclo de la lluvia.
Pero todo eso cambió. Desde hace unos diez años, estima la gente en Tacajalve, el clima ya no es el mismo. “Dicen que esta es tierra fría, pero ya no”, lamenta la joven lideresa comunitaria, Antonela Huinac. “A estas alturas de mayo [hace diez años] ya estaba lloviendo, pero vemos que el clima hoy en día es de mucho calor”, agrega. En tiempos de crisis climática no solo el calor se vuelve extremo, el frío también.
La aparición más frecuente e incierta de otros fenómenos como las heladas es una grave amenaza cuando la subsistencia está basada en la agricultura. Cuando la temperatura desciende tanto y de manera imprevista, puede acabar con cultivos enteros en las comunidades.
Es por eso que un grupo de 25 jóvenes, entre ellos 18 mujeres, se han convertido en promotores climáticos que comparten la información que se obtiene en las estaciones meteorológicas de la Asociación de Cooperación para el Desarrollo Rural de Occidente (CDRO). Los jóvenes interpretan los datos y generan boletines para las comunidades de Tacajalve, Chivarreto, Chuicruz, Chuipachec, Xejuyup, Juchanep y Paxtocá. Equipados con anemómetros y veletas, estos jóvenes interpretan información climática y la convierten en mensajes que ya han salvado cultivos de las heladas.
Monitorear un clima cambiante
A unos treinta kilómetros de Tacajalve se encuentra el Sendero Ecológico El Aprisco, un parque natural privado ubicado en las montañas de Totonicapán y manejado por CDRO —organización de base comunitaria que, desde hace 40 años, ha coordinado proyectos que buscan mejorar las condiciones de vida de más de 132 comunidades en el occidente de Guatemala—. Este refugio natural se utiliza como un espacio de sensibilización y educación ambiental para quienes lo visitan, especialmente niños y niñas.
El Aprisco es un bosque de 13 hectáreas conformado principalmente por pinos y cedros. La presencia de esta vegetación brinda una sensación de frescura, muy distinta a la de San Francisco El Alto y la cabecera municipal de Totonicapán. Durante el invierno, los trabajadores deben utilizar chaquetas que los protejan del frío, que ha alcanzado los -5 °C.
El parque está conformado por una serie de senderos. Al final de uno de ellos, y a un lado de la carretera, se encuentra una especie de jaula que protege un artefacto metálico con varios elementos que sobresalen, entre los cuales está un tubo de unos tres metros de alto y apenas unos 20 centímetros de diámetro. Se encuentra en un área libre y lejos de los árboles.
“Conozca de meteorología: las estaciones meteorológicas permiten predecir y analizar las condiciones meteorológicas y de los fenómenos atmosféricos como ciclones, huracanes, tormentas y sequía”, se lee en un cártel ubicado en la entrada.
Los objetos que sobresalen son un anemómetro, un objeto con tres medias esferas que giran y miden la velocidad del viento, y una veleta, una especie de flecha metálica que indica su dirección. No puede verse desde la superficie, pero debajo de la tierra hay un pluviómetro que registra la cantidad de lluvia que cae y permite determinar cuánta agua y humedad hay debajo de la tierra.
CDRO instaló esta estación meteorológica en 2018 como una herramienta para que los productores agrícolas puedan conocer los futuros eventos climáticos y prepararse para responder ante ellos. Es una de las cuatro que la organización tiene en el departamento de Totonicapán, a las que recientemente sumó otras cuatro en el área entre Cunén y Santa Cruz del Quiché, en el departamento de Quiché.
Alan Pérez, técnico de CDRO encargado del monitoreo climático, detalla que la estación del Sendero Ecológico El Aprisco “recolecta datos del ambiente para tener información más clara sobre los sucesos meteorológicos que pueden ocurrir en esa área”.
Luego, CDRO entrega estos datos a los promotores climáticos que han sido formados para interpretarlos. Con base en los hallazgos, ellos generan boletines con recomendaciones agrícolas y forestales.
El principal objetivo es que la información llegue a la mayor cantidad de personas. Algunos boletines se publican en redes sociales, como grupos de Facebook, se envían por mensajes de Whatsapp e incluso por mensajes de texto. Otros, con el permiso de los líderes comunitarios, se pegan en lugares clave de las comunidades como los centros de salud. Con apoyo de profesionales de radio, también se han realizado 33 spots en lenguas Ki’che’ y Kaqchikel. Todo esto ha permitido que la población tome decisiones informadas.
En una ocasión, los promotores climáticos lograron informar a una vecina de Santa María Chiquimula —otro municipio de Totonicapán— de la llegada de una helada la mañana siguiente. Que la información llegara a la mujer, productora de hortalizas, representó toda una hazaña, pero demostró que el esfuerzo por divulgar la información valía la pena.
La mujer no tenía un teléfono inteligente y era analfabeta, así que no tenía manera de leer la información en redes sociales o por WhatsApp. Los monitores tuvieron que recurrir al envío a través de SMS a la hija de la agricultora para que le leyera el mensaje y le diera las indicaciones: debía regar la plantación en la noche o en la madrugada y utilizar tapescos (tejidos planos hechos con caña) para cubrirla.
Y así lo hicieron. El brócoli y la coliflor sobrevivieron mientras las mismas hortalizas de su vecina —que no se enteró de la helada— se perdieron. “Esta es una experiencia que nos ha motivado a seguir trabajando porque sí es de utilidad. Es una cosa tan sencilla, pero que le cambia la vida a una familia”, asegura Antonia Xuyup, directora del Sistema Ambiental Comunitario de CDRO.
Entre certezas e incertidumbres
Aunque el monitoreo climático no puede predecir con certeza la llegada de una helada con muchos días de anticipación, sí permitió que los jóvenes identificaran la prevalencia de condiciones que podían favorecerlas. Monitorearon las temperaturas mínimas diarias, la entrada de masas de aire frío (generalmente del norte), la humedad, la nubosidad y el viento.
“Las noches despejadas y con poco o ningún viento favorecen una mayor pérdida de calor del suelo, por lo que, si además se esperan temperaturas cercanas o por debajo de 0 °C, aumenta el riesgo de helada durante la madrugada o al amanecer del día siguiente”, explica Xuyup.
Durante el último invierno —entre noviembre de 2025 y enero de 2026—, la aldea de Tacajalve enfrentó no solo una sino varias heladas fuertes. En las noches, la temperatura disminuyó y osciló entre los 4 y 6 °C.
Las mujeres del grupo de jóvenes promotores establecieron una rutina para responder a este fenómeno. Cada noche colocaban cobijas y chamarras para proteger las semillas de aliso que apenas germinaban. La hora en la que lo hacían dependía de su propia percepción de la temperatura del ambiente. En los días muy fríos lo hacían desde las seis de la tarde y, en los días que eran un poco más frescos, las cubrían después de la medianoche.
Las jóvenes volvían al invernadero a las 5 o 6 de la mañana del siguiente día y debían retirar las chamarras para que los rayos de sol alcanzaran a las semillas. De esta manera, garantizaron que las plantas experimentaran un desarrollo normal.
“Las comunidades pueden tirar rastrojo para cubrir las raíces de las plantas para que no mueran ni se pierda el cultivo”, resume Pérez.
Por su parte, Antonela Huinac reconoce que las heladas de hace unos meses fueron un gran reto para ellos, “pero las plantas se cuidaron de la mejor manera porque nos adaptamos”, celebra.
Aún con todos los logros que han tenido, los jóvenes promotores y los profesionales de CDRO tienen algo claro: el monitoreo climático no reemplaza los saberes ni el conocimiento ancestral de la población k’iche’. Más bien, se complementan. Es por eso que los boletines también incluyen datos relacionados a la fase lunar en la que se encuentran. Según una tesis de la Universidad del Valle de Guatemala (UVG), se observó que al cosechar durante la luna llena los granos presentan menos humedad y por lo tanto menor número de insectos y menor daño durante el almacenamiento.
“Esto es fundamental porque los abuelos y abuelas saben que no en cualquier momento se puede sembrar un árbol”, explica Xuyup.
Reforestación: una herramienta para enfrentar el cambio del clima
La historia del grupo de promotores climáticos empezó en 2024 con el verde de los árboles. Al notar que la temperatura y la sensación térmica aumentaban en Tacajalve, Antonela Huinac, junto a la pastoral juvenil de la iglesia católica a la que asiste, decidió unirse a una jornada de reforestación en San Antonio Sija, otra aldea de San Francisco El Alto.
El Grupo Intergubernamental de Expertos sobre el Cambio Climático (IPCC, por sus siglas en inglés), en su informe global de 2022, ya indicaba que la protección y restauración de bosques puede moderar el calor local mediante sombra y evapotranspiración. En ciudades, la evidencia sintetizada por el IPCC señala que aumentar la vegetación reduce el calor y los extremos térmicos, mientras que en áreas rurales también hay beneficios microclimáticos, pero se intersectan con otras variables como el tipo de paisaje y el agua disponible.
Aunque la ciencia ya había hablado de esto, en Tacajalve se dieron cuenta que los árboles jugaban un papel central en la ecuación climática acudiendo al dato empírico. En la zona donde la carretera atraviesa la comunidad, el sol pega con fuerza y “se siente la diferencia porque allí no hay árboles que refresquen”, dice Huinac. Ella y sus jóvenes compañeros empezaron a preguntarse: “¿Cómo podemos ayudar a nuestra madre tierra, a nuestra naturaleza?”.
Decidieron pasar de las palabras a la acción, buscaron posibles donantes de árboles y fue así como dieron con CDRO.
En mayo de 2024, la organización les dio 150 cipreses (Cupressus) y 150 árboles de pino blanco (Pinus chiapensis), especies nativas en Guatemala. Realizaron la jornada de siembra el día 24 de ese mes. CDRO también les impartió talleres sobre reforestación y el cuidado de ciertas especies de plantas.
Al finalizar el proceso y luego de ver el interés de los jóvenes, CDRO les ofreció instalar un vivero en su aldea. Ellos aceptaron y consiguieron un terreno —que la familia de Antonela Huinac prestó— donde construyeron esa “sala cuna de árboles”. En especial las mujeres del grupo se encargaron, con palas y picos, de nivelar el suelo que se ubicaba en una pendiente y, actualmente, son quienes garantizan el cuidado de las semillas y plántulas que posteriormente se convierten en árboles para reforestar.
En 2026, ellas y grupos organizados de la comunidad, como los comités de agua potable, ya han sembrado 500 plántulas de aliso (Alnus acuminata) que fueron cuidadas en el vivero. Además, junto con las autoridades comunitarias, han planificado plantar 2000 más a partir de septiembre, cuando esperan que llegue la lluvia.
Huinac ha asumido el liderazgo de la iniciativa de reforestación y motiva a sus compañeras a seguir en el proceso, al tiempo que trabaja desde su casa en el oficio de corte y confección de ropa.
La información climática no debería ser un lujo
Raquel Sigüenza, representante de la Unión Internacional para la Conservación de la Naturaleza (UICN) en Guatemala, considera que el monitoreo climático reduce la vulnerabilidad de las comunidades al sustituir la incertidumbre por información climática local y oportuna. Esto permite, según la experta, que las inversiones sean sostenibles a los efectos extremos del cambio climático. Es por eso que la organización internacional, a través de su proyecto Altiplano Resiliente, apoya la labor de CDRO con sus estaciones de monitoreo meteorológico.
“El enfoque de la UICN no se centra sólo en establecer sistemas de monitoreo que arrojen datos técnicos, también se enfoca en asegurar que esa información llegue a actores locales para quienes históricamente la información climática no es accesible, ayudando de esta manera a reducir la brecha de acceso a la información climática. Es una forma de justicia climática”, explica Sigüenza. “La información climática ya no es un lujo al alcance de pocos”.
La UICN no solo apoya en Guatemala a la iniciativa de monitoreo climático de CDRO y los jóvenes promotores. También acompaña otros proyectos relacionados con la adaptación de prácticas agroforestales con las que han llegado a 132 000 personas pertenecientes a los pueblos indígenas k’iche’, Kaqchikel y Mam. Especialmente a mujeres, jóvenes y hogares monoparentales femeninos.
En medio de los esfuerzos, Sigüenza reconoce que el monitoreo climático ha enfrentado dificultades en la región. Las principales están relacionadas con capacidades técnicas y operativas limitadas en los municipios y organizaciones comunitarias, barreras culturales reflejadas en resistencia a nuevas prácticas de restauración y brechas de género.
Las dificultades mencionadas por Sigüenza se viven también a escala mundial. Actualmente, la gran mayoría de las redes comunitarias operan gracias a asignaciones temporales de fondos de la cooperación internacional o proyectos de ONG que, al expirar, dejan a las comunidades sin presupuesto para reponer equipos dañados, comprar sensores o mantener activas las plataformas de comunicación.
Además, en cuanto a brecha de género, según datos de la Organización de las Naciones Unidas para la Alimentación y la Agricultura (FAO, por sus siglas en inglés), si las mujeres agricultoras tuvieran el mismo acceso que los hombres a recursos productivos, sus rendimientos podrían aumentar entre 20 % y 30 %.
Aún así, tanto UICN como CDRO y los jóvenes promotores consideran que el monitoreo climático es una iniciativa que debe continuar porque sí ha tenido un impacto positivo en reducir la pérdida de cosechas. “Vale la pena porque con este tipo de pérdidas las familias quedan muy dañadas, no solo en la parte productiva, sino emocional y psicológica”, finaliza Xuyup.
*Este reportaje es una alianza periodística entre Agencia Ocote y Mongabay Latam.

title: The house that unlocked a family's history
content:
The house that unlocked a family's history
When Fred Miller, an Air Force veteran, purchased the white, Gothic Revival-style house with the green roof near his childhood home in southern Virginia, he wanted a large space to host gatherings for his close extended family. He was not expecting to unlock hidden chapters from his family's past.
Miller did not know it at the time, but his new property was once a plantation. Named Sharswood, it was built in the 1850s by a slave-owning uncle and nephew who shared his last name.
"If I had known there was a 'Miller Plantation,' I maybe could have… put a connection with the last name Miller and that plantation," Miller told 60 Minutes in 2022. "But I'd never heard of a 'Miller Plantation' or a 'Miller' anything."
This Sunday on 60 Minutes, correspondent Lesley Stahl interviewed Fred Miller and members of his family at Sharswood, speaking about what they unearthed about the property and its past inhabitants.
Fred Miller's sister Karen Dixon-Rexroth, who initially convinced her older brother to buy the property, and their cousins Dexter Miller and Sonya Womack-Miranda, did most of the research into Sharswood's past.
"Something drew me to knowing the history of this place," Dixon-Rexroth told Stahl. "I knew it was an old place from the 1800s, so I started from there, as far as looking at the previous owners, and also any records that were available online."
With time and the help of Karice Luck-Brimmer, a local historian and genealogist, the Millers were able to uncover documents that proved that their own ancestors were once enslaved at Sharswood.
"Since the revelation… I know that when the slaves brought food into the main house, they came up through the basement stairs," Fred Miller told 60 Minutes. "And there's a distinct wear on the basement stairs from years and years of traffic, of people walking up those stairs, I'm thinking, 'Wow, these are my people.'"
When the 60 Minutes producing team of Shari Finkelstein and Braden Cleveland Bergan first visited Sharswood to meet the family and scout the location, they were part of a conversation between Dexter Miller and his former coworker Bill Thompson, whose family bought the property in 1917 and owned it for more than a century. Thompson's sister sold it to Fred Miller in May of 2020.
It was during this conversation that Miller asked Thompson the one question that had been on his mind for a long time.
"I said, 'Bill, there's one question that's been bothering me: Where is the slave cemetery?' He said, 'Dexter, it's right over there.' I said, 'Right over where?' He said, 'You see those trees over there?'"
And with that revelation, as seen in the video above, the 60 Minutes team accompanied the Millers to a cluster of trees just beyond Fred's property line, where for the first time they saw the likely burial site of their enslaved ancestors. Several weeks later, Lesley Stahl visited the site with Fred, who then lived in California, and his sister Karen.
"It was heart-wrenching', I'll tell you that," Fred Miller said about seeing the cemetery for the first time. "Just to think that all these years of me wondering, and it was right under my nose the entire time, right here."
Since our 60 Minutes story first aired in May 2022, Fred Miller moved back home to Virginia and established a non-profit Sharswood foundation to maintain the slave quarters and cemetery. He also offers tours of the house.
You can watch Lesley Stahl's full report on Sharswood below.

title: Heal the Land, Heal Our People: Still Fighting to Free the Klamath River
content: Heal the Land, Heal Our People: Still Fighting to Free the Klamath River tia.roberts Tue, 09/15/2026 - 17:06 CSQ Issue 50-3. Cultural Sovereignty: Self-Determination Through Indigenous Governance September 2026 Read on Issuu Buy a copy Subscribe Many believe the Klamath River is free, but it’s not—not yet. Four of the six dams on the Klamath River were removed in 2023-2024, prompting major media outlets, prominent environmental organizations, and even other Indigenous people to proclaim that the river is free. The fight is not over—we still need to remove the Keno and Link Dams and heal our watershed. The misinformation about our sacred ambo (water in Klamath/Modoc) has made many Klamath Tribal members feel like we are experiencing termination all over again. The Termination Era was a period where the U.S. government targeted Tribal Nations whose land they wanted to steal, like the Klamath Tribes, with lands rich in natural resources. They “terminated” our status as a federally recognized sovereign Indigenous Nation in 1954. Our home was once a massive watershed filled with lakes, rivers, wetlands, and marshes, historically known as ancient Lake Modoc. A biodiverse ecosystem, once the third-largest salmon run on the Pacific coast. The Klamath River starts in our homelands and ends in the Pacific Ocean, in Yurok territory. The Klamath watershed historically connected many Tribal Nations: the Klamath, Modoc, Pit River, Karuk, Hupa, Yurok, and other Tribes. Photo taken July 2026. The start of the Klamath River flows out of the Upper Klamath Lake. The Link Dam is shown below, and in the photo, the remains of two natural reefs that were nearly destroyed during its construction. The rocky area before the dam and the green area near the dam. The Klamath Tribes are three Tribes—Klamath, Modoc, and Yahooskin Paiute—all forced onto a single reservation. We are the maqlaq and neme, located at the heart and lung of the Klamath watershed. We ceded over 22 million acres of land to the U.S. government via the Treaty of 1864 in exchange for a 2-million-acre reservation and reserved treaty rights to hunt, fish, gather, and trap, including water rights. We are the only Tribal Nation along the Klamath River with a ratified treaty, and hold the most senior water rights. We did what we could to survive colonization and sold timber to support our people. Our sales made us one of the wealthiest Tribes in the U.S., which gave us the financial ability to advocate. We stewarded our land with fire until the government outlawed its use in 1911. We were an impediment to the government, which wanted to log our forests, steal water for irrigation to farm cattle, mass produce non-native agriculture, construct railroad lines, and create hydroelectric energy with dams. Sadly, all was accomplished throughout the 1860s,1870s, and continues. In 1905, the Klamath Project was authorized under the 1902 Reclamation Act, allowing irrigation development for 200,000 acres in the Klamath Basin. Construction of the first of six dams began in 1909, marking the beginning of our severance from our c’iyaals (salmon). The government wanted full control over our home, so they broke our treaty. In 1954, the U.S. ceased to recognize us as a sovereign Indigenous Nation. Our delegates traveled to the termination hearings in Washington, D.C., to tell Congress we would never give up our rights, but it did not matter. We were terminated, and so were our c’iyaals— a near genocide of our culture. Aerial drone image post 2021 Bootleg Fire. The areas not burned were stewarded with fire by the Klamath Tribes. After termination, we could no longer hunt, fish, gather, or steward our lands until we successfully advocated to restore our treaty rights in 1974, which helped lead to recognition as a sovereign Nation again in 1986. Our recognition was restored, but with no land. We are salmon Peoples who have been without our c’iyaals for over 100 years; the only Tribe along the Klamath River that was, and remains blocked from our salmon relatives. Colonization and termination had catastrophic impacts on the Klamath River. We are the namesake, being located at the headwaters. What happens in our headwaters impacts all downstream. Today, toxic water continues to flow from our headwaters. Our sacred watershed is sick, crying for help, and our aquatic relatives are on the brink of extinction. When we hear others say the Klamath River is free, it feels like colonial erasure, the termination of our Peoples and animal relatives all over again. We are still healing from termination. The government was almost successful in their genocide, but, like our c’iyaals, we are finding our way back home. After the removal of four dams, c’iyaals were spotted in our upper watershed in October 2025. We do not know how they made it over the remaining two dams, as the fish ladders are not designed for salmon. Miraculously, our c’iyaals are coming home, but return to deadly, toxic waters. Lighting a prescribed fire in a culture and fire workshop. Using Fire to Restore Our Sacred Watershed Indigenous Peoples’ use of loloqs (fire) has shaped landscapes and cleaned water for thousands of years. Our homeland is a volcanic plateau, a fire-dependent ecosystem that provides pristine water to the Klamath watershed and is interconnected throughout the upper and lower basins. Fire acts as a natural selection process, creating resilience and resistance to future disturbance by favoring fire-dependent and adapted species, while reducing accumulated fuels, disease, and invasive species. It renews soils, stimulates the growth of culturally important plants, enhances wildlife habitat, reduces hazardous fuels, and increases an ecosystem’s resistance to severe wildfire, pests, and climate stress. Fire is the solution to fighting mega fires, but also the medicine to heal our watershed and people. Without intentional burns on our landscape, we get massive wildfires. In 2021, Oregon’s Bootleg Fire obliterated over 400,000 acres. It ravaged through the canopy and when it reached the areas treated by the Klamath Tribes, it dropped to the understory and walked across the forest floor. Drone footage captured the effectiveness of our stewarding. We co-steward with the U.S. Forest Service since 1999, but have limited capacity to fully steward all of our homelands. The portions we managed were the proof needed to change the national perspective on fire in the U.S. What happened in our homeland during the Bootleg was what we have known about fire since time immemorial. Post Bootleg Fire meadow portion of the burn, 2021. Our lands would burn on average, every 10-13 years, anywhere from 300,000–500,000 acres at a time; smaller fires would burn more frequently. Our ancestors spread fire for many reasons; managing the watershed was one of them. Over the past decade, fire suppression has created a fuel load of dense, down woody fuels and layers of duff. To relieve an overloaded fire suppressed forest from mega fires, cattle are being introduced to steward the land and reduce fuels, replacing Indigenous Traditional Ecological Knowledge in the system and destroying the once-pristine waterways. Fire is essential for our culture, spiritual practice, land, water, and has been the primary tool for thousands of years. The government severed our ability to steward the land with fire and created pollution with cattle, pesticides, plastics, and dams, sickening our homelands. The majority of our watershed is toxic. Upper Klamath Lake is choking with algae blooms. Because the connection between Lower Klamath Lake and the Lost River has been fragmented, dammed, and poisoned, our sacred fish are unable to reproduce or reach their original spawning grounds. Traditionally, we would cremate our loved ones and place them back into the water, something we can no longer do with the fracturing of our watershed. Post Bootleg thicket burn 2021, photo taken Spring 2022. Our creation story is tied to our sacred c’waam (lost river sucker) and koptu (short-nose sucker), who are found nowhere else in the world except in our ambo. We are spiritually tied to these fish, and if they suffer, we do. In our stories, animals came first, and then later our Peoples. The most powerful bird that worked alongside Creator is Ka-ak (Old Raven), the supreme ally to Creator, who watches over the people and has oracular powers. Ka-ak is guiding us back to our old ways. As our Elders have told us, we must build it as it was before. This is why, as Co-executive Directors of tonip ka-ak (5 Raven) Alliance, we are working together to advocate for the change needed to heal our lands. We have the solutions to healing the Klamath watershed; remove the dams and use fire to heal our watershed and Peoples. Juliette A. Jackson and Anna Merritt are enrolled members of the Klamath Tribes and Co-directors and Co-founders of tonip ka-ak (5 Raven) Alliance, a Native women-led nonprofit in Chiloquin, Oregon, whose core mission is to “heal the land, heal the people.” Top photo: Culture and fire workshop on the Sprague River, Oregon. All photos courtesy of Tonip Ka-ak (5 Raven) Alliance. Main Image

title: SPOTLIGHT: Health policy trailblazer Precious Matsoso credits patience, faith and The Beatles
content:
Leading negotiations on the world’s first pandemic treaty, South African health policy trailblazer Precious Matsoso dealt with “occasional adversarial and intense engagements” by bursting into song. In her melodious church voice, Matsoso sang All You Need Is Love by The Beatles, imparting a message of co-operation to delegates from 194 countries gathered in Geneva, the headquarters of the World Health Organization (WHO).
She recalls: “It was very funny because a Brazilian delegate was saying, ‘Why are we treating each other like this?’ And that’s when I sang that song.” There was also a moment, she says, where she sang the theme song of the movie Mission Impossible.
After 30 years of negotiating health policy on national and global levels, Matsoso says: “When elephants fight, the grass suffers. Here, patients suffer.” She is referring to vulnerable sick people slipping between the cracks, with life-and-death stakes, as health sector stakeholders clash.
Following her three-year tenure as co-chairperson of the International Negotiating Body for the WHO Pandemic Agreement, earlier this year TIME magazine named Matsoso on both its TIME 100 Health 2026 and 100 Most Influential People in the World 2026 lists.
A collective refusal
In her acceptance speech, Matsoso distilled the aim of the pandemic treaty as “a collective refusal to repeat the devastation and inequities we witnessed during Covid-19”.
Driven by the memory of how African countries were pushed to the back of the queue for diagnostics, protective equipment and medicine during Covid-19, the deliberations saw her speak up for equitable access to (and local manufacturing of) pandemic-related health products.
In her speech following the TIME accolades, she added: “[The world] had vaccines in just under a year, an unprecedented achievement in research and development. But half the world, notably Africa, lacked access to diagnostics, therapeutics, and vaccines. That was not an accident. That system was designed for charity after the fact, not equity from the start.”
This, she said, is what the pandemic agreement intends to fix.
The pandemic treaty was adopted in May 2025 with a working group still drafting final aspects such as an annex on “pathogen access and benefit sharing”. According to a WHO statement in July, this is “a system that enables the rapid sharing of pathogens with pandemic potential while ensuring the fair and equitable sharing of benefits arising from their use, including pandemic vaccines, diagnostics, and therapeutics”. To Spotlight, Matsoso says this final section is “arguably the most important test of whether global health rules can alter power relations”.
Our interview is happening inside a central city hotel near the Cape Town International Convention Centre, where earlier in the day she delivered a plenary speech on the pandemic treaty at the World Congress on Public Health.
Matsoso’s CV is a long document detailing countless leadership roles in South Africa and at global health bodies, and many awards over the years, including the South African Medical Research Council’s Lifetime Achievement Award last year.
Presently, she heads the Health Regulatory Science Platform at the University of the Witwatersrand, where she works adjacent to Professor Helen Rees, founder and director of the Wits Reproductive Health and HIV Institute and chair of the South African Health Products Regulatory Authority. The two collaborated in the past, shaping South Africa’s medicine landscape in the time of HIV and Aids denialism.
Soweto childhood filled with music, science and uprisings
Across a pin-cushion protea in a vase, Matsoso recounts her Soweto childhood: how it was filled with music and science. Her father, a self-taught mechanic, and her mother, a maths teacher, loved music and their home echoed with anything from Bach and Tchaikovsky to The Beatles and Tom Jones, she says.
At 15-years-old Matsoso witnessed the 1976 Soweto student uprisings, she says, a pivotal moment that forced her into early political consciousness. In high school, she relished science and particularly chemistry, which she excelled at and taught to her classmates.
“There was somebody called William Smith who used to run Star School [science supplements published in The Star newspaper], it was incredible,” she says.
“He made organic chemistry easy. I loved chemistry very much, but also wanted to be in the health sector. And so pharmacy was the nearest thing.”
