Matsoso turned down a bursary in computer science at the University of the North in Polokwane (now the University of Limpopo), in favour of studying toward a Bachelor of Pharmacy at the same university, thanks to funding from a family friend in Soweto. But soon campus politics would force her to Cape Town, where she finished her degree at the University of the Western Cape. Reflecting on student uprisings and her activism at the time, Matsoso says: “The police were looking for us, we were on the run. It was a very sad time, I lost my friend, they killed him during detention.”
In time, her other qualifications would include a diploma in Health Management from the University of Cape Town and a Master of Laws in Healthcare Law and Ethics from the University of Dundee in Scotland.
Health reforms and Aids denialism
In 1995, after having worked as a public sector pharmacist, including at Chris Hani Baragwanath Academic Hospital in Soweto, and in the private sector as a pharmacy owner, Matsoso was recruited to head pharmaceutical services at the newly established National Department of Health under then health minister Dr Nkosazana Dlamini Zuma.
Here, Matsoso was in charge of managing drug procurement for the public sector, formalising South Africa’s National Drug Policy in 1996, and also for compiling the country’s Essential Medicines List that same year. With pride she recounts: “I was appointed in 1995, and the Essential Medicines List was produced in 1996. The very first one. And since, it has grown from strength to strength.” The Essential Medicines List is a list of medicines that are considered vital for the health of the country, like antiretrovirals or insulin. The health department undertakes to supply medicines on this list to the public health sector, normally via tenders.
In 1998, she stepped into the demanding role of registrar of the Medicines Control Council, today called the South African Health Products Regulatory Authority. Her appointment followed what some described as a purge of senior leadership at the MCC in early 1998. Highly respected leaders like Peter Folb and Johan Schlebusch were forced out following their decision to suspend a clinical trial of Virodene, a toxic industrial solvent pushed by a group of Pretoria researchers as a cure for HIV. (The affair is set out in detail in chapter 8 of Nathan Geffen’s book Debunking Delusions.)
To Spotlight, Matsoso relays four highlights of her time as registrar of the MCC.
Firstly, she says she refused to register Virodene.
“[Professor] Helen Rees was the chair [of the Medicines Control Council] at the time and I was the registrar. I refused. So we didn’t register it,” says Matsoso.
Secondly, she says she approved the antiretroviral Nevirapine for the prevention of mother-to-child transmission of HIV, and thirdly she granted “special permission” for the import of Daphnach, the generic antifungal used to treat oral thrush which often leaves people living with advanced HIV unable to swallow or eat.
“The tablets that Zackie Achmat and them [Aids activists with the Treatment Action Campaign] brought into the country from Thailand, those were difficult times,” she says, chuckling dryly.
And fourth – “the most significant and which almost got me into trouble, was that the MSF [Médecins Sans Frontières] wanted to conduct a study using cheaper generic antiretrovirals in Khayelitsha. So I approved it, and I was told to withdraw the approval by [then] trade and industry minister Alec Erwin. And I said ‘Well, there’s nothing in the law that says I must withdraw.’”
Early Pepfar negotiations
In 2003, Matsoso was involved in negotiations around the establishment of the United States President’s Emergency Plan for Aids Relief (Pepfar), an aid initiative estimated to have helped save in the region of 26 million lives. The Trump administration has over the last year and a half scaled Pepfar back dramatically.
Matsoso recalls chairing a meeting on the creation of Pepfar in Gaborone, Botswana: “During the Bush era [former American president George W. Bush], there were debates about why the US was establishing a parallel process when we had the Global Fund. I was chairing, and civil society and the US government were fighting in the room. I said: ‘I’m going to kick all of you out of this room, because this meeting is about HIV/Aids. We are not going to do this in my meeting.’ So I was very firm. And the meeting was a big success.”
The global stage beckons
Eventually she was forced out of her job at the MCC.
“So while I was busy, I get a call on behalf of minister Manto [then health minister Dr Manto Tshabalala-Msimang] that I’m basically fired. I think it was just harassment. But anyway, I applied for a job at the WHO as a director of Public Health Innovation and Intellectual Property. That’s why I left and I went to Geneva for six-and-a-half years.” She took along her children, then aged 18 and 13, saying: “My son and daughter were able to integrate, making friends with children from different parts of the world.”
In this role, Matsoso remembers chairing negotiations through the night to establish a health emergency programme, post-Ebola: “It was difficult. We negotiated through the night for two days. On the first day, we finished at about 9pm; on the second day at about 6am…”
A new health minister
Back in South Africa in 2010, Matsoso was appointed director-general of the country’s health department under the new health minister, Dr Aaron Motsoaledi – a job she would stay in until 2019. This saw her commute between the administrative offices in Pretoria and Parliament in Cape Town up to twice a week. A highlight of this time, she says, was driving the establishment of South Africa’s first independent Health Ombud within the Office of Health Standards Compliance. In 2016, Professor Malegapuru Makgoba would assume this role. He has since been succeeded by Professor Taole Mokoena.
Reflecting on creating new health policy, she says: “In legislative drafting, political parties rarely agree. Because you introduce the law, you have to defend it, sell it, and get them to support the legislation. It’s a different set of skills. Sometimes you face people with limited technical understanding who speak politically. You have to maintain your cool, be patient, and help them understand. In both multilateral and national settings, there is one key ingredient: patience. You must be patient.”
After hours
Given her negotiating skills, from where does her grasp of humanity stem? “Well, I go to church,” says Matsoso.
“I’m very spiritual, people don’t know this because it’s my private space. I also have a group of women that I work with. We have an orphanage that we support in Atteridgeville [a township in Pretoria]. So we’ve seen those children grow up. At the end of each year, we throw them a Christmas party and buy them clothes.”
The well-travelled health diplomat cites some of her favourite countries to visit as Zambia and Japan. Reading and books are central, too.
“So in my bedroom, I have shelves of books within easy reach. This is apart from the bookshelves in my study,” she says.
Earlier this year, Matsoso ended her TIME magazine acceptance speech with words that might well capture her ethos: “To science that is rigorous and accessible,” she said. “To policy grounded in evidence and empathy, and to global health systems where every frontline worker is protected, and to a fairer and safer world.” DM
This article was first published by Spotlight – health journalism in the public interest. Sign up to the Spotlight newsletter.

title: Clean seas, safe coasts: How India is transforming its 11,000 km coastline through citizen power
content:
Opinion Clean seas, safe coasts: How India is transforming its 11,000 km coastline through citizen power
Somewhere between the India that once measured its wealth in coral and catch, and the India of today, the ocean began sending us a message written in litter. This is the story of how we began writing back
There is a memory the sea keeps that no monsoon can wash away. Walk along any of India’s 11,098 kilometres of coastline at first light, and you will find it in the same tide that once carried spice ships to Malabar and pearl divers to the Gulf of Mannar: A restless, ancient rhythm that has shaped how Indians live, trade, worship and dream. But walk that same shore today, and increasingly the tide brings back something else too — a torn fishing net tangled with a shampoo sachet, a turtle hatchling nosing past a bottle cap mistaken for food, a fisherman’s morning catch thinner than his father’s, and heavier with plastic than with fish. Somewhere between the India that once measured its wealth in coral, cowrie and catch, and the India of today, the ocean began sending us a message written in litter. This is the story of how, over the last decade, we finally began writing back.
For too long, the coast lived at the edge of our imagination the way it lived at the edge of our map — visited, admired, occasionally mourned after a cyclone, but rarely defended as a shared inheritance. Ocean governance earlier was, in the main, an administrative afterthought scattered across departments, driven by disaster response rather than daily stewardship, with no national platform that asked the ordinary citizen to see the sea as theirs to protect. Meanwhile, the threat was quietly compounding. Plastic waste, much of it single-use, was finding its way through our rivers and drains into estuaries and open water, breaking down not into harmlessness but into microplastics — fragments smaller than five millimetres that fish mistake for food, that enter the catch on our plates, and that we now know travel silently up the food chain into our own bodies. Marine animals were dying entangled in abandoned nets. Coral reefs, mangroves and fish stocks that sustain the livelihoods of millions of coastal families were absorbing a slow, invisible injury. It was, by any honest reckoning, one of the most under-addressed environmental challenges of our time, hiding in plain sight along a coastline that touches nine states and four Union Territories.
What changed was not merely a policy. It was a decision, taken consciously by the Modi government, that cleanliness could no longer be treated as somebody else’s job. It had to become, as the Prime Minister put it when he launched the Swachh Bharat Mission in 2014, a Jan Andolan, a movement of the people. That civilisational instinct — Mission LiFE, a Lifestyle for Environment that asks each citizen to make sustainability a daily habit rather than an occasional virtue — has since travelled from our streets to our shores. As the Ministry entrusted with the science of our oceans, atmosphere and Earth systems, we asked ourselves a simple question: If India could mobilise a nation to clean its cities, could it not do the same for its seas? The answer arrived in 2022, in the form of Swachh Sagar Surakshit Sagar — Clean Seas, Safe Coasts — a campaign conceived not as a one-day photo opportunity but as a sustained, science-backed, citizen-powered movement, timed each year to converge with International Coastal Cleanup Day, the third Saturday of September, a global tradition that began in 1986 and today draws volunteers in more than a hundred countries to their nearest coastline with nothing but gloves, bags and resolve.
The comparison, even within this campaign’s own short life, tells its own story of scale. In its first year, Swachh Sagar Surakshit Sagar ran for 75 days and reached 75 locations, largely through the efforts of our own ocean research institutes. But as other ministries joined hands, as voluntary organisations such as Seema Jagran Manch and Paryavaran Sanrakshan Gatividhi lent their networks, and as the idea began to travel by word of mouth along the coast, that same campaign, within the same year, had grown to touch 836 coastal locations and mobilise more than a lakh volunteers. That is not incremental growth; that is a movement finding its feet and then finding its stride. Four editions later, as we launch Swachh Sagar Surakshit Sagar 5.0 this September, the coalition has widened further still — the Indian Coast Guard and Navy, the Ministry of Ports, Shipping and Waterways, the Ministry of Youth Affairs and Sports, the NCC and NSS, Scouts and Guides, schools, universities, corporates and, crucially, fisherfolk associations and women’s groups who know these waters as intimately as their own courtyards. Our own institutes — the National Institute of Ocean Technology in Chennai, the National Centre for Coastal Research, INCOIS in Hyderabad, and sister institutions along both coasts — are coordinating clean-up drives across more than a hundred beaches this year alone, with partners like Bisleri independently bringing another 50 locations under the same banner. This is what a Jan Andolan looks like when it matures.
What makes this year’s edition distinctive is not only its reach but its rhythm. From September 12 to September 19, the coastline will host, in effect, a week-long festival of stewardship rather than a single ceremonial gesture. There will be a cyclothon along both the eastern and western seaboards, young people pedalling from town to town in a living relay of intent. There will be a Fit India morning on the sands, a marathon, and on World Ozone Day, a clean-up drive that quietly reminds us that the health of the atmosphere above and the ocean below are two chapters of the same story. There will be a human chain along our beaches, hands linked from Gujarat to the Sundarbans, from Kanyakumari to the Andamans, and an Ocean Olympiad that turns marine science into a contest young minds will remember long after the trophies are handed out. Students will compete in drawing and essay competitions that ask them to imagine the sea their children will inherit. Young volunteers will ride to the beach in the Bike-to-Beach campaign and post their clean-up as an Eco-Selfie, because a movement that wants to last must also learn to speak the language of the generation that will carry it forward. And on September 19, International Coastal Cleanup Day itself, it will all converge in the campaign’s largest single-day clean-up, geo-tagged and digitally logged so that every bag of waste collected becomes data, not just diligence — a record we can measure, publish and improve upon next year.
That last detail matters more than it seems. Technology has quietly become this movement’s backbone. Volunteers register digitally, drives are mapped and geo-tagged in real time, and participants receive digital certificates that turn a morning of hard, sweaty work into a recognised act of citizenship. This is governance choosing to trust its citizens with data and, in turn, being held accountable by them.
But behind every statistic in this campaign is a face I keep returning to when I think about why this work matters. It is the fisherman off the Odisha coast who tells you his net now needs an extra hour of sorting before the catch is clean enough to sell. It is the mother in a Keralam fishing hamlet who worries less about polio these days and more about what her children’s food carries invisibly within it. It is the small hotel owner in Goa or Puducherry whose livelihood depends entirely on a beach staying beautiful enough for a family to want to return to it next year. Clean seas are not an abstraction for these citizens; they are grocery money, school fees, and the health of a child. When we speak of the Blue Economy — of oceans as engines of trade, tourism, fisheries and energy that can power a Viksit Bharat — we are also speaking, in the most literal sense, about their kitchen tables.
I have often said that India’s relationship with nature was never meant to be transactional; it was meant to be filial. Swachh Sagar Surakshit Sagar is, at its heart, an attempt to recover that relationship at scale. We are not asking India to fall in love with its coastline. That love was always there, written into our festivals, our fishing songs, our pilgrimages to the sea. We are simply asking India to act on it, one beach, one bag of plastic, one Saturday in September at a time — until safe seas are no longer a season’s campaign, but simply how we live.
The writer is Union Minister of State (Independent Charge) for Science & Technology and Earth Sciences; Minister of State, PMO, Department of Atomic Energy, Department of Space, and Ministry of Personnel, Public Grievances & Pensions

title: Como a Turquia transformou resíduos em riqueza
content:
Como a Turquia transformou resíduos em riqueza
Projeto Lixo Zero combina reciclagem, conservação de recursos e educação ambiental e já movimentou US$ 3,48 bilhões
Projeto Lixo Zero combina reciclagem, conservação de recursos e educação ambiental e já movimentou US$ 3,48 bilhões
Desde que foi lançado, em 2017, o Projeto Lixo Zero (Zero Waste) da Turquia vem mostrando que políticas de gestão de resíduos podem produzir efeitos que vão além da redução do lixo enviado aos aterros. A iniciativa combina reciclagem, economia de recursos naturais, redução de emissões e conscientização da população, com impactos também sobre a economia do país.
Idealizado por Emine Erdoğan, primeira-dama da Turquia, e implementado pelo Ministério do Meio Ambiente, Urbanização e Mudanças Climáticas, o programa tem como objetivo incentivar o gerenciamento dos resíduos de acordo com princípios de desenvolvimento sustentável e reduzir a poluição.
De acordo com dados do ministério, o projeto já evitou a emissão de 3,9 milhões de toneladas de gases de efeito estufa. A iniciativa também resultou na economia de mais de 530 milhões de quilowatts-hora de energia e 572 milhões de metros cúbicos de água. Os resultados se estendem à conservação de recursos naturais, o programa evitou o abate de 347 milhões de árvores, impediu a queima de 87 milhões de barris de petróleo e reduziu o consumo de 650 milhões de toneladas de matérias-primas
Desde o início da iniciativa, 33,8 milhões de toneladas de resíduos deixaram de ser encaminhadas para aterros e foram direcionadas à reciclagem. O volume inclui 20,4 milhões de toneladas de papel, 5,4 milhões de toneladas de plástico, 2,3 milhões de toneladas de vidro, 500 mil toneladas de metal e 5,2 milhões de toneladas de resíduos orgânicos. Além de reduzir a pressão sobre os recursos naturais, a reciclagem também gerou retorno financeiro. Segundo o governo turco, os materiais recuperados movimentaram o equivalente a US$ 3,48 bilhões na economia do país.
Outra frente do programa é a mobilização da população. A iniciativa busca ampliar o conhecimento sobre a geração de resíduos e estimular hábitos de consumo e descarte mais sustentáveis. Até o momento, cerca de 16 milhões de cidadãos turcos foram informados sobre os benefícios das práticas de lixo zero, segundo dados do Ministério do Meio Ambiente, Urbanização e Mudanças Climáticas.
Os resultados fizeram o projeto ganhar visibilidade fora da Turquia. A iniciativa recebeu reconhecimento do Programa das Nações Unidas para o Desenvolvimento (PNUD) e do ONU-Habitat, além de ter sido apontada como uma experiência promissora em um relatório da Organização para a Cooperação e Desenvolvimento Econômico (OCDE) publicado em 2019. Mais recentemente, Emine Erdoğan recebeu do Banco Mundial o prêmio de Liderança em Clima e Desenvolvimento, em reconhecimento ao trabalho desenvolvido por meio do Projeto Lixo Zero.

title: Alice Duncan-Kemp was an empathetic observer of Mithaka culture, but her legacy is complicated
content:
Alice’s dreaming is centrally about the childhood, memories and writings of Alice Duncan-Kemp (1901-1988), who grew up on a pastoral property named Mooraberrie in the first decades of the 20th century.
Mooraberrie was a vast sheep and cattle station located in the Channel Country between Birdsville and Windorah in inland south-western Queensland. A 2015 native title determination recognised Mithaka people as the traditional owners of the region.
Duncan-Kemp published four books in her lifetime and another was published posthumously. All of these works drew on a childhood spent in intimate contact with Mithaka people. Her extraordinarily detailed and empathetic observations formed part of the documentary basis for the 2015 native title determination.
Review: Alice’s dreaming – Tom Griffiths (Black Inc.)
What then of the word “dreaming” in Tom Griffiths’ title?
According to the historian Patrick Wolfe, the word “dreamtime” entered the Australian lexicon via the early anthropological research collaboration between Frank Gillen, the postmaster at Mparntwe (Alice Springs), and Baldwin Spencer, a professor of biology at the University of Melbourne. Their famed partnership resulted in a huge collection of objects, images and films, which has been digitised.
The Arrernte term “alcheringa” was translated by Gillen as the “dream-times”: a long-distant epoch in which the world was created and rules of conduct were laid down.
Wolfe was critical of the generalisation of Spencer and Gillen’s notion of the “dream-times”. He showed that dreams were a counterpoint to European scientific rationalism; the connection between “dreaminess” and Aboriginal people reinforced some of the racist presumptions of both 19th-century anthropology and the popular imagination.
The mid-20th century anthropologist W.E.H. Stanner preferred the term “Dreaming”, which better captured the complexity of an “impalpable and subtle” concept that refers to cosmogony as well as institutions, totemic affiliations and ever-present responsibilities to Country.
Specific, local terms are more preferable still. Arrernte people today conceive of the “Altyerra” or “Altyerre” , rather than “alcheringa”, and Yawuru people in and around Broome conceive of the “Bugarrigarra”, to mention just two examples.
Griffiths, an emeritus professor of history at Australian National University, insists his book is about “Alice’s dreaming”: a different concept again when it is attached to a white child.
He certainly leans on the general idea of dreaminess, but then Alice’s perspective was that of an enchanted and imaginative child. Her writings seem to indicate and induce a state of reverie.
But Griffiths also means to suggest Duncan-Kemp’s incorporation into Mithaka understandings of their Country and the ancestral beings, stories and songs that animate it. When Alice was two years old, she survived an accident as she was travelling in a buggy crossing the flooded Bullo River. She might have been killed by a flowering branch of a bauhinia tree, but was unscathed. This event confirmed a connection between little Alice and Yammacoona, a powerful Dreaming mother-figure associated with the bauhinia.
This story is told in the first section the book, the most absorbing of its four parts. Here, Griffiths makes use of Alice’s extensive writings, beautifully enhancing her insights. Country pulses; it is intimately known and crammed with people, meanings and resources. Mithaka people are constantly hunting and harvesting.
Alongside this powerful evocation of the vitality of Country, Griffiths provides an account of Aboriginal labour in the pastoral economy. Mithaka people were skilled at working with horses and stock. Women performed domestic labour. All of this was unwaged. It seems to me, however, that these exploited Mithaka workers did not suffer a “social death”, to use slavery scholar Orlando Patterson’s influential term.
Mithaka people also attended to intensive ceremonial activities, such as the “goose corroboree”, which entreated magpie geese and other wildfowl to come to the lagoons and waterholes, ensuring a bounty. These ceremonial efforts and the everyday activities more usually classified as “work” provided for the necessities of life.
Duncan-Kemp, too, is often hard at work throughout this section of the book. She recalled that some children learned to muster from horseback as young as six or eight. Griffiths usefully clarifies how commonplace this was: children on the pastoral frontier in the early 20th century were granted adult responsibilities.
Less convincing is Griffiths’ sweeping statement in the prologue: “Aboriginal people were the respected ‘landlords’ of the pastoralists.” By this, he means Duncan-Kemp’s father referred to the Mithaka people who lived, worked on and had input into the running of Mooraberrie as “landlords”.
The designation tells us something about William Duncan. But it did not make Mithaka people landlords. Patently, they did not enjoy legal title to property and did not extract rent from tenants.
A portrait of cultural dynamism
Sequencing is important, as Griffith acknowledges. In the second part of the book, he backtracks from the early years of the 20th century to the violent period preceding Alice’s birth. “More than a dozen major massacres are known and remembered in the Channel Country,” he records, “most of them well organised and intended to kill the maximum amount of people.”
The massacres often took place at waterholes, “precious jewels” in a region prone to droughts and floods, and generally involved the Native Mounted Police.
The seemingly large populations that feature in Duncan-Kemp’s childhood reminiscences in fact represent a “greatly reduced community”. One of her key teachers is Bogie, whose mother and sister were killed in a massacre when he was a teenager.
The sequencing is effective. Griffiths explains that after the passage of a repressive 1897 Act, which provided for the mass institutionalisation of Aboriginal people on reserves across Queensland, being “attached to a station and valued by a white leaseholder became a crucial passport to survival and to continuing tenure of one’s Country”.
All of this is crucial to understanding the roles of Alice’s carers and teachers, and their attachment to Mooraberrie. Griffiths’ considered organisation of the material allows the reader first to appreciate the thriving cultural world that Duncan-Kemp encountered, as she perceived it, before grasping that this is a portrait of Aboriginal cultural dynamism in the wake of immense disruption. The book is describing efforts at revitalisation, rather than simply giving an account of local “traditions”.
But the long-windedness that Griffiths acknowledges as a feature of Duncan-Kemp’s accounts of her childhood begins to emerge as a problem in his own book. Griffiths writes of the “intricate web of capillaries” that sustain the alluvial floodplains of Mithaka Country, and his book, too, has a branching structure. In the last two sections, I frequently lost track of his inquiry into the meaning and contemporary significance of Duncan-Kemp’s words.
Griffiths explores Duncan-Kemp’s compulsion to write, some biographical details of her adulthood, and the very serious problems with plagiarism in her books. He also muses about the importance of reading, sets out the environmental history of the region, and talks of its truffles and birds. He explains the importance of Aboriginal grindstones, which were used to process endemic grain species.
I became disoriented reading a book that is about so many things and began to wonder what, exactly, it is about.
Contemporary collaborations
The book’s fourth and final section is more focused than the third. In this section, Griffiths turns to a life lived in parallel to Duncan-Kemp’s: that of Bill Gorringe, who was born to Mithaka woman Nuncaleer and an older stockman, George Gorringe, around the same year as Alice.
Nuncaleer and George’s descendants have been involved in recent alliances between graziers and Aboriginal people to protect Country from large-scale irrigation and mining proposals. Bill’s daughter, Rainy McKellar, now collaborates with Alice’s grandson Will Kemp, pouring over Duncan-Kemp’s archive as part of contemporary efforts to reinvigorate cultural knowledge of Mithaka Country.
Perhaps perversely, what this book isn’t about also becomes a problem towards its end. As I have noted, Griffiths makes clear that Mithaka people worked for no wages on Mooraberrie. He is one of Australia’s most eminent historians, yet he does not mention the important scholarship on slavery, stolen wages and pastoralism.
Also, Griffiths opens the chapter titled “Treaty” with an anecdote about the Queensland government’s Path to Treaty initiative. This is a literary framing device for a chapter dealing with an 1889 negotiated settlement that brought to a close decades of violence in the Channel Country. But there is no discussion of the fact that the Crisafulli government repealed the Path to Treaty Act in 2024.
It’s not that I object to hopeful and revelatory stories: I’m desperate for them. But redemptive narratives surely must, somewhere and in some way, engage with the intensifying racism of the present.

title: Residents purchase land under their homes to keep their housing locally owned and affordable
content:
Residents of the Hidden Circle Mobile Home Park in Jay, Maine, have purchased the site for $1 million in an effort to keep the land under their 31 homes locally owned and affordable.
Mobile home park residents usually own their home and pay rent for the lot—and in recent years, investors have been buying up sites across the U.S., frequently raising lot fees to increase profits.
In 2023, Maine State Governor Janet Mills signed “Opportunity to Purchase” legislation requiring mobile home park owners to give advance notice to residents of their intent to sell, giving them the chance to submit a competing offer. Last year, Mills strengthened those protections by signing legislation giving residents the right to match a third-party offer, effectively giving them first right of refusal on any mobile home park sale.
Hidden Circle’s purchase is the 14th of its kind in Maine, and the fourth since Mills signed the new protections.
“No one should lose their home to exploitative companies looking to make a profit,” Mills said, “which is why I worked with the legislature to pass and sign legislation that gives residents of mobile homes the first chance to buy the land they reside on before big companies can displace them.
“No one should lose their home to exploitative companies looking to make a profit.” – Maine State Governor Janet Mills
“Congratulations to the residents of Hidden Circle Mobile Home Park for taking their futures into their hands, becoming owners of this land, and working together to create a lasting foundation for their community for years to come,” Governor Mills added.
“It hasn’t been an easy process, but we never gave up,” said Hidden Circle resident Travis White, who serves as president of the cooperative’s volunteer board. “We had to purchase the park because the alternative could be worse. Someone could come in here and hike up the rents and eventually push people out of their homes. Now, people can feel financially safe in their homes.”
The residents formed the co-op last year with the support of the Cooperative Development Institute, a New England nonprofit that supports communities in making transitions to resident ownership.
Financing for the purchase came from the Mobile Home Park Preservation Fund created by Governor Mills and administered by MaineHousing, the Brunswick-based Genesis Community Loan Fund, and the donors of the Maine Community Foundation.
“Hidden Circle demonstrates what’s possible when residents, community organizations, and public partners work together to preserve affordable housing,” MaineHousing director Dan Brennan said.
“The Mobile Home Park Preservation Fund was designed to help residents compete for ownership of the communities they call home, and today that investment is creating lasting benefits for families in Jay. Resident ownership not only protects affordability—it gives people a stronger voice in their future and helps ensure these communities remain stable and vibrant for generations to come,” Brennan added.
“The Hidden Circle residents demonstrated remarkable determination throughout this process,” said Nora Gosselin, director of resident acquisitions at the Cooperative Development Institute. “From the very start—be it septic challenges or survey hurdles—they hung together and got it done.”
Genesis Executive Director Liza Fleming-Ives said: “Every successful resident-owned community strengthens this model and gives more mobile home community residents confidence that they can protect their homes. Genesis will continue working with partners across the state to expand this proven model, helping ensure stable, affordable homes for Maine families.”
“Every successful resident-owned community strengthens this model and gives more mobile home community residents confidence that they can protect their homes.” – Liza Fleming-Ives, Executive Director, Genesis Community Loan Fund
The Maine Office of Community Affairs has launched the Manufactured Housing Community Data Dashboard, a new tool to provide information on licensed manufactured housing communities across the state.
“The dashboard will be updated annually and allow residents, policymakers, park owners, housing practitioners and the general public to track, for the first time, annual lot increases at all Maine manufactured housing communities.”

title: First Nations netballers driving change, bringing cultural safety
content:
Netball's First Nations Tournament part of creating culturally safe spaces
While netball may be Australian girls' and women's top participation team sport, it has long fallen short of producing — or at least nurturing — elite Indigenous talent.
Just three Indigenous Australian women have represented the Diamonds: Marcia Ella-Duncan, Sharon Finnan-White and, after a 22-year gap, Donnell Wallam.
In 2024, Wallam left Australia for New Zealand, taking a swipe at her former club, the Firebirds, on the way out.
At the time, she wrote that the New Zealand clubs' "respect for inclusion and culture" was a key factor in her decision to leave, while she eventually returned to the Sunshine Coast Lightning this year.
Netball Australia was not idly watching.
As accusations of a 'toxic culture' at the Firebirds were aired, the governing body launched an investigation and kickstarted a series of measures to enshrine 'cultural safety' for First Nations athletes in the sport.
This included the introduction of Australia's inaugural First Nations team, the Black Swans, following the appointment of Ali Tucker-Munro, Netball Australia's General Manager First Nations and former Diamonds squad member.
Tucker-Munro was also influential in establishing the First Nations Tournament, a yearly national championship currently being held in Melbourne, and the Spirit Series, which launched in 2026 and saw the Black Swans go undefeated against Australia's Pacific neighbours.
Speaking from the State Netball and Hockey Centre, Tucker-Munro, alongside players Gabby Coffey and Scarlet Jauncey, said the measures had begun to address the lack of visible role models for First Nations netballers, with more work to be done.
Embraced in Alice Springs
Twenty-six-year-old Coffey, representing the Northern Territory, is one of several First Nations netballers who have been stuck at the cusp of national competition.
The defender spent four years as a Melbourne Vixens training partner before eventually making the decision to move to the UK to further her netball career.
She represented Birmingham over two seasons, and has since returned to Alice Springs.
Coffey had seen the writing on the wall at the Vixens.
"I knew there wasn't much movement in their defensive end, and the same with a lot of defensive ends around Australia," Coffey told ABC Sport.
While she has not given up on a professional career, she is also at peace with the idea that her role may be to support other First Nations athletes with their sporting aspirations.
The Wiradjuri woman grew up in Alice Springs, away from mob and country, but remembers being embraced by the community in Arrente.
"When you grow up on other Indigenous land and tell people you're Indigenous, they pull you into their culture, so [my family and I] were super lucky and blessed to grow up in the centre of Australia where arguably their Indigenous culture is very sacred and traditional," she said.
Determined to pursue netball, she was advised by coach Gillian Lee to move down south, and remembers the transition to Melbourne as a difficult one.
"It was really hard being away from home," Coffey said.
"I was really lucky with the team I entered [the Vixens] and the support I did have, but it's not the same for everyone. There's a lot of girls who do get those opportunities to move and then don't last because there's just not that support in place."
Hailing from the Northern Territory, Coffey said, was an additional barrier.
"Even with competitions like these, we don't get together until we're here, and we're training away from each other, so it can be quite a challenge."
Visible Indigenous role models key
Asked what more could be done to help First Nations netballers make it to the elite level, Coffey said role models were key.
"If you can't see it, you can't be it," she said, pointing out that there are only two Indigenous players currently in Super Netball.
Coffey said her own experience of spending multiple years as a train-on player, without breaking into the elite environment, showed how difficult it was to make it into a professional team in Australia.
"We get a number of internationals [coming to Super Netball], which I think makes the game better and more exciting, and I don't think [that] should be restricted," she said.
"But I do think there should be more focus on bringing Indigenous girls into the elite level."
She pointed to Netball Australia's plans to introduce two new teams into the competition, saying this would open further list spots.
A New Zealand team, she added, may take pressure away from the Australian players vying for contracts.
Scarlet Jauncey has spent the last year as a training partner for the West Coast Fever, pinching herself to line up on names like Jhaniele Fowler-Nembhard at training.
A Yaruwu woman from Rubibi/Broome in Western Australia, Jauncey agreed with Coffey that cutting international talent was not a solution.
"We're happy to be playing against the best in the world, that's what we want," the defender said.
Like many of her teammates, Jauncey grew up idolising Wallam.
"I think it just gives us something to strive towards, knowing that we can be in that space," she said.
In 2025, Jauncey captained the Black Swans, in turn becoming a role model to other First Nations players.
"It was the best tournament I've played in, the best teams I've been with," she said.
"I think just being able to come to First Nations tournaments and having that connection with each other has been really great."
Coffey agreed, saying the experience had given her "goosebumps".
"I think it gives not only myself, but a lot of players so much power and push to keep going and play at the highest level," she said.
Cultural safety means listening to community
Tucker-Munro smiles when hearing the players' responses to playing for the Black Swans.
It has been one of her signature initiatives, alongside the First Nations Tournament and Spirit Series.
"These tournaments are aspirational in terms of trying to inspire the next generation of our kids — who we know love sport and netball in particular — to trial for their respective state and territory," she said.
"It's about the kids that are here this week wanting to aspire to take that next step into the big leagues in terms of Super Netball and Australian representation as well."
Tucker-Munro acknowledged that while it was important to bring First Nations netballers into elite environments, those environments had to be culturally safe.
"First Nations people come into these spaces with our culture and community on our back, as well as cheering us on, so you want to do them proud," she said.
"It's also a tough journey, especially for the kids who have to relocate, so it's about thinking strategically about how we can support them."
Since her appointment, the code has put in place a First Nations Cultural Council, and last year ran a cultural safety review in collaboration with community.
The review considered the perspectives of the wider netball workforce, including coaches and umpires as well as athletes
Tucker-Munro conceded there are "multi-faceted" barriers to having more elite Indigenous netballers, including financial constraints and geographical barriers to access.
"For too long our voice has been very silent," Tucker-Munro said.
"We're not a homogenous people, so it's really important that we make sure we're hearing the voices of many.
"One thing we're really big on in our community is not to do things for us or to us, you've got to do it with us.
"There's real intent and good will to actually drive some of this change across the sporting landscape of netball in Australia."

title: Autismo España celebra la aprobación de ocho millones más para mejorar la atención educativa al alumnado con autismo
content:
Autismo España celebra la aprobación de ocho millones más para mejorar la atención educativa al alumnado con autismo
Basado en hechos observados y verificados directamente por nuestros periodistas o por fuentes informadas.
Elígenos como tu fuente preferida en Google.
El Gobierno prevé que la financiación alcance los 20 millones de euros mediante una segunda aportación de 12 millones en 2027.
Autismo España celebró este martes la aprobación por el Consejo de Ministros de un crédito extraordinario de ocho millones de euros para financiar el Programa de Cooperación Territorial de educación inclusiva y mejora de la atención temprana para el alumnado con trastorno del espectro del autismo (TEA), una medida que consideró "un avance" en el cumplimiento del Plan de Acción de la Estrategia Española en TEA.
La Confederación destacó que esta financiación materializa parte del compromiso anunciado por el Gobierno en noviembre del pasado año para impulsar actuaciones destinadas a "garantizar el derecho a una educación en igualdad de condiciones" y reforzar la atención temprana de los niños y niñas con autismo.
Según explicó Autismo España, la aprobación de estos fondos responde a una de las principales reivindicaciones que la entidad ha trasladado al Gobierno durante los últimos meses mediante su labor de incidencia y seguimiento ante las administraciones públicas.
El programa, cuya ejecución está prevista entre el 1 de octubre de 2026 y el 31 de agosto de 2027, busca "consolidar centros educativos seguros, accesibles y predecibles" que favorezcan la participación, el bienestar emocional, el progreso escolar y la continuidad educativa del alumnado con autismo. El Gobierno prevé que la financiación alcance los 20 millones de euros mediante una segunda aportación de 12 millones en 2027, con el objetivo de "abarcar los cursos 2026-2027 y 2027-2028".
Autismo España reclamó que los recursos aprobados se traduzcan en "actuaciones concretas", eficaces y evaluables, con apoyos adecuados, accesibilidad, formación de los profesionales y coordinación entre las administraciones educativas y sociales.
La entidad subrayó además la necesidad de que el reparto de los fondos "sea equitativo entre comunidades autónomas" y se adapte a las necesidades de cada territorio, contando con la experiencia del movimiento asociativo del autismo y sus profesionales.
Para Autismo España, los ocho millones aprobados constituyen un "avance", pero no el punto de llegada, por lo que mantiene su reivindicación de que se cumpla el compromiso de alcanzar los 20 millones de euros previstos y de que las medidas contempladas en la Estrategia Española en TEA se traduzcan en "recursos y derechos efectivos para las personas autistas".

title: 7ª Mostra Pankararu de Música, realizada no Sertão de Pernambuco, abre inscrições para edição de 2026
content:
A 7ª Mostra Pankararu de Música recebe inscrições para a edição de 2026, que acontece de 9 a 12 de outubro, na Aldeia Bem-querer de Cima, no Território Indígena Pankararu, em Jatobá, no Sertão de Pernambuco. A programação reúne música, manifestações artísticas, conhecimentos ancestrais e práticas culturais do povo Pankararu em uma experiência de imersão no território. Os formulários estão disponíveis para o público geral, instituições de ensino e vendedores da comunidade local.
A proposta da Mostra vai além da realização de apresentações musicais. O encontro é organizado como uma etnovivência pedagógica, artística e cultural, criando espaços para a troca de conhecimentos e para o contato com diferentes dimensões da vida no território Pankararu.
Durante os quatro dias de programação, temas relacionados à memória, à educação ancestral, à natureza, à espiritualidade e às práticas de cuidado integram a experiência. A iniciativa também valoriza formas próprias de produção e transmissão de saberes, colocando a comunidade e o território no centro das atividades.
Quem deseja participar da Mostra como público deve preencher o formulário destinado ao público geral. A modalidade é voltada às pessoas interessadas em acompanhar a programação e vivenciar as atividades realizadas no território.
Também há uma inscrição específica para instituições de ensino que pretendem participar com grupos de estudantes. A proposta busca aproximar os conhecimentos construídos no território de outras experiências educativas. No caso de instituições interessadas em permanecer na comunidade durante os dias da Mostra, é necessário fazer contato prévio com a organização por meio dos canais indicados no formulário.
A terceira modalidade de inscrição é exclusiva para vendedores da comunidade local. O cadastro permite a comercialização de produtos durante o evento e não está disponível para pessoas que não fazem parte do território.
A 7ª Mostra Pankararu é realizada em parceria com o Instituto Aió Conexões Pankararu e a Funarte. A iniciativa busca fortalecer uma programação construída a partir do próprio território, valorizando os saberes, as práticas culturais e a produção artística do povo Pankararu.

title: Casi medio millón de niños y adolescentes tienen ya gafas y lentillas gratis
content:
Casi medio millón de niños y adolescentes tienen ya gafas y lentillas gratis
Campaña con Manolito Gafotas
Sánchez presenta la nueva edición del Plan Veo, dotado con 73 millones de euros y en el que participan el 75% de las ópticas del país
Manolito Gafotas, nacido de una familia trabajadora de Carabanchel, lleva gafas desde los 5 años. Él, un niño curioso que todo lo mira y lo quiere saber, está orgulloso de sus lentes, porque con ellas puede ver bien el mundo que le rodea. ¿El problema? Que cuando se le rompían, sus padres debían esperar “unos meses” para disponer de ese dinero para pagarlas. “Me ponían celo y a correr”, relata este personaje de la escritora Elvira Lindo. Ahora las tiene gratis, gracias al Plan Veo, puesto en marcha en diciembre del año pasado para menores de 16 años: 100 euros al año para la compra de gafas y lentillas infantiles. La ayuda estará disponible hasta el 31 de diciembre.
Esta es la campaña que han presentado esta mañana el presidente del Gobierno, Pedro Sánchez, y la ministra de Sanidad, Mónica García, quienes han reconocido que los beneficiarios han superado las previsiones, por lo que se ha tenido que ampliar el presupuesto a 73 millones de euros.
Según los datos facilitados por García, casi medio millón de niños y adolescentes se han acogido a este programa (en marcha desde el 17 de diciembre del 2025), que ha llegado a todos los rincones de España gracias a la colaboración de unas 7.800 ópticas (casi el 75% de las existentes) y 13.000 profesionales.
“Gracias a este plan, miles de niños y adolescentes pueden jugar sin miedo, dejar de heredar las gafas de otros, ponérselas cuando les corresponde y no meses después o ir con los cristales rayados o con niebla”, señala García, quien recuerda que esta prestación se ha incorporado a la sanidad pública de manera universal (sin distinción de la situación económica de la familia), porque “los derechos son universales”.
Estas medidas, añade, son las mejores armas contra la desigualdad. “Las gafas de Manolito ya no son un problema”, dice García, quien, emulando a este personaje, señala: “Que ningún niño vea peor porque en su casa no hay dinero mola un pegote”.
Sánchez ha defendido este plan, que apuntala los derechos y la sanidad pública. El presidente del Gobierno ha recordado que más de 700.000 de los niños sufren pobreza visual y que uno de cada tres estudiantes con malos resultados académicos podría tener un problema visual no diagnosticado. Para paliar esto, nació el Plan VEO, indica.
Sánchez ha aprovechado el acto para recordar cómo su Gobierno ha reforzado el Estado del bienestar aumentando en 145.000 millones la inversión destinada a las prestaciones sociales y ha ampliado derechos, incorporando, entre otros, nuevos cribados neonatales y ampliando las edades de los programas de detección precoz del cáncer.
“No vamos a dejar que ese sistema se debilite, se desmantele. Y no vamos a aceptar que aquello que pertenece a todos los españoles, singularmente la sanidad pública, termine dependiendo del bolsillo de cada uno, o acabe en el bolsillo de unos pocos”, ha finalizado.

title: La tasa de analfabetismo en el país es la más baja en la historia
content:
La Unesco reconoce que 96% de los mexicanos saben leer y escribir
Miércoles 9 de septiembre de 2026, p. 9
San Juan Chamula, Chis., En el marco del Congreso Mundial por el 60 aniversario del Día Internacional de la Alfabetización 2026, la Organización de Naciones Unidas para la Educación, la Ciencia y la Cultura (Unesco) felicitó a México por sus progresos en materia de alfabetización, al ser un país que “avanza en esta materia”.
Lo anterior, luego de que el país alcanzara la tasa de analfabetismo más baja de su historia: del total de la población de 15 años y más, quienes no saben leer ni escribir representan 3.8 por ciento; es decir, más de 96 por ciento son alfabetizados.
Lidia Arthur Brito, subdirectora general de la Unesco, quien encabezó la ceremonia oficial en esta comunidad, en el corazón de los Altos de Chiapas, destacó la conducción de la presidenta Claudia Sheinbaum Pardo en dichos progresos.
“Quiero reconocer el liderazgo de la Presidenta, quien es la primera mujer en llegar a este cargo en México, y es además, una gran científica. Sabemos que ella, con todo su equipo, con todo el pueblo mexicano, continúan el sueño de Benito Juárez, de Justo Sierra, de José Vasconcelos, y claro, de Jaime Torres Bodet, el segundo director general de la Unesco, y dos veces titular de la Secretaría de Educación Pública, quienes ponen a México en la ruta de un país completamente alfabetizado”, afirmó en la Plaza de la Paz de esta comunidad, ante miles de indígenas de todas las etnias del estado.
Afirmó que los avances de nuestro país y, en particular, de comunidades indígenas como San Juan Chamula, “demuestra que la alfabetización no consiste únicamente en adquirir competencias de lectura y escritura, sino también en fortalecer la identidad, preservar las lenguas y ampliar las oportunidades de desarrollo para todas las personas”.
Chiapas, declaró, es un ejemplo de diversidad que distingue a México. Sus pueblos han mantenido vivas las tradiciones, conocimientos y formas de organización, que “constituyen un patrimonio invaluable para la humanidad”.
Acompañada del titular de la SEP, Mario Delgado Carrillo y del gobernador de Chiapas, Eduardo Ramírez Aguilar, Brito destacó que la educación “es más poderosa cuando dialoga con las culturas, las lenguas y los saberes”.
Antes de la entrega de los Premios Internacionales de Alfabetización Unesco 2026, que en esta edición reconocieron a seis proyectos innovadores en México, Líbano, Nigeria, Colombia, Países Bajos y Tailandia, entre ellos el Programa de Alfabetización Chiapas Puede, la subdirectora general de la Unesco admitió que, pese a los avances alcanzados en las décadas recientes, pues la tasa de jóvenes alfabetizados en el mundo pasó de 75 a 93 por ciento entre 1975 y 2024, “tenemos que reflexionar sobre lo que realmente significa la alfabetización en el siglo XXI”.
Admitió que la alfabetización “va más allá de la escritura y la lectura, porque abarca los conocimientos, las competencias y las capacidades necesarias para desenvolverse plenamente en la sociedades actuales, y navegar por un mundo muy complejo”.

title: 'Construimos Comunidades Accesibles' hace más amable la ciudad a personas con problemas de comprensión
content:
Así es 'Construimos Comunidades Accesibles', iniciativa que hace más amables las ciudades a personas con problemas de comprensión
Basado en hechos observados y verificados directamente por nuestros periodistas o por fuentes informadas.
Elígenos como tu fuente preferida en Google.
Con este proyecto, Plena Inclusión España, a través de sus entidades y federaciones locales, busc mejorar la accesibilidad cognitiva en distintas localidades.
Tras cuatro años de espera, por fin ayer se aprobó en Consejo de Ministros el real decreto que desarrolla la Ley 6/2022 de Accesibilidad Cognitiva, por la que se regulan las condiciones básicas para garantizar que las personas con dificultades de comprensión puedan ejercer sus derechos en igualdad de condiciones.
Tras su entrada en vigor, la accesibilidad cognitiva se convierte en derecho, y hacer que el entorno sea comprensible para todas las personas ya no será una opción, sino una obligación.
Hasta que este decreto, al que no se ha asignado una financiación concreta, aterrice en todos los entornos pasará tiempo, y se deberá hacer con la ayuda indispensable del movimiento asociativo de la discapacidad intelectual, que lleva décadas adaptando entornos y materiales. Ceacog (Centro Español de Accesibilidad Cognitiva ), por ejemplo, aunque es un organismo público, es gestionado por Plena Inclusión y cientos de entidades de todo el país llevan años colaborando con administraciones locales o autonómicas para hacer más accesibles los entornos públicos. Aunque muy despacio, se van dando pasos, unos pasos que con la nueva legislación deberán acelerarse.
Una de las iniciativas más desarrolladas en accesibilidad cognitiva es ‘Construimos Comunidades Accesibles’, un proyecto con el que Plena Inclusión España, a través de sus entidades y federaciones locales, busca nuevas soluciones para mejorar la accesibilidad cognitiva y darlas a conocer a otras organizaciones, a empresas y a la administración pública. "Nace con la idea de generar ciudades, espacios y entornos que sean comprensibles para todo el mundo. Porque cuestiones que para nosotros son cotidianas, como coger un autobús, visitar un museo o disfrutar del arte de nuestra ciudad, para las personas que tienen dificultades de comprensión se convierte en todo un reto y en casi una actividad de riesgo", explica Vanessa García, gerente de Plena Inclusión Castilla y León.
Dentro del proyecto tienen varias iniciativas, pero García destaca sobre todo dos: un proyecto para hacer más comprensible y fácil viajar en autobús por la ciudad de Valladolid y otro con el que quieren acercar el arte a todos los ciudadanos y hacer accesibles las visitas a los museos de la comunidad.
Cuestiones cotidianas, como coger un autobús o visitar un museo, para las personas que tienen dificultades de comprensión se convierte en todo un reto
Moverte por la ciudad de manera autónoma
Desde el año pasado, los autobuses de Auvasa, que dan servicio a la ciudad de Valladolid, son accesibles para las personas con dificultades de comprensión, lo que facilita su autonomía a la hora de moverse por la ciudad. A través de la metodología de la accesibilidad cognitiva y del uso de pictogramas, Plena Inclusión y la Federación de Autismo de Castilla y León facilitan a las personas con trastorno del espectro autista o con otras dificultades de comunicación, la comprensión del ciclo del viaje: subirte, pagar, usar la tarjeta, sentarse, llamar a una parada…
Estas secuencias, que están tanto en los autobuses como en las paradas, se completaron con una guía interna para que los trabajadores de Auvasa supieran dirigirse y ayudar a estas personas si lo necesitaban. "Estas iniciativas facilitan un montón la vida a muchísimas personas, y ya no solo personas con dificultad de comprensión, sino a cualquier ciudadano que tiene otras dificultades de comprensión, que no maneja nuestro idioma…", explica Vanessa García.
En Valladolid, las personas con discapacidad intelectual o con problemas de comprensión han recibido la iniciativa con los brazos abiertos, pues les ayuda a moverse solos. "Es muy satisfactorio poder tener más autonomía, porque al final no es tanto que ellos no tengan capacidad de hacerlo, sino que el entorno a veces es muy difícil de entender, hay muchos estímulos, a veces hay muchos carteles explicando diferentes cosas… Poder entenderlo fácilmente es algo muy positivo para su desarrollo y para su autonomía, pues les permite moverse por la ciudad como cualquier otro ciudadano".
Acercar el arte a personas con problemas de comprensión
Antes incluso de esta iniciativa, impulsaron otra, un proyecto para hacer accesibles los museos de la ciudad y acercar el arte a todas las personas. Para conseguirlo, adaptaron folletos de exposiciones a lectura fácil, folletos validados por personas con discapacidad intelectual. "Hemos hecho esta adaptación para que todas las personas puedan comprender lo que ven y lo que visitan, porque a veces los folletos de los museos no son fáciles de entender, aunque no tengas dificultades de comprensión".
Gracias a estas colaboraciones ha nacido además La Guía Arte para todas las personas, que ha contado con el asesoramiento del Museo Nacional de Escultura, donde explican de forma sencilla qué épocas y qué tipos de arte existen en la historia del arte español. "Queremos acercar a todas las personas algo que 'a priori' puede ser un poco más complicado, más ajeno, más distante a las personas con dificultades de comprensión, pero queremos que ellas también puedan disfrutar de la maravilla del arte", insiste la gerente de Plena Castilla y León.
Además del transporte y el arte, la entidad tiene otra iniciativa, esta vez para acercar la tecnología a las personas con problemas de comprensión. Por un lado, han creado los manuales Digitalizarte, unos textos digitales accesibles, en lectura fácil y gratuitos que permiten estudiar y aprender sobre la tecnología, que pueden ser, como asegura Vanessa García, "un aliado estupendo o pueden aumentar la brecha entre las personas con o sin discapacidad. En estos manuales trabajamos competencias digitales con la teoría básica para poder sacar un certificado de competencias digitales que otorga la Junta de Castilla y León".
Por otro, han creado una guía en lectura fácil sobre ciberseguridad y un Manual de inteligencia artificial para que todas las personas puedan "navegar de forma segura en Internet y disfrutar de las ventajas de la IA y alertarles de sus riegos".
Se necesita financiación, porque detrás de la accesibilidad cognitiva hay personas trabajando
Lectura fácil y validadores: claves del éxito de la accesibilidad cognitiva
Reglamentos como el que se acaba de aprobar pueden ayudar a impulsar la accesibilidad cognitiva, pero para que sea una realidad se necesitan a las entidades, que llevan décadas de ventaja a las administraciones, y presupuestos para llevarlas a cabo. "Cualquier paso que se dé para asegurar y para garantizar la accesibilidad cognitiva es una excelente noticia, pero también es un reglamento de mínimos que necesita la colaboración de las comunidades autónomas y es necesario acompañarlo de una financiación para que el derecho se convierta en realidad, porque detrás de la accesibilidad cognitiva hay personas trabajando".
Y es que para adaptar cognitivamente los espacios se necesitan sobre todo dos cosas: formación y personas. Formación en accesibilidad cognitiva, en lectura fácil -hay que seguir una serie de normas- y validadores, que son personas con discapacidad intelectual que comprueban que la accesibilidad cognitiva se ha hecho correctamente. "Lo normal es que las administraciones recurran a nosotros, que nos digan que quieren accesible algo y establezcamos vías de colaboración, pero para eso se necesita profesionalizar y financiación para poder llevar a cabo estos proyectos".
Además, puede suponer una gran oportunidad laboral para las personas con discapacidad intelectual, un nicho de empleabilidad muy valioso, porque como insisten en Plena Inclusión, "el valor que tiene toda la metodología de accesibilidad cognitiva es que tienes a los propios validadores, que son los que te garantizan si lo que hacemos se está entendiendo, nos sitúan en la realidad".
Una realidad de la que, además, se puede beneficiar más gente de la que parece: "Yo invitaría a todas las administraciones públicas a poner esto ya en marcha porque es una obligación para ellas, pero sobre todo es un derecho de todos los ciudadanos. Y porque es algo que beneficia a todos. Cuando hemos tenido experiencias con las administraciones, por ejemplo, de traducir a lectura fácil formularios de la administración que son súper complejos, y han quedado encantados, han visto que esto beneficia a todos los ciudadanos", concluye Vanessa García.

title: How fantasy fans are keeping a Turkish blacksmithing tradition alive
content:
Kemeralti Bazaar, Izmir, Turkiye – To the casual passer-by, the Akdemir family’s workshop could be any traditional blacksmith’s forge. Dozens of hammers and tongs hang from the walls; kebab skewers, knives and axes lie across the benches; a length of steel glows in the fire. But for those familiar with fantasy worlds and gaming, a second look may be required.
Just a few steps inside the workshop's shutter-style doors, an enormous forged fantasy sword rests across a countertop, similar to the one wielded by the Lich King in the popular video game World of Warcraft. Elsewhere are weapons inspired by TV series and video games, including Game of Thrones and League of Legends, rendered in steel.
At the forge, Suleyman Akdemir, a large man with a furrowed brow, grips a glowing length of metal with long tongs, draws it from the fire, and lays it across the anvil. A few metres away, his father, Omer, 54, reaches for a tool. Then the power hammer crashes down, its blows reverberating through the narrow workshop and out into the covered streets of Izmir’s Kemeralti bazaar, forcing conversation to wait.
Suleyman, 30, wears a brown leather apron over a black T-shirt, his hands encased in black gloves. His father rarely stops working while he talks; Suleyman often pauses, turning towards his customers before returning to the forge.
Between father and son, exchanges are calm, almost formal. Here, they seem less like family than two craftsmen who have spent years learning how to work around one another.
When the hammer falls silent, Suleyman turns from the forge.
“Ever since I was a child. I’d say since I first learned to walk, I've been working here with hot forging,” he says, breaking into a smile.
The surroundings bear that history. The fantasy weapons are newcomers to a workshop where Suleyman's family has practised blacksmithing for generations. Yet, incongruous as they look among the agricultural tools and barbecue skewers, they may be one reason the forge is still running.
“Thank God, we can make anything we see,” Suleyman says.
That conviction has taken the Akdemirs somewhere his predecessors could hardly have imagined. Customers from around the world now send Suleyman images and ideas inspired by weapons they have seen on screen, which he interprets as individually designed, hand-forged pieces.
Kemeralti has been a commercial centre of Izmir for centuries, with its dense network of streets and hans stretching inland from the city's waterfront.
For Suleyman, one of his earliest memories is of its power hammer at his father’s workshop. He was seven or eight, he says, when he became fascinated by the machine, which weighs about 1.5 tonnes.
He watched it rise and fall over the incandescent iron.
“I was spellbound when I saw it,” he says. “I knew right then that I would do this for a living."
By 12, he was using a hammer himself. The first object he forged was considerably less dramatic than the weapons now surrounding him: everyday cooking utensils.
After school, he returned to the workshop, learning to make hoes, billhooks, axes, skewers and other household objects.
Blacksmithing was not his only possible future. Suleyman trained in taekwondo and considered pursuing sport professionally. But the difficulty of building a sustainable career in sport eventually brought him back to the trade he had known since childhood.
By then, the business he was inheriting was beginning to change.
Two or three decades ago, the family says, agricultural tools and basic hardware accounted for nearly all its production. Their customers came largely from Izmir and the surrounding countryside, looking for practical objects made for work. Then some of that work began to disappear.
Factory production could make many everyday tools more cheaply, while changes in the work around them erased the need for others. As tobacco farming declined, so did orders for the needles the Akdemirs once made for growers. Shoemakers who had relied on their hand-forged sole-cutting blades turned instead to laser-cutting technology. Other agricultural tools increasingly faced competition from mass-produced alternatives.
One by one, some of the objects that had kept the forge busy were becoming obsolete.
Omer's generation had inherited a craft. Suleyman was confronting a different question: what happens when people no longer need the things that craft traditionally produces?
"The work my father and his generation do appeals to a specific demographic," he says. "They make general hardware products. But in truth, they craft them with such artistry that I felt it belonged somewhere far beyond."
In 2014, he decided to see how far and opened an Instagram account.
Initially, the internet brought relatively ordinary requests.
Suleyman's first online customer was a police officer in Erzurum who wanted a hand-forged machete for outdoor use. Making it was easier than sending it: the courier repeatedly refused to accept a parcel containing such a sharp blade.
"I went back and forth to the courier four times for a single product," he recalls.
Then, in 2016, an order came in that pointed to an entirely different market.
The Turkish historical drama Dirilis: Ertugrul (Resurrection: Ertugrul) was attracting a huge following at the time. The series would eventually be broadcast in more than 60 countries. One of its main characters, Turgut Alp, carried a distinctive axe.
A customer in Turkiye called the workshop and asked Suleyman to make one; it took him almost a week.
Then another request arrived, and another.
"We made that axe. After that, people started asking, 'Can you make this, can you make that?'” he says. “As we kept doing it, we grew to love it."
The commissions became progressively stranger. Instead of bringing Suleyman an object to copy or describing a familiar tool, customers began sending images from films and games.
A fictional weapon presents a peculiar problem for a blacksmith. On screen, it does not necessarily have to obey the rules of weight, balance or construction. In Suleyman's hands, it must.
When an unfamiliar commission arrives, he sits at a computer at the side of the working area, and rewatches film scenes, pauses gameplay footage to study details before sketching his own version and working out how its components might fit together
"This isn't something you can just 'strike, forge, and hand over.'” he says. “It's an entirely custom design. How will it fit together, how will I cast the mould ... I research every single detail."
For the most complex pieces, developing the first version can take two and a half to three months. Once Suleyman has solved the design, making another becomes easier.
He says he has never looked at a request and thought it impossible. For him, the challenge is simply figuring out how.
Omer has spent most of his life here. He describes a chain of blacksmiths stretching back generations.
"My father's master's master was an apprentice here during the Greek occupation,” he says, referring to the Greek occupation of Izmir between 1919 and 1922. “Then came my father's master, my father, myself, and now my son."
The workshop's history predates the Akdemir family. According to Omer, a man named Sabri Alim was an apprentice there during the Greek occupation, and later took over from his own master, Suleyman Acarlar. In 1955, Omer's father, Suleyman Akdemir, arrived from Konya and began working under Sabri as an apprentice. He eventually took over the workshop himself, before passing the craft to his son Omer.
The family cannot establish that every generation worked in this exact room; what has endured is the blacksmithing tradition within Kemeralti.
Omer studied blacksmithing at vocational high school and later trained in lathe operation, but says the workshop was his real education.
When he began, the workshop produced shoe-sole cutting blades, tobacco needles, and agricultural tools. Laser cutting eventually displaced the blades they made for shoemakers. Tobacco farming declined. Other products simply stopped being ordered.
If that disappearance bothers Omer, he shows little nostalgia for it.
"I am open to progress of any kind,” he says, continuing to work as he talks. “If you stay fixed in one place, you cannot grow. The work we used to do disappeared. What were we supposed to do, insist on making things no one needed?”
Nor does he see anything particularly radical in his son's use of the internet. To Omer, it has simply changed who can find them.
"Suppose someone in a village in Kastamonu wants something custom,” he says, referring to the province in northern Turkiye. “Under normal circumstances, that person could never reach me. But through the internet, they do."
He gestures towards the workshop. "And since we have no shortage of craft skill, we can make whatever anyone asks for."
Almost on cue, the automatic shutter opens. A man walks in carrying an old axe with a loose handle.
Omer takes it to his workbench and begins repairing it. The customer, meanwhile, looks around. His attention moves from the everyday tools towards the swords and oversized axes.
"Did you really make these here?" he asks.
A few minutes later, his axe repaired, he disappears back into Kemeralti.
The transition looks almost seamless now: old axe through the door, fantasy sword on the wall. But it wasn't.
For years, the family's daytime business still revolved around its conventional orders. If Suleyman wanted to experiment, he had to wait until everybody else had finished.
"I worked here at night for nine years."
When Kemeralti's shutters came down, he started again.
He relit the forge, tested quenching temperatures, experimented with moulds and worked through designs he had never attempted before. Some nights, he slept in a small room he had set aside inside the workshop. Then, he got up and returned to work.
As orders grew from one to two, three, five and then 10, the family's initial scepticism turned to curiosity. Suleyman says business volume more than doubled within a year of starting online sales.
Eventually, the experiments he had squeezed into the night became the larger part of the business.
Custom and specialised products now account for roughly 80 to 90 percent of revenue, he says. The workshop handles about 450 orders annually, with customers in countries including Germany, the Netherlands and Switzerland; exports generate about 35 percent of revenue.
A piece that might sell for 2,000 Turkish lira ($40) domestically can command considerably more overseas, Suleyman says.
But the story he enjoys telling most is not about financial success; it’s about a lost axe.
A customer had taken one of his hand-forged axes hiking in the Kaz Mountains, between Balikesir and Canakkale in western Turkiye, and lost it. Months later, someone else found it.
There was no brand or maker's stamp on the steel. Yet, Suleyman says, the finder recognised his workmanship.
"If anyone made this," Suleyman recalls with a laugh, "it has to be Suleyman."
The axe, he says, eventually found its way back to its owner.
At the back of the workshop, another craftsman is quietly working with his hands. But his route here was very different.
Away from the heaviest hammering, wood shavings cover a smaller bench. Yagiz Can Sonmez, 33, works at the sanding station in protective goggles, busily shaping a handle.
Unlike Suleyman, he wasn’t born into blacksmithing, but went looking for it.
Sonmez had previously worked as a sadekar, a goldsmith artisan, in Istanbul's Grand Bazaar. After studying at university, he moved to Izmir and opened a shoe boutique in Alsancak with his wife.
"One day, while sitting in the store, my fascination with hot metalwork resurfaced," he says. "I started researching online to see who was doing this in Izmir. That's how I found Suleyman."
At first, he came just to watch. Then he started returning on weekends, picked up the hammer, and began learning. Eventually, he closed the boutique and moved into blacksmithing full-time.
"What drew me here is the ability to project what's in your mind and soul onto a hard metal,” he says. “It comes from within. You start a project with nothing specific in mind, and as you progress, something takes shape. In the end, the final piece is something you couldn't have even envisioned at the start."
His background in goldsmithing gives him a different approach to the work.
"Suleyman leans toward classic designs. I focus more on intricate, detailed work. Blending those two approaches works well for us; it’s like two opposing poles coming together."
"Our styles are different," Suleyman says, smiling.
A neat symmetry seems to run through their journeys into the craft. Suleyman had turned to the internet to find people interested in what an old forge could make, while years later, Yagiz used the internet to find someone who could teach him how to forge.
Suleyman hopes eventually to establish a creative space locally where visitors could try blacksmithing and encounter woodworking and leathercraft alongside it.
There are not many places left in Kemeralti where someone like Yagiz could have done this.
According to Akin Oz, vice president of the Izmir Ironworkers Craftsmen and Artisans Chamber, Solomon Metal is now the only active hot-blacksmithing operation remaining in the historic bazaar.
The decline is visible in the objects Omer no longer makes: blades replaced by laser cutting, tobacco needles left behind by changes in farming, tools undercut by industrial production.
Traditional craftsmanship is one of five forms of “intangible cultural heritage” recognised under a UNESCO convention adopted in 2003 and ratified by Turkiye in 2006. The designation is concerned less with preserving the objects craftspeople produce than with safeguarding the knowledge and skills used to make them, and ensuring those skills are passed on.
Inside the Akdemir workshop, that distinction is easy to understand.
It is knowing how to judge the heat of iron by eye; how to bring the hammer down at the correct angle; how to temper the steel. It is knowledge acquired by standing beside somebody who already knows, says Suleyman.
By late afternoon, Kemeralti begins to empty. Tea sellers collect empty glasses. The crowds in the narrow alleys thin. Inside the workshop, the three men are still at their stations. After pounding through the workshop for much of the day, the power hammer finally falls silent.
Generations ago, the customers seeking out the family's blacksmiths needed tools for the work immediately around them. Today, some live thousands of kilometres away. They find Suleyman through a screen and send him images of objects that may never have existed outside one.
And despite everything that has changed, the request often comes down to something remarkably simple. Can you make this?
Suleyman has spent most of his life working out the answer. "I can."

title: 4 Indian places where water shapes everyday life
content:
India’s diverse landscape is home to settlements where water is much more than a scenic backdrop. For some communities, lakes and rivers are roads, workplaces and sources of food; for others, homes and agricultural spaces have evolved around constantly changing water levels.
From Manipur’s floating phumdis to Kashmir’s lake settlements and Assam’s river islands, these places offer a glimpse into lifestyles shaped by water.
If one landscape in India most closely resembles a floating world, it is Loktak Lake in Manipur. The lake is known for phumdis — floating masses of vegetation, soil and organic matter that have accumulated over time. Fishing communities have traditionally used these waters for their livelihoods, with small huts and boats scattered across parts of the lake.
Loktak is also home to Keibul Lamjao National Park, the world’s only floating national park. The protected area sits on the lake’s phumdis and is famous for the endangered sangai, or Manipur brow-antlered deer.
Srinagar’s Dal Lake is best known for its houseboats and shikaras, but the lake is also closely intertwined with the lives of communities that live and work on and around its waters. Floating gardens grow vegetables, and boats transport the produce to markets. Early-morning vegetable markets on the lake are among the most distinctive experiences for visitors.
Houseboats, shikaras, fishing and water-based cultivation have together created a way of life that is difficult to separate from the lake itself.
Majuli is technically a river island rather than a floating village, but its existence is deeply tied to the Brahmaputra. Located in Assam, the island has long been home to communities whose lives have adapted to the river’s seasonal flooding, erosion and shifting channels. Agriculture, fishing and boat transport remain important parts of life.
The island is also an important centre of Assamese Vaishnavite culture, with its Satras and traditions of mask-making, music and performing arts.
In the Sundarbans, villages exist within one of the world’s largest mangrove delta systems, where rivers, creeks and tidal channels dominate the landscape. It isn’t a floating village in the literal sense. Instead, it shows communities adapting to a landscape where the boundary between land and water is constantly shifting.
Boats are an important means of transport in many parts of the region, while fishing, crab collection, honey gathering and agriculture support local communities. Life here is also shaped by the challenges of living in a tidal landscape. Cyclones, flooding, erosion and increasing salinity can affect homes and livelihoods.

title: Keeping Kadazandusun and Iban alive for the next generation
content:
But many are at risk of fading, with an estimated 65% of Sabah’s Dusunic community no longer speaking their mother tongue.
It might be surprising to learn that efforts to keep some of these languages alive are taking place in peninsular Malaysia. In 2010, Universiti Pendidikan Sultan Idris (UPSI) in Tanjong Malim, Perak, became the first higher education institution in the country to offer tertiary programmes in Kadazandusun and Iban.
Julita Norjietta Taisin joined UPSI that year to teach Kadazandusun, her area of expertise. At the time, Kadazandusun and Iban were offered only as minor programmes under the department of Malay language and literature.
