In 2024, UPSI introduced Semai and expanded all three into majors under its Bachelor of Education programme.
Some students are also pursuing master’s and PhD degrees, helping to build a wider pool of teachers and specialists in these languages.
Iban was officially introduced in primary schools in 1968 and secondary schools in 1988, while Kadazandusun followed via pilot projects in primary schools in 1997 and secondary schools in 2006.
Yet a major challenge remains: there is a critical shortage of qualified teachers formally trained to teach these languages.
“I’ve noticed that more and more young people no longer use Kadazandusun in their daily conversations,” said Julita, who hails from Tuaran, Sabah.
“The biggest challenge is not simply that young people do not want to learn – they need to have the opportunities and reasons to use the language.”
She also highlighted the need for more learning materials, applications, and creative digital and social media content in Kadazandusun.
“As the number of native speakers dwindles, not only is the language itself threatened: expressions, folklore, proverbs, traditional knowledge and cultural values are also at risk of being lost.
“If we lose our language, we lose our identity,” she said.
Beyond the classroom, Julita said UPSI’s Sabah Native Student Association organises annual activities that give Malay, Chinese and Indian students the opportunity to learn Kadazandusun.
A similar effort is under way with Iban. Saripah Anak Banseng has been a lecturer at UPSI since 2020, specialising in the language. She initially pursued science before changing paths and eventually earning a PhD focusing on her mother tongue.
“I’m from Sri Aman, Sarawak, and I grew up in a longhouse community living the Iban way of life,” she told FMT Lifestyle.
“When I was young, we had no electricity, and we had to walk for more than an hour to school and travel by boat to reach the town.”
Saripah said all UPSI students currently taking the language programme are native speakers, but factors such as mixed marriages and living away from Sarawak mean Iban is not always part of their everyday lives.
Around 35 students are enrolled in UPSI’s Iban major programme, while an estimated 100 took the minor programme between 2024 and 2026. There are also 11 master’s and three PhD students.
“A language cannot simply be documented in a museum,” she said. “Even in my classes, I remind students that language does not exist only on paper – we need to use it outside the classroom.
“Perhaps one day, Iban may even become a medium of instruction in peninsular Malaysia.”
Although she grew up speaking Iban, Saripah said further study opened her eyes to the language’s intricacies, structure and uniqueness – aspects she had previously understood only instinctively.
“At first we may see language simply as a tool to communicate, but when we study it deeply, we understand the world better,” she added.
Speaking a week before Malaysia Day, Julita reflected on what the occasion means to her as a Sabahan living in peninsular Malaysia.
“Malaysia Day reminds me of Sabah’s role and position in the formation of Malaysia. I will continue to be proud to carry my Sabah identity and culture with me wherever I go,” she said.
For Saripah, Malaysia Day carries an equally important reminder: that Malaysia’s diversity must be understood and appreciated beyond a single day of celebration.
“We always talk about harmony, but harmony doesn’t only happen when we get together to celebrate one day. It is also about understanding one another’s way of life, language, history and culture.”

title: One quarter of Australian kids are 'developmentally vulnerable' when they start school
content:
We know the first five years are a crucial time in a child's life. Early experiences, such as family relationships or exposure to trauma, shape brain architecture, which lays the foundation for children's learning, behavior and health.
Worryingly, a significant proportion of young Australians are not getting the positive early experiences they need. As of 2024, almost 25% of Australian children were identified as "developmentally vulnerable" by the time they start school. This means many children lack the self-regulation, thinking, language, resilience and social skills needed for learning and getting along with their peers.
Without early intervention, problems with brain development and antisocial behavior become entrenched and can have a lasting impact.
But our research, based in Australian child care centers, shows that intensive, high-quality education and care can help children catch up.
How the intervention works
Research shows high-quality early education programs can help prevent or reduce the disruptive impact of trauma and stress on vulnerable children.
In 2009, we designed a program to operate in a child care center for Australian children living with significant social disadvantage and exposure to trauma, abuse or neglect. This can include family violence or alcohol or substance abuse. We have since replicated and tested it in various locations.
To participate in our program, children are referred by community health and child protection professionals. Children attend the program for five hours a day, five days a week for three years. There is no cost to families.
The program is currently being run at three sites in partnership with three child care providers in Victoria and Queensland, with 108 children participating.
What's involved?
The program is more intensive than usual early learning and care to match the complex needs of the children and families.
Educators are supported by an expert team that includes early childhood education leaders, infant mental health specialists and social workers who work with families with complex needs. The expert team provides practical advice to educators to help them work with these families and children.
Children are provided with nourishing, homemade food for breakfast, morning snack, lunch and afternoon snack every day at the center. Learning is individualized to meet children's interests and abilities. There are purposefully designed indoor and outdoor play spaces and equipment.
Families also get wraparound support without judgment from the staff team. For example, if parents ask for help with sleep routines or feeding problems, staff respond in respectful and practical ways. Every interaction with a parent is welcoming and kind.
The program is designed to provide children with a stable, safe, holistic, high-quality, relationship-focused education and care model. Evidence indicates this reduces the impact of trauma so children can engage in play and learning and helps families connect with local community support.
Does it work?
Children's outcomes are assessed independently after one and two years by qualified clinical researchers.
A recent evaluation of the program shows that after one year, children saw an average increase of 11.6 points in scores for resilience, capacity for self-regulation and capacity to form attachments with others (according to a standard scale).
Children also showed a 7.2-point increase in language development and a 4.6-point increase in IQ.
We will next assess children after two years in the program, before they start school.
These mirror other findings
These findings are similar to those from an original trial of our program. In 2022, we published the results of a randomized controlled trial of the model.
Here, we tracked 72 children who had participated in our program and compared their development outcomes with those of 73 children with similar backgrounds who participated in a mix of parental care and usual early education programs. The differences in outcomes between the two cohorts indicate that intensive, targeted programs are highly beneficial for children living with significant family stress and disadvantage.
We found large, significant positive cognitive and social-emotional outcomes for children after two years. We also found improved language outcomes after three years' participation compared with children who had not been in the program.
The outcomes from the 2026 evaluation are particularly noteworthy because the children entered the program with more family risk factors than the original group we studied.
What next?
Children's outcomes from our program suggest there is a role for targeted, intensive programs in the early education and care system for children from disadvantaged backgrounds.
Our research provides evidence that intervening early—well before children start school—has the potential to make a significant difference to children's life trajectories.
Our research also suggests that families and children are living with increasingly complex and heightened levels of risk and hardship. It is unrealistic to expect early childhood educators to manage these complex risks without the support of other professionals, such as infant mental health practitioners.
This means we need additional targeted funding to support multidisciplinary, experienced and qualified leaders and educators in early learning services.
Then we can directly help children living with high levels of disadvantage to ensure they start school on an equal developmental footing with their peers.

title: Displaced by a typhoon, Taiwan’s Bunun people fear for the future of their culture
content:
- More than a hundred Bunun Indigenous people were forced to resettle in lowland areas after 2009’s Typhoon Morakot destroyed the only road leading to Tengjhih, their mountain settlement, in southern Taiwan.
- The Bunun, who believe the connection to their ancestors is a pillar of their identity, still wish to return to their ancestral land, saying it would allow them to preserve rituals and traditional knowledge.
- Each year, however, climate change is making rainfall more destructive, wreaking havoc on efforts to rebuild and reopen the road to Tengjhih.
- Indigenous communities have heavily criticized the government’s resettlement program, under which families receive ownership of the apartments they are given, but not of the land on which the buildings stand.
TENGJHIH HAMLET, Taiwan – Nestled high on a mountain slope in southern Taiwan, Tengjhih was a key settlement of the Bunun Indigenous people. Today, however, little remains but memories of the hamlet.
Wild grass sprouts around abandoned houses. Stray dogs have made the empty streets their territory. The children’s toys and chairs scattered across the ground hint at a hurried departure.
Bunun leader Dahu Ismahasan is visibly moved as he looks at what is left of his village.
“When we were children, we played here. We were happy, innocent,” he says.
But “now the village is destroyed,” says Dahu, who is president of the Bunun tribal council.
Dahu and fellow villagers had to leave Tengjhih in the wake of Typhoon Morakot, which killed 755 people in 2009 across Taiwan. The deadliest storm in the island’s recorded history brought torrential rainfall, causing floods and landslides primarily in mountainous Indigenous territories.
At the time, Indigenous peoples accounted for only 2.1% of Taiwan’s total population; yet in the aftermath of Morakot, around 70% of areas deemed unsafe by the government were located in Indigenous territories.
Nobody in Tengjhih died during Morakot, but the typhoon destroyed the only road leading to the hamlet.
With Tengjhih declared a “high-risk zone”, authorities in 2009 began permanently resettling its 150 residents, mostly in surrounding lower-elevation areas like Kaohsiung, Taiwan’s third-largest city, and Liouguei District, Dahu says.
Morakot also displaced other highland Indigenous communities such as the Tsou, the Paiwan and the Rukai. Like the Bunun, they were also resettled in lower-altitude areas.
Typhoon season typically runs from July through September in Taiwan. Climate change has led to more destructive levels of rainfall during these months, wreaking havoc on efforts to rebuild and reopen the road to Tengjhih.
Authorities halted repairs shortly after a typhoon in 2012 washed away a section of the road. Attempts to fix the route faced another setback in 2021, also due to extreme weather.
In 2023, 14 years after Morakot, the road was finally rebuilt. But just a few months later, another typhoon washed it away. Repeated torrential rains, intensified by climate change, saturated the mountain soil, triggering landslides and putting the settlement at risk. In 2025, another typhoon tore away yet another section of the mountainside.
Preserving cultural heritage
Dahu, 60, now lives in Liouguei, but still makes occasional trips to his ancestral home to reconnect with the mountain.
It is a risky journey. To reach Tengjhih, he has to drive along an alternative mountain road that’s narrow and has no safety barriers.
On the way back, he makes a stop at the neighboring hamlet of Erjituan to visit his 85-year-old mother, Clrenge Ismahasan. Erjituan and Tengjhih are two of the three hamlets that make up Baoshan village, home to the Tengjhih Forest Recreation Area.
In a school classroom, Clrenge and two other elderly Bunun women sit at a table drawing as they listen to traditional Indigenous songs.
Dahu’s mother, who moved to Erjituan after Morakot, still has vivid memories of the day the typhoon struck. “That day, it was pouring,” she tells Mongabay. “Everything was flooded. We couldn’t get down from the mountain.”
She remembers that in Tengjhih, people grew corn, millet and beans. “The men would go hunting and come back two or three days later.”
When asked what they miss most about their ancestral home, the women all look down at their drawings and give no answers.
“It’s too painful for them,” Dahu says. “They know they will never see the village again in their lifetime.”
For the Bunun people, the connection to ancestors is a pillar of their identity. Dahu, who now lives in Liouguei, says returning to their ancestral land is important, as it allows them to preserve traditional rituals and knowledge, from hunting and gathering to cultural practices and ways of teaching younger generations.
Nearly 20 years after the typhoon, Dahu and other villagers still regularly write to the local government to make their case. They are still hoping — and fighting — to return home.
“If this village disappears, our people will disappear too,” Dahu says.
Clrenge says she harbors the same wish. “If we can’t return to the village, who is going to pass on these practices?”
Back in Tengjhih, Saminat Maliklan is one of five residents who still refuse to relocate, choosing to stay in her small wooden house that was spared by the typhoon.
As she prepares tea made from leaves picked from her garden, she looks at her 11-year-old granddaughter visiting from Kaohsiung, a city around 60 kilometers away.
To preserve her culture, Saminat, a Bunun cultural guide, teaches traditional songs and the Bunun language to children in the community.
“I pass on everyday Bunun practices to my granddaughter: carrying wood, pulling weeds, planting things,” she says. “And when it comes to language, I try as much as possible to speak with her in our mother tongue.”
Fading connection
Traditionally, young Bunun people would leave the mountains to study at secondary schools and universities in the lowlands, then return to the village to settle down and start families. However, they no longer have that choice.
“Today, when they come back, there is no village and no work,” says 55-year-old Saminat.
Instead, they are uprooted from their ancestral land, she adds: “They have to adapt to an unfamiliar environment, and their ties with elders gradually fade. Our rituals and ceremonies are disappearing.”
Tengjhih’s economy mainly relied on tourism and agriculture. Morakot and successive typhoons have not only destroyed the access road but also forced the government to indefinitely close the surrounding Tengjhih forest area, which supported livelihoods.
For people like Bi’ Ismahasan, who grows tea and coffee in a settlement near Tengjhih and runs a small business catering to tourists, these sources of income are no longer viable.
“When a major typhoon hits us, I have no income for the entire year,” says the 70-year-old woman. “In 2026, I lost my entire harvest. Every year is worse than the previous one.
“I lost all the customers who used to come to visit Tengjhih. Today, I survive on government assistance.”
Her children and grandchildren all now live in Kaohsiung.
“In the cities, young people from the same communities form associations and organize cultural activities so they don’t forget our seasonal rituals,” Bi’ tells Mongabay. “But deep down, I’m afraid that the emotional connection will slowly fade.”
There are also worries of spiritual disconnect. “Our children will no longer be able to bury us in the mountains,” Dahu says. “And our souls will not be able to return to our ancestral land. We will be condemned to wander far away. It’s truly pitiful, isn’t it?”
No prior consultation
In 2005, four years before Morakot, Taiwan passed the Indigenous Peoples Basic Law, of which Article 21 explicitly establishes the principle of “free, prior and informed consent” (FPIC) for Indigenous tribes. It stipulates that the government must consult with tribes and obtain their consent before carrying out development projects on Indigenous lands.
“But in the case of the Bunun, the relocation of the villages was decided without prior consultation,” says Tunkan Tansikian, a Bunun and an Indigenous rights and policy scholar at National Dong Hwa University. “This naturally led to a loss of trust in the government.”
A report published in April 2022 by Taiwan’s Control Yuan, the government’s audit office, recommended incorporating Indigenous perspectives and traditional knowledge into the reassessment of sites at risk from natural disasters. The government responded with reforms, which the Control Yuan summarized in a report in May 2026. However, the document does not list all at-risk settlements and does not name Tengjhih.
Indigenous communities have heavily criticized the Morakot resettlement program. Families receive ownership of the apartments they are given, according to news reports, but not of the land on which the buildings stand. As a result, they cannot sell, expand or rebuild their homes.
“The purpose of the resettlement program was to persuade residents to abandon their mountain villages, which were considered dangerous, in order to reduce safety risks,” Tunkan says.
“For Indigenous peoples, however, land is a core part of their culture, rather than being treated as a tradable and easily relinquished commodity, as mainstream society does.”
The Taoyuan District Office, which oversees Tengjhih, has ruled out allowing the Bunun to resettle in their ancestral home.
“The site is not suitable for habitation due to landslides, and the option under consideration would be to let residents build a temporary shelter there for short stays, without settling permanently,” it tells Mongabay.
Dahu disagrees, saying that authorities have cited no in-depth geotechnical study to justify their refusal, instead simply invoking the risk of landslides.
After years of campaigning, he eventually secured the construction of an alternative road that would provide, at least, access to the settlement. It is scheduled to open in January 2027, he says. Despite the hope it has brought, continued climate instability makes its opening uncertain.
“We still have hope,” Dahu says. “The wind and rain won’t last forever. One day, the road will be better, and the lives of the people here will be better too. We keep that hope in our prayers.”

title: Hundreds recruited to help foster kids visit birth families in NSW
content:
NSW overhauls supervised foster care visits with new Family Time team
In short:
NSW's approach to foster care supervised visits has been revamped with new specialist workers.
Family Time helps kids build connections with their birth families, and ease the impact of separation.
Parents and children will now catch-up at "beautiful venues" like parks or ice skating rinks to create "positive memories".
Thousands of children in foster care are improving ties with their birth families, as part of an overhauled supervision system in New South Wales.
More than 300 specialist workers have now been recruited by the Department of Communities and Justice to accompany children on supervised family visits.
These Family Time visits can vary widely in setting — from picnics and sports events, to theme parks and zoos.
Kylie Stone is among the recent recruits, whose own childhood experience of family separation motivated her to join the team.
She grew up in outer-western Sydney, where her father grappled with addiction and went to prison when she was aged 11.
"I just remember waiting for all my letters to come or waiting for phone calls and wanting to go and see my dad," she said.
Now, Ms Stone is determined to make a difference to other families' lives in her old neighbourhood.
One of her proudest moments in the job involved a young mother and her child who had been removed from her care while she sought treatment for an addiction.
"I started working with her when her baby was three months old. We shared her first Easter, her first birthday, her first Christmas together,"she said.
"There were days that she did struggle and she's like, 'I don't know if I can do this', and she's actually now gone through final orders and she's getting her little girl back.
"Honestly, it gives me goosebumps."
Ms Stone acknowledges while permanent family reunification is not always feasible, supervised contact provides a "safe place" to build connections and ease the impact of separation.
Supervised family visits have long been a feature of the state's foster care system, but previously they were run by caseworkers in the private sector.
It was a system that Families and Communities Minister Kate Washington argued was plagued by poor training and a high staff turnover, which would often make it a distressing experience.
"When a different person was turning up to their door every single time, they didn't know the child, they didn't know the families,"she said.
Ms Washington said bringing the program in-house had ensured there was rigorous oversight and training of workers.
There is also a strong focus on making sure Family Time workers are culturally-matched, and to date, almost 20 per cent of the team identifies as Aboriginal.
Growing focus on Aboriginal kinships
One of the new program officers is Cody McGrady Miller, a Gomeroi and Wonnurua man who was 12 years old when he was removed from his mother's care by caseworkers and police.
He and his sister were placed in the care of his great-aunty in south-west Sydney, and said the turnover of casework teams "make it really difficult".
"Back then, there was not much understanding around Aboriginal kinship systems and the way in which our communities support children," he said.
Now he works with the Family Time team in Tamworth, and has led efforts to ensure supervised visits are culturally appropriate.
"For us as Aboriginal people, I think that connection is one of the most significant parts of culture, and with the lived experience, I feel like that I can really contribute to ensuring that there's a better experience for children and young people in care," he said.
Building a 'legacy' for families
Supervisors typically write detailed reports after each visit, which is often used for family law or court proceedings.
But Nicholle Andreuzza from the Department of Communities and Justice said there had been a move away from the "clinical" approach to supervising family visits.
"What we're seeing now is beautiful venues," Ms Andreuzza said.
"We're seeing kids and mum and dad at soccer fields with the support of their Family Time work, we're seeing kids having experiences like ice skating, we do some visits in home when safe to do so."
Ms Andreuzza said the Family Time workers also played an important "legacy" role, by taking pictures during the visits.
"So for kids when they get older … they're able to look at photographs and look at all of the positive moments that they've had with their mums, dads, brothers, sisters, uncles, aunties," she said.

title: THE CONVERSATION: What happened when a South African school switched from English to bilingual science tests
content:
South African no-fee primary schools use African languages as well as English for teaching and testing. Before 2025, children started learning in their home language in the first three years and then switched to English in Grade 4 (aged 10 and 11). Now, bilingual education is extending gradually into the upper primary grades.
South Africa’s public basic education system serves roughly 12.7 million learners. 80% of these learn through a language that is not their home language.
I am an education researcher with a special interest in language across the curriculum in multilingual contexts. In a recent case study of a bilingual science learning intervention in a Cape Town school, I wanted to know how effective it was to teach and test in more than one language, and what parents thought of the approach. Past studies hadn’t made it clear whether parents usually supported it.
The study found that teaching and testing science topics in the children’s home language and English produced much better results than using English only, and that parents were in favour of it.
The results suggest that bilingual classroom teaching and assessment could be used more widely, and it’s important to make sure parents understand why.
Better test results using two languages
The study took place in a school in Khayelitsha, in the Western Cape. The no-fee school attracts learners from a wide area because it is well run. At the time of the study, the school language policy was English medium in all subjects in Grade 4, including science. The principal, however, agreed to try the bilingual approach in science for the study.
We gave 168 Grade 4 learners a bilingual science textbook in English and isiXhosa, their home language. The same teacher taught four classes bilingually, and learners used both languages in writing in their exercise books. One class was given a bilingual test while the others wrote the conventional English-only test.
The findings showed that children were more engaged in their learning in class compared with similar aged children who were learning in English only. In our study children contributed more to class discussion and wrote more in their exercise books.
In addition, those who wrote the bilingual test, with all questions written in isiXhosa and English, scored an 86% pass rate. Those who wrote the English-only test scored a 51% pass rate.
What parents said
The parents of the children in the study said during a feedback session after the test was written that they were very happy with the programme. They commented on how the bilingual textbook connected them with their child’s learning at home. Parents said their children taught them about science while at home – making links between the world around them and the concepts they were learning at school.
One parent said:
My child came back home more interested in things happening around us.
Another mentioned their own ability to get more involved in their child’s schoolwork when using their own language:
Sometimes a parent may be busy cooking, so when they ask a question you are able to answer even if you didn’t see the question.
Similarly, a parent said:
I went through the pages and read for myself without calling my child and asking what it said.
Parents also described how using more than one language was common in their neighbourhoods. Their children were multilingual and translated for one another when something was not understood. Therefore, the bilingual model of language use at school was closer to language use at home.
One parent noted that they had high hopes for their child continuing with science as a career one day because of this strong start. Parents also wanted to know if mother tongue based bilingual education would be rolled out across the country and in all grades.
None of the parents expressed a concern about their children losing out on English.
Debates on language in the classroom
This last point is important because the dominance of English in society leads to a popular belief that the earlier children learn through English only, the better equipped they will be for the world of higher education and the workplace later on. Teachers report feeling a pressure from parents to avoid code-switching from English into an African language.
In reality, research shows that English-only education contributes to the low achievement of South African children, especially in subjects such as mathematics and science.
When parents have been surveyed on their opinions about language in education, they have usually been given an unenviable choice between monolingual English or monolingual African language instruction.
Furthermore, parents have had little to no exposure to strong models of bilingual education in English and an African language to draw on in their responses. Often the only association black South Africans have with home language teaching is with Bantu Education, the inferior system that the apartheid state designed for black children between 1953 and 1979.
Bilingual programmes can succeed
The bilingual science study demonstrates that when a bilingual programme is well resourced with teaching, assessment and bilingual learning materials it can produce excellent results.
Furthermore, when parents are well informed about bilingual learning, they support it. Parents can appreciate the positive impact of children’s full participation in their learning, both for school and for life outside school. DM

title: Indigenous Futurism: Kichwa Art as Memory in Motion
content: Indigenous Futurism: Kichwa Art as Memory in Motion tia.roberts Tue, 09/15/2026 - 16:12 CSQ Issue 50-3. Cultural Sovereignty: Self-Determination Through Indigenous Governance September 2026 Read on Issuu Buy a copy Subscribe For as long as I can remember, art and story-telling have surrounded every corner of my life. Embraced through every detail, showing up in music, songs, textiles, food, and celebration, for me, art, culture, and identity are inseparable. They are roots that expand from my body to my homelands, grounding me to my community no matter what territory I find myself in, always strong, always present. The love I have for my culture and for the people I come from has always been the reason to channel that collective memory, that collective love of our community. I come from a culture where people carry art into all aspects of their lives. I am the daughter and granddaughter of artisans, musicians, textile weavers, and mindalaes, who are artists, merchants, musicians, dancers, and cultural carriers. They have built systems of commerce across territories, creating paths that allowed Kichwa Otavalo communities to sustain themselves economically around the world. I was never formally taught how to draw or paint. Our art is intergenerational, influenced and guided by the love of all those who came before us. Today, I call myself an artist through digital illustration, photo embroidery, murals, and wearable art. Wherever I go, I am proudly Kichwa Otavalo, carrying the Imbabura mountain in my body and the love, knowledge, and memory of my grandparents and ancestors; a whole universe of generations compacted in my heart. “water yourself” (2024). Wherever Kichwa Otavalo people migrate out of necessity, we carry our culture with us. There is no way to separate our bodies from our territory. It is so deeply embedded in our memory that it traverses colonial borders and generations. Our art has always been a way to sustain ourselves, creating those spaces while being away from home. At the root, it has been the beating heart of the Kichwa Otavalo Peoples. Drawing and illustration entered my life during college. What began as something fun and grounding became a way of processing identity, memory, and belonging. As I continued creating, I noticed I was constantly drawing variations of the same image: myself wearing my traditional clothing, the anaco. Over time, I realized that every drawing held something deeper than a woman in traditional clothing. When I wear my anaco, I feel the most elegant and the most beautiful. Those drawings transported me back to being a little girl, my mom helping me get dressed, placing each piece, teaching me how to wear it. My mother, my first teacher, the first storyteller I met, the first artist I knew. Through drawing, I was bringing those memories, those relationships, those raw feelings, pieces of home, into every space I occupied. It took me years to confidently call myself an artist, despite coming from a culture that lives and breathes art. Yet the more I created, the more intention it carried, and I began to find language to describe why creating Kichwa art in the present matters. For me, art has always been political and never separate from resistance. Every illustration, every mural, every piece of wearable art is a way to assert our presence. That same force moved me to create work in response to the violence my community was facing—artwork that took direct action and broke into the news cycle, making the message land. That is what brought me to Kichwa Futurism. “Pawkar Szn” (2025). Indigenous Futurism as a term has always resonated with me, but Kichwa Futurism is how I name it from where I stand, explicitly centering my people, our territory, and the Global South in a conversation that often looks only northward. It is the belief that Kichwa people belong in the future just as much as we belong in the past and present. Too often, Indigenous people are imagined only through books, museums, or tokenized narratives. Yet our communities are living and continuously creating new ways of expressing our existence in the world. Kichwa Futurism is alive across every creative form our people are working in, bringing our identity into spaces where Indigenous music, visual art, film, photography, and fashion haven’t always been centered. I am equally inspired by Kichwa artists and creatives in the diaspora, those of us creating from distance, holding our culture with the love that comes from knowing what it means to be far. Indigenous Futurism creates space to imagine ourselves beyond settler colonialism, asking what is possible when Indigenous people can visualize and manifest our own futures. Our art and our futures are an extension of our bodies, universes, galaxies, the manifestation of the dreams of all our relatives. Every time I create, I am pushing back against the idea that we can only be seen through a settler colonial gaze. Art has allowed me to contribute to representation that goes beyond visibility. It has become a way to reclaim narratives and ensure that our voices actually take up space. When people from my community see themselves in my work, I am always reminded of how powerful that is, not only for newer generations, but for little me, who never saw herself reflected anywhere. Sharing my work online opened something I didn’t expect. It brought me to other Kichwa youth in the diaspora, people who saw my work and recognized themselves in it, and from those connections grew some of my deepest friendships. Creating art has allowed me to contribute a part of myself to the collective history of our community, a way to show up as a Kichwa Otavalo warmi (woman) from the diaspora, raw and unromanticized, outside of any tokenized frame. “Ñuka Adina” (2021). Within Ecuador, Indigenous identities are constantly co-opted by nationalist narratives, the idea that our culture belongs to everyone, that it is simply part of being Ecuadorian. Yet, Indigenous communities continue to face discrimination, exclusion, and racism, celebrating Indigenous aesthetics while actively erasing Indigenous people. Every year when I go back home for Inti Raymi, I see it firsthand: Ecuadorians and tourists wearing our clothing, playing dress-up in the name of celebration, as if our identity were a costume available to anyone who wants to try it on. But this is not only a phenomenon of Inti Raymi. Brands use the Kichwa language for business names, our symbols for marketing, our people as props, and call it appreciation. Politicians wear our clothing to get votes. Folklore dance groups perform our dances outside any cultural context. Even in the diaspora, the appropriation of our identity continues, people claiming identity without community attachment, while the extraction of our culture and bodies goes unnamed. I see this most visibly in the anaco. For Kichwa women, our traditional clothing is not simply an outfit or a symbol of Ecuadorian heritage. It is a political act of resistance. Every time someone treats it as a costume, they are not just borrowing an aesthetic. They are participating in the erasure of what it actually means to wear it, to carry it, and everything it took to still be able to wear it till this day. This is why it is so important for Indigenous people to create from our own eyes and experience. To tell our own stories from memory, responsibility, and lived experience that cannot be replicated from the outside. To move away from stereotypes and create space for how we want to be seen. “Ñuka" (2021). For me, art is both self-expression and responsibility. It is a way of honoring the people who came before me and honoring the futures that will come after me. Every work I create becomes part of the collective memory of who we are. It is my little seed for the future generation of Kichwa youth, artists, and creatives. Kichwa art lives in our bodies, and we carry our homelands wherever we go. The most radical act of love we can do is to speak from our experiences into every space we walk into. Adina Farinango is an Indigenous Kichwa Otavalo artist and designer based between Lenapehoking/New York City and Ecuador. Learn more about her work at adinafarinango.com and follow her Instagram account @adinasdoodles. Top image: “Sapi” (2021). All art by Adina Farinango. Main Image

title: Víctor M. Quintana S.: La lucha lagunera abre vía para defender el agua
content:
uienes más defienden el agua en este país –y en casi todo el planeta– no son los estados, sino muy diversas organizaciones y movimientos de base. No es extraño: quienes más sufren de la escasez o de la contaminación del vital líquido son las comunidades rurales, los usuarios urbanos, los pueblos indígenas y los pequeños y medianos agricultores.
En toda nuestra geografía bullen los movimientos en defensa del agua: en la Huasteca, comunidades indígenas y mestizas, así como organizaciones del noreste del país, se oponen al fracking y exigen un blindaje presidencial, porque reducirá y contaminará el agua de todas y de todos; el colectivo Tierra Mestiza lucha contra la apropiación del agua por parte de embotelladoras y empresas privadas en la región de Cholula, Puebla; las y los ciudadanos de la zona metropolitana de Guadalajara luchan contra la privatización del líquido y por tener agua verdaderamente potable; en Ascensión, Chihuahua, las y los ejidatarios se oponen a los pozos clandestinos y al tendido de líneas que los electrifican, porque están abatiendo sus acuíferos y los niveles freáticos se contaminan de metales pesados. En varias lenguas indígenas, en castellano, con acentos del sur, del centro y del norte del país, el grito es el mismo: “Agua para todas y para todos, agua para la vida”.
Para todos ellos ha abierto una brecha importante el triunfo esculpido a pulso por las organizaciones ciudadanas de la Comarca Lagunera. La Suprema Corte de Justicia de la Nación (SCJN) acaba de rechazar el intento de la Comisión Nacional del Agua (Conagua) y la Consejería Jurídica de la Presidencia por modificar la sentencia número 543 que protege el acuífero principal de la Comarca Lagunera. La ejecutoria del amparo en revisión 543/2022 ordenó cesar las acciones que agravan la sobrexplotación del acuífero mencionado, y al dejar sin materia el recurso de Conagua y la Consejería Jurídica, la Corte determina que la resolución del amparo sigue vigente, firme y con plena fuerza ejecutoria.
Ya habíamos relatado en estas mismas páginas la saga de las organizaciones sociales de la comarca: Prodefensa del Nazas, Encuentro Ciudadano Lagunero y Desarrollo Cardenista para el Campo Lagunero, que en 2019 interpusieron un amparo contra la Secretaría de Medio Ambiente y Recursos Naturales (Semarnat) y la Conagua, porque sus acciones y omisiones incidían en la sobrexplotación del acuífero y no garantizaban el derecho humano al agua de la población. Cuatro años después, el 1º de marzo de 2023, la primera sala de la SCJN emitió la sentencia 543, en la que aprueba por unanimidad otorgar el amparo de la justicia federal contra la sobrexplotación del acuífero Principal Región Lagunera y ordena a la Conagua, la Semarnat y al organismo Cuencas Centrales del Norte que paren de dar concesiones de nuevos pozos y que hagan programas que reparen el nivel del acuífero.
A la lentitud por parte de las tres dependencias para poner en marcha el acuerdo judicial se sumó el recurso legal interpuesto por 29 concesionarios del agua subterránea, sobre todo lecheros, para anular la sentencia 543. Las organizaciones se manifestaron y lograron que el 12 de marzo pasado, un tribunal colegiado rechazara el recurso de los concesionarios.
El conflicto escaló, pero también la terquedad ciudadana lagunera: ante la presión de las empresas concesionarias, hizo que la Consejería Jurídica de la Presidencia, en representación expresa, presentó ante la Corte el oficio 100.CJEF.06053, pidiendo delimitar y modificar los alcances de la sentencia, estableciendo que no podía limitarse la actuación de la Conagua en materia de derechos de los concesionarios sobre el agua subterránea, incluidas las prórrogas de concesión. Las organizaciones laguneras denunciaron públicamente este hecho como injerencia del Ejecutivo en el Judicial de poderes, y con toda la argumentación jurídica en la mano, hablaron con el presidente de la SCJN y la ministra ponente, la licenciada Lenia Batres Guaderrama. Así lograron que la Corte declare firme y vigente la sentencia 543, que protege el acuífero principal de la Comarca Lagunera.
El triunfo de la ciudadanía se logró con base en la continua denuncia e información al público, una sólida defensa jurídica llevada a cabo por abogados jóvenes y competentes y una inquebrantable voluntad de lucha. Gracias a eso se logró preservar el derecho humano al agua para más de un millón de habitantes de la comarca, se impidió una violación a la división de poderes, se acotaron las atribuciones de la Conagua y la Semarnat y se ponen límites muy claros a la concentración de concesiones y sobrexplotación de los acuíferos por unas cuantas empresas.
Pero tal vez lo más importante es que la lucha de estas organizaciones laguneras (que, por cierto, aún tienen algunas batallas legales por delante), como todos los movimientos sociales, abre un inédito viable, es decir, muestra que es posible hacer uso de las instancias e instrumentos legales, sobre todo del juicio de amparo, para proteger los bienes comunes y derechos de todas y de todos.
Eso les agradecen todas las comunidades, personas y organizaciones que luchan por el agua y el territorio en nuestro México.

title: Opinion: On Sept. 11, the memorial ceremony at Peace Arch reminds us that some things rise above borders
content:
Opinion: On Sept. 11, the memorial ceremony at Peace Arch reminds us that some things rise above borders
Opinion: Canadians and Americans gather at the annual ceremony to honour those who answered the call, support those who continue to serve, and demonstrate that some values transcend borders
On Sept. 11, 2001, the world changed forever. Like millions of people, we watched in disbelief when we learned that thousands of innocent lives had been taken in acts of unimaginable violence. We watched in disbelief as first responders rushed toward danger while others fled. Many never came home.
Twenty-five years later, those memories remain vivid. But equally enduring is something else: the extraordinary spirit of service, courage and unity that emerged in the days, weeks and years that followed.
That is why Canadians and Americans gather beneath the Peace Arch to remember.
The annual Northwest 9/11 Memorial Ceremony has never simply been about looking back. It is about honouring those who answered the call, supporting those who continue to serve, and demonstrating that some values transcend borders.
This year marks the 25th anniversary of 9/11, and that milestone carries particular significance.
A generation has grown up with no personal memory of Sept. 11. Many of the young police officers, firefighters and paramedics attending our ceremony were children, or not yet born, when the attacks occurred. Yet they understand the responsibility they have inherited: to remember those who came before them and to uphold the ideals of public service, sacrifice and courage.
This year’s ceremony will be especially meaningful as we welcome four first responders who served in New York City on Sept. 11, 2001. Their presence reminds us that history is not confined to books or documentaries. It lives in the experiences of those who answered the call that day and in the commitment they continue to demonstrate decades later.
Their stories are deeply personal, but they also belong to all of us.
Over the years, this ceremony has grown into far more than an annual commemoration. It has become a gathering of communities, agencies and individuals who understand that service knows no borders. Canadian and American first responders work together every day. Border officials cooperate to protect our shared communities. Military personnel train alongside one another. These partnerships endure because challenges do not stop at the border, and neither does the willingness to help.
This year, that message carries added significance. Canada and the United States are experiencing a period of heightened economic and political tension, with trade talks having broken down and disagreements testing a relationship that has long been among the closest in the world. Those differences are real, and their consequences matter to people and communities on both sides of the border.
But moments of disagreement can also remind us of what should never be lost. The relationship between Canadians and Americans has always been about more than governments, trade agreements or the political issue of the day. It has been built over generations by neighbours, families, communities and people who have repeatedly stood together when it mattered most.
When police officers from Vancouver stand beside retired members of the New York Police Department, when firefighters from British Columbia honour colleagues from the FDNY, and when border officers from both nations stand shoulder to shoulder beneath the Peace Arch, they demonstrate something profoundly hopeful: friendship, cooperation and shared purpose endure.
That message is every bit as important today as it was 25 years ago.
Guy Morall is founder of the annual 9/11 Memorial Ride in B.C. Henry Hollander is a retired deputy chief, North Whatcom Washington Fire and Rescue. Cody Stamberger is from the Ferndale Washington Fire and Rescue. Tim Armstrong is a retired chief, New Westminster B.C. Fire Service. Howard Blank is a Vancouver-based entertainment executive and philanthropist.
More than 400 first responders, military and border services personnel, public officials and members of the public are expected to gather beneath the iconic Peace Arch at the Canada-U.S. border, at 11 a.m. on Friday, Sept. 11 for the Northwest 9/11 Memorial Ceremony.

title: Farmer's legacy lives on in wildflower he discovered before tragic death
content:
Farmer killed fighting WA bushfire honoured by planting of native flower he discovered
In short:
A West Australian farmer killed fighting a bushfire last year has been honoured for his discovery of a potentially new plant.
Mark Mudie discovered an unusual red-flowering hakea during seeding season about two years ago.
What's next?
Work is underway to determine the taxonomy of the plant, which locals hope will be named in Mr Mudie's honour.
A West Australian farmer who died fighting a devastating bushfire has been posthumously honoured with a native flowering plant he discovered two years before his death.
Ravensthorpe Shire deputy president and farmer Mark Mudie died in December last year while battling a blaze at West River that destroyed more than 5,000 hectares of farmland.
The plant, believed to be a hybrid species of hakea, is being planted today in Ravensthorpe, about 500 kilometres south of Perth, to remember and celebrate his life.
Mr Mudie's son Nathan said his father often wandered the bushland around the community, drawn to region's native flora.
"I remember the day dad found it, driving in the truck during seeding, and he called me up and said, 'I found a plant that I've never seen before'," he said.
"I didn't think much of it, but he was very excited about it and got some samples taken away.
"It was a bit of a rare thing to have out in our area, but Dad was very proud to find it."
Sitting adjacent to the Fitzgerald River National Park, the region's biodiversity attracts visitors from around Australia every year for its natural wildflower displays.
Nathan Mudie said the flowers were one of his father's passions, which he often shared with the family.
"He quite enjoyed the wildflower season in Ravensthorpe and used to always pick a bunch of wildflowers and bring it back home for Mum," he said.
"He was right into his wildflowers."
Plant returned to family
Ravensthorpe Wildflower Show and Herbarium coordinator Sue Leighton said Mark Mudie would often send her photos of flowers he saw to learn their names.
When he discovered the unusual hakea, she was one of the first people he called.
"He sent me a photo and said, 'Sue, I don't know what this is, I've never seen it before?'"Ms Leighton said.
"He sent a picture of this hakea that was about two-and-a-half metres high and about two-and-a-half wide and full of big blooms on it."
Ms Leighton said three of the herbarium staff went out to examine the plant and take cuttings for further examination.
"One taxonomist has said that it's just a subspecies of another one, but there's never been any seed on it at all, so we do believe it is a hybrid," she said.
"I've got those two plants that Kings Park has given us, and we're doing a ceremony planting of the one that will go in the herbarium garden at Ravensthorpe, and the other one will go to his wife, Elaine."
Kings Park senior plant breeder Digby Growns said it was an impressive specimen, and worthy of horticultural attention.
"It was covered in these globular flowers, similar to Hakea laurina, and we presumed it was a hybrid with that species and another unknown species," he said.
Mr Growns took several cuttings in a bid to propagate the plant.
"First to bring it into cultivation and protect it, given there was only a single plant," he said.
"And then to have a look at it, to see if there was any opportunity for making it commercially available."
Mudie Surprise
Ms Leighton said it could take years for the taxonomy of the plant to be finalised, but the herbarium was hoping, in time, the hakea could be named in honour of Mark Mudie.
"If it was something that could be grown as a hybrid, it could be given a name," she said.
"It won't have a species name on it, it will just have a trade name ... It could be called Mudie Surprise."
Nathan Mudie said with just the planting of the hakea, the remembrance and recognition of his father's discovery had touched the family.
"It's a very nice tribute that the community and everyone's decided to do, and for us as a family, it was very, very touching for us, and it's very nice to be here," he said.
"I think he'll be very proud of that and of how the community rallied together, and it shows the person that he was."

title: Vijftien bomen geven hun herinneringen prijs in Midden-West-Vlaanderen: "Verhalen van liefde en hoop"
content:
Het is Open Monumentendag, en in de regio Midwest lanceren ze daarom een bijzonder erfgoedproject: 'Markante bomen'. Vanaf vandaag kan je in de 15 gemeenten van Midden-West-Vlaanderen 15 bomen met een bijzonder verhaal ontdekken. Van oorlogsverhalen tot kleine menselijke gebeurtenissen: elke boom onthult een herinnering.
Vijftien bomen geven hun herinneringen prijs in Midden-West-Vlaanderen: "Verhalen van liefde en hoop"
"Bomen maken al eeuwenlang deel uit van ons landschap, maar dragen ook bijzondere verhalen met zich mee", zegt de Roeselaarse schepen Mieke Vanbrussel (CD&V). "Gebouwen verdwijnen, wegen worden verlegd en plaatsen krijgen een nieuwe invulling. Maar sommige bomen overleven die veranderingen. Ze blijven als herkenningspunt achter op plekken die er vandaag heel anders uitzien."
Oorlogsherinneringen
Vijf thema's komen aan bod: religie en , verdwenen plekken, symboliek, oorlog en herinnering, en traditie en volkscultuur. Onder de geselecteerde bomen zitten onder meer de herinneringseik in Ledegem en een in Meulebeke, die allebei bij het thema oorlog en herinnering horen. Ook bomen in het Keuneleutebos in Westrozebeke en aan het Bomkapelleke in Koolskamp maken deel uit van het project. "We hebben gezocht naar een goede spreiding van de bomen", zegt Vanbrussel.
"Cultuur en erfgoed houden niet op aan een gemeentegrens", zegt Kurt Windels, clustervoorzitter cultuur en erfgoed van regio Midwest. "We willen onze inwoners het bijzondere erfgoed in hun regio zelf laten ontdekken."
Geen droge geschiedenis
Toneelgezelschap De Verenigde Vrienden uit Rumbeke en comedian Hans Cools werkten mee aan het project. Bij de bomen staan infoborden met meer informatie over de plek, en via een digitale bomenkaart kunnen bezoekers nog meer bijzondere bomen in de regio ontdekken.
Audiomaker Wim Chielens maakte de podcasts bij het project. "Achter elke boom schuilt een menselijk verhaal", zegt hij. "Dat heeft me enorm getroffen. Geen droge geschiedenis, maar verhalen over liefde, verlies, hoop en verbondenheid. Die verhalen vertel ik op verschillende manieren: via interviews, maar ook via een lied of een stukje toneel."
